This deck teaches the vocabulary the rest of the course depends on. When Chapter 5 says “optimize risk responses” or Chapter 8 says “engage stakeholders”, it assumes you already know what those phrases mean here, so time spent on this deck pays off in every later chapter. A software project manager rarely writes the code. The job is making sure many people’s work adds up to something the organization actually wanted, on time and within budget. That is why this is a management course inside a software engineering degree. Study this deck in two passes: first get the big picture (what is a project, who does what), then return to memorize the lists (12 principles, 8 domains). Introduction SE423: Software Project Management 1
Outline

The opening explains why anyone should care: organizations lose real money when projects are run badly. History shows the field did not appear from nowhere. Each development, such as separating technical and managerial leadership or creating PMOs, solved a problem people actually had. This part moves from the discipline to the person: what a PM is accountable for and which abilities separate good ones from bad ones. PMBOK is the reference standard the course follows, and it is where most exam questions from this deck come from. Expect to spend most of your revision time here. Outline as a story: why it matters → how it developed → who does it → what rules they follow. Outline • Introduction • Project Management History • Project Managers • PMBOK 2
Introduction (section)
Section divider. The next three slides answer one question: what is project management, and why are organizations paying attention to it? Introduction 3
What is Project Management?

Each of the four nouns does a different job. Knowledge is what you understand (how estimation works). Skills are what you can do well (running a tense meeting). Tools are the things you use (a Gantt chart, Jira). Techniques are the methods you follow (critical path analysis). The definition lists all four because owning a tool without the skill to use it isn’t project management. A PM guides the work rather than performs it. Think of a film director: the director doesn’t act or operate the camera, but without one, the actors and crew would not produce a coherent film. On a software project the developers write the code, while the PM keeps that work pointed at the outcome the organization wanted. The approach is a choice, not a rule. Predictive means plan it all up front, which suits fixed requirements such as a regulated banking system. Adaptive means build in short cycles and adjust, which suits a new app whose users’ needs are unclear. Hybrid mixes them. The slide’s point is that good project management does not depend on one method. KiTTenS : Knowledge, Tools, Techniques, Skills. Project management guides the work. If an option says the PM “does” or “writes” the work, be suspicious. Project management is the application of ______ to project activities to meet project requirements. A PM spends the week removing blockers, aligning the team on priorities and checking that the work still leads to what the client needs. She writes no code. Which statement describes this? A team must follow fixed regulations and has stable requirements, so it plans the entire project up front. Which approach is this? What is Project Management? • Project management • The application of knowledge, skills, tools, and techniques to project activities to meet project requirements. • Project management refers to guiding the project work to deliver the intended outcomes. Project teams can achieve the outcomes using a broad range of approaches (e.g., predictive, hybrid, and adaptive). 4
Introduction

The interest is growing because more of what organizations do now takes the form of projects: new systems, new products, digital transformation. Work that used to be routine operations increasingly has a start, an end and a specific result. Read these numbers as “demand is much larger than supply”. 87.7 million is the total number of people needed in PM-oriented roles by 2027, while 2.3 million is how many new people must enter each year. Many of those people won’t hold the title “project manager”, since team leads and engineers also run project work. For you, this means PM skills are useful even if you stay technical. Don’t memorize the exact figures first. Remember the message, a global talent gap , then attach the numbers: 87.7M total by 2027 and 2.3M new per year to 2030. According to PMI, how many people will employers need in project management–oriented roles by 2027? PMI’s Talent Gap report says 2.3 million new project management employees will be needed each year to meet global demand by 2030. Introduction • Many people and organizations today have a new or renewed interest in project management • The Project Management Institute reported that by 2027, employers will need 87.7 million individuals working in project management–oriented roles. • According to PMI’s 2021 Talent Gap report, 2.3 million new project management employees will be needed each year to meet global talent demands by 2030. 5
Introduction

Employers’ top three skills for graduates are not technical: teamwork, problem-solving and verbal communication. Project work builds all three because it forces you to agree on a plan, handle things going wrong and explain decisions to others. The waste figure is the business case for this course. Out of every $1 billion spent on projects, $97 million (about 10%) produces nothing useful, usually because of unclear requirements, poor planning or weak control. A company spending $50 million would lose about $5 million, which easily justifies paying for good project management. The Saudi numbers make this local. A national strategy expected to grow the AI market to $135.2 billion by 2030, plus the world’s highest government technology spending ($24.7 billion in 2025, 21.7% of national spending), means many large projects will need people to run them, here in Saudi Arabia. $97M per $1B ≈ 10% wasted. Remember the percentage, and you can always rebuild the number. Which set lists the top skills employers look for in new graduates, according to the slide? A company spends $2 billion on projects. Based on PMI’s Pulse of the Profession figure, about how much would it waste? What does the slide say about Saudi Arabia’s government technology spending in 2025? Section divider. These slides show where the profession came from and what it now expects of its members. Project Management History 7
The Project Management Profession

The profession is growing because the world’s work increasingly comes in the form of projects, and organizations have seen what poorly managed ones cost them. The slide names three threads to follow. History explains why the job looks as it does. Professional societies like PMI set shared standards and certifications, which is what makes it a profession rather than just a job title. Software made serious planning practical: a schedule with hundreds of tasks is unmanageable on paper but easy to update in a scheduling tool. SHiP : Software, History, Professional societies. These are the three things the slide says you should understand. Which three things does the slide say help you understand the project management profession? According to the slide, the project management profession is growing slowly as companies move away from formal management. The Project Management Profession • The profession of project management is growing at a very rapid pace • It is helpful to understand the history of the field, the role of professional societies like the Project Management Institute, and the growth in project management software 8
History of Project Management

The pyramids count as projects in the modern sense because they were unique, had a clear goal and eventually ended. “Some people argue” matters here: without written methods, nobody can show that they used project management as we know it. The Manhattan Project , the US effort to build the atomic bomb during the Second World War, is the usual starting point for modern project management. It involved huge scale, a hard deadline and work spread across many sites, so informal coordination could not work. Its key lesson is the split between a project manager and a technical manager . Knowing the physics and running a three-year, $2 billion program are different jobs. Software teams still do this: an engineering lead makes the technical decisions, while the PM handles schedule, people and budget. Picture two chairs at the head of the table : one for managing the project, one for leading the technology. That image is the Manhattan Project’s lesson. Which project is usually considered the first to use “modern” project management? What was distinctive about how the Manhattan Project was organized? A $2 billion (1946 dollars), three-year effort: what do these numbers tell you about why modern project management emerged? History of Project Management • Some people argue that building the Egyptian pyramids was a project, as was building the Great Wall of China. • Most people consider the Manhattan Project (led by Pr. Oppenheimer) to be the first project to use “modern” project management. • This three-year, $2 billion (in 1946 dollars) project had a separate project manager and a technical manager. 9
History of Project Management

Companies in the 1990s suddenly had dozens of projects running at once, sharing the same people and budgets. Each PM could run their own project well and the organization could still end up with chaos, such as three projects needing the same database expert in the same week. PMOs were created to solve that. Focus on the word coordinating . A PMO doesn’t usually run each project. It gives projects a common way of working (templates, standards, training), sees across all of them, and tells senior management how they are doing. Think of a university registrar: it doesn’t teach courses, but it makes all of them work together. PMO = air traffic control. Pilots still fly the planes (PMs run projects), while the tower keeps everyone from colliding. What is a Project Management Office (PMO) and its role in organizations? Why did many companies begin creating PMOs in the 1990s? A PMO is best described as: History of Project Management • In the 1990s, many companies began creating PMOs to help them handle the increasing number and complexity of projects • A Project Management Office (PMO) is an organizational unit responsible for coordinating the project management function throughout an organization 10
Global Issues

Organizations struggle to find capable project and program managers, which matches the talent gap on slide 5. So they treat growing them as a strategic concern, through training, mentoring and career paths. “Core competency” means this is now a basic expectation. A software engineer may be asked to lead a small feature with its own plan and deadline, without ever being called a PM. Markets change quickly and requirements shift, and a plan made a year ago may no longer fit. So organizations want approaches that deliver in small pieces and adjust based on feedback. Chapter 4 covers this. Finishing on time and on budget used to be enough to call a project successful. Now organizations ask whether the promised benefit arrived. A mobile app delivered perfectly but used by nobody has no realized benefit. CoBAlT : Core competencies, Benefits, Agile, Talent. These are the four global dynamics on the slide. Delivered ≠ done. Benefits realization asks: “Did it actually help?” A project finished on time and on budget, yet six months later almost nobody uses the system. Which global issue from the slide does this highlight? A company adds “can plan and track a small project” to every engineer’s job requirements. Which dynamic is this? Struggling to find enough experienced program managers, a company launches a mentoring path for them. Which dynamic does this respond to? The slide says organizations want to use less agile approaches to project management. Global Issues • Several global dynamics are forcing organizations to rethink their practices: • Talent development for project and program managers is a top concern • Basic project management techniques are core competencies • Organizations want to use more agile approaches to project management • Benefits realization of projects is a key metric 11
Project Management Certification

A profession needs a body that defines good practice. PMI plays that role for project management, and it publishes the PMBOK standard this course is built on. So when these slides say “the standard says”, they mean PMI. A PMP is the professional-level certification. It signals to employers that someone has real experience and has passed a demanding exam, like a professional engineering license does in other fields. That is why demand for it keeps rising. The CAPM is the entry-level option, intended for students and people early in their careers who don’t yet have the project experience the PMP requires. This is the one relevant to you now. CAPM starts with C , think “Come in”: the entry door. PMP = the “Professional” who has already got experience. Which organization is described as the leader in advancing the project management profession? A third-year student with no project experience wants a PMI certification. Which one does the slide point to? The number of people earning PMP certification is decreasing quickly. Project Management Certification • The Project Management Institute (PMI: http://www.pmi.org/) is the leading organization in advancing the project management profession • PMI provides certification as a Project Management Professional (PMP®) • The number of people earning PMP® certification is increasing quickly • Students can join PMI at a reduced fee and earn the Certified Associate in Project Management (CAPM) certification(see PMI for details) 12
Ethics in Project Management

The key word is personal values : ethics deals with what you believe is right and wrong, not only with what is legal. An action can be legal and still be unethical, like quietly reporting “on track” to a client when you know the project is not. A dilemma is a situation where the choices are all uncomfortable. A sponsor pressures you to hide a delay until after the funding decision. A friend’s company bids for your project’s contract. PMs face these often because they sit between clients, staff and executives who want different things. Agreeing to the code is a requirement for earning the PMP, and the exam tests professional responsibility. So ethics isn’t a side topic: the profession treats it as part of being qualified. The four values come on slide 55. Ethics quick test: “Would I be comfortable if the client and my manager both saw exactly what I just did?” Ethics is loosely defined as: The sponsor asks the PM to report the project as “green” until the funding decision, although it is two months late. What is this? What must applicants agree to in order to earn the PMP certification? The PMP exam includes questions related to professional responsibility, including ethics. Ethics in Project Management • Ethics, loosely defined, is a set of principles that guide our decision making based on personal values of what is “right” and “wrong” • Project managers often face ethical dilemmas • In order to earn PMP® certification, applicants must agree to PMI’s Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct • Several questions on the PMP® exam are related to professional responsibility, including ethics 13
Project Managers (section)
Section divider. The next slides move from the field to the person: what a project manager answers for and what makes one good. Project Managers 14
Project Managers

The PM answers for anything that threatens the project, even when someone else caused it. Schedule, budget and quality pull against each other: finishing sooner usually costs more money or lowers quality, and much of the job is deciding which one to protect when you can’t keep all three. “Depending on the project scale” means a small project may blur these, while a large one may assign specialists to each. Delivery means the finished product reaches the customer in a usable state: deployed, documented and accepted, not merely “code complete”. Locking in resources means securing people and equipment early. Your best database engineer can be pulled onto another project unless you’ve secured them, and that can damage your schedule more than a technical bug would. New PMs expect to spend their days on strategy, and instead they ask “is that done yet?” all day. Each task’s status lives in someone’s head, and the PM can’t make decisions without it. That is why status meetings, dashboards and tracking tools exist. SQuaBbLeD : Schedule, Quality, Budget, Locking in resources, Delivery. Triangle trick: picture time, cost and quality at three corners. Pull one corner, and the others move. Define the term ‘project constraints’ and explain how they influence project planning and execution. Provide at least three examples of common constraints and discuss their interrelationship. A client wants delivery a month earlier with the same features. What should the PM expect? Another project is about to take the only security engineer next month. Which PM responsibility from the slide applies? What does the slide say consumes most of a project manager’s time? The issues a project manager handles stay the same regardless of the project’s scale. Project Managers • Project Managers are mainly responsible for all issues related to the software project; issues may vary depending on the project scale, some of the common issues are: • Schedule • Budget • Quality • Delivery of products • Locking in resources • As a project manager you will notice that most of your time is consumed chasing and collecting the status of project tasks. 15
The Project Manager

Notice that all four responsibilities (planning, scheduling, coordinating, working with people) involve other people or their work. Job titles and descriptions vary across companies, but this core stays the same, whatever the industry. The 97% statistic is about experience . A PM who has seen projects fail recognizes warning signs early, knows who to talk to, and can influence the conditions for success. You can’t get that from a textbook alone, which is why junior PMs benefit from working under senior ones. These three skills address different things. Change : requirements and people will shift, and a PM who is upset by that won’t last. Understanding the organization : knowing who holds power and how decisions get made often matters more than the plan itself. Leading teams : you usually have no authority over the people on your project, so you get results by earning their cooperation. SPaCeWalk : Scheduling, Planning, Coordinating, Working with people. COoL : Change, Organization, Lead. These are the three skills, and a PM needs to stay cool under pressure. Which list matches the responsibilities most PM job descriptions include, according to the slide? What does the 97% statistic on the slide tell you? A PM is talented technically, but keeps getting surprised that a department head can quietly block decisions. Which skill from the slide is missing? Halfway through, the client changes direction, and the PM calmly replans instead of resisting. Which skill is this? The Project Manager The Role of the Project Manager • Job descriptions vary, but most include responsibilities like planning, scheduling, coordinating, and working with people to achieve project goals • Remember that 97% of successful projects were led by experienced project managers, who can often help influence success factors Skills for Project Managers Project managers need a wide variety of skills, They should: o Be comfortable with change o Understand the organizations they work in and with o Be able to lead teams to accomplish project goals 16
Competencies for Project Managers

People skills, leadership, listening and verbal communication are at the top because a PM’s only real tool is other people’s work. Listening earns its own line since a PM who talks more than they listen misses the early warnings from the team. Most PMs have no formal authority over their team, so people cooperate only if they believe the PM. Trust is what makes them do what you ask, and integrity and consistency are how you earn it. A PM who treats people differently from one week to the next quickly loses their trust. These are for situations with competing interests. Conflict resolution handles disagreements inside the team. Negotiating gets resources from other managers. Influencing the organization gets decisions made above your level. Balancing priorities and critical thinking are how you decide what matters when everything feels urgent. Only one of the 14 is technical, and it is last on the list. A PM needs enough technical understanding to spot nonsense and earn the team’s respect, not to be the best engineer. This surprises many engineers who become PMs. Sort the 14 into three buckets rather than memorizing a list: People (skills, listening, verbal, teams, mentoring), Character (integrity, trust, leadership), Decisions and politics (conflict, critical thinking, priorities, negotiating, influencing). Then add Process and technical as the odd one out. Scenario trick: look at what is going wrong . People arguing → conflict resolution. Need budget from another manager → negotiating. Decision stuck above you → influencing. Two senior developers keep arguing about the architecture in every meeting, and the rest of the team has stopped contributing. Which project manager competencies does this call for, and what should the PM do? A PM needs a database expert who reports to another manager, and must agree on how many days she can have him. Which competency does this use? A PM keeps the same standards for everyone and always does what she says she will. Over time, the team tells her about problems early. Which competencies explain this? A senior engineer spends an hour a week helping a new graduate learn how to estimate tasks. Which competency is this? A key decision has been stuck with senior management for weeks. The PM builds support among other department heads to move it forward. Which competency is this? Three urgent requests arrive at the same time, and the PM decides which one matters most for the project goals. Which competency is this? Most of the 14 competencies for project managers are technical. Competencies for Project Managers 1. People skills 8. Conflict resolution, conflict 2. Leadership management 3. Listening 9. Critical thinking, problem solving 4. Integrity, ethical behavior, consistent 10.Understands, balances priorities 5. Strong at building trust 11.Negotiating 6. Verbal communication 12.Influencing the Organization 7. Strong at building teams 13.Mentoring 14.Process and technical expertise 17
Advantages of Using Formal Project

Without formal PM, money, equipment and people get spent wherever someone shouts loudest. With it, there is a plan and a budget to compare against, so overspending shows up early instead of at the end. Productivity and profit improve because people spend less time on the wrong work and on redoing it. Most delays and defects come from unclear requirements and late changes. Formal PM reduces both by agreeing on the work early and checking it regularly, which is why time and quality can improve together. Customers notice too, since they are told what is coming rather than being surprised. When teams plan together, they stop stepping on each other’s work, which is “better internal coordination”. Strategic goals benefit because projects are how a strategy gets carried out: if projects deliver, the strategy happens. People notice this benefit last, but it’s very real. Poor planning leads to last-minute crunches, so staff work late and quit. Planned work spreads the effort, giving higher morale and less stress , which then feeds back into quality. Group the ten into four: Money (control of resources, lower costs, profit), Delivery (time, quality, customers), Coordination/Strategy (internal coordination, strategic goals), People (morale, not overworked). Remember “ CaMPeD ”: Coordination, Money, People, Delivery. How does project management contribute to organizations in achieving their strategic objectives? Please elaborate. Which is NOT listed on the slide as an advantage of using formal project management? After adopting formal PM, a team stops doing weekend crunches before each release. Which listed advantage does this show? The finance team can now see what each project spends and which staff it uses. Which listed advantage is this? Two departments stop duplicating work because their project plans are shared. Which listed advantage is this? Advantages of Using Formal Project Management • Better control of financial, physical, and human resources • Improved customer relations • Shorter development times • Lower costs and improved productivity • Higher quality and increased reliability • Higher profit margins • Better internal coordination • Positive impact on meeting strategic goals • Higher worker morale (less stress) • Less overworked personnel 18
Project Management Body of Knowledge (section)

Section divider. PMBOK (the Project Management Body of Knowledge) is PMI’s reference for the profession. These slides use its 7th edition, which is organized around principles and performance domains rather than step-by-step processes. Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK) 19
The Purpose of The Standard for Project

“Basis for understanding” means the standard gives everyone a shared language. When a contractor from another country says “stakeholder” or “deliverable”, you can both mean the same thing. It explains what project management is for rather than telling you exact steps to follow. The standard applies to a bank, a hospital, a five-person startup or a national program, and to agile or waterfall teams. If it depended on one industry or method, it couldn’t work as a shared language. Exam options that limit it to large, IT or waterfall projects are false. The slide says the standard looks beyond the project itself: governance (who makes decisions), functions (who does what), the environment (what surrounds the project) and how it relates to product management (what happens to the product after the project ends). A project’s success depends on all of these, not only on its internal plan. SLID : Size, Location, Industry, Delivery approach. The standard applies regardless of these, so if an answer limits it by any of them, it’s wrong. The four things it describes: FiG PiE — Functions, Governance, Product, Environment. The Standard for Project Management applies only to large projects that use a predictive delivery approach. What does the Standard for Project Management provide? Besides the project itself, what does the standard describe? The Purpose of The Standard for Project Management • The Standard for Project Management provides a basis for understanding project management and how it enables intended outcomes. • This standard applies regardless of industry, location, size, or delivery approach, for example, predictive, hybrid, or adaptive. It describes the system within which projects operate, including governance, possible functions, the project environment, and considerations for the relationship between project management and product management. 20
Project Management

Principles describe how to behave , not what steps to take. Stewardship means treating the money, people and trust you’ve been given as if they were not yours to waste: reporting honestly, spending carefully, thinking about consequences beyond this project. Team and Stakeholders are both about people, but in different directions: inward and outward. A team with trust raises problems early. Stakeholders involved from the start tell you what they need before you’ve built the wrong thing. These three set direction. Value asks, “Is this worth doing?” rather than “Did we finish the list?” Systems thinking reminds you that a change here can break something elsewhere. Leadership means setting the example with integrity, and the slide’s “adaptability and empathy” means adjusting to what people need. These three shape how the work gets done. Tailoring : no method fits every project, so adapt it. Quality : building it in from the start is cheaper than fixing it at the end. Complexity : some things can’t be fully predicted, so expect that and stay alert. These three deal with an unpredictable future. Risk : find what might go wrong (or right) and act before it happens. Adaptability and resiliency : bend when conditions change, and recover after a hit. Change : help people move to the new way of working, since a delivered system nobody adopts fails. Remember them in four groups of three: People-with-care (Stewardship, Team, Stakeholders), Direction (Value, Systems, Leadership), How we work (Tailoring, Quality, Complexity), The future (Risk, Adaptability, Change). Sentence trick for the order: S ome T eams S ee V alue, S ystems, L eaders; T hey Q uickly C onquer R isk A nd C hange. 12 principles = how to behave. 8 domains = what to focus on. The bigger number is behaviour. Which of the following best reflects the principle of “Stewardship” in project management? A project team has limited resources and must choose the feature that will provide the greatest benefit to users. Which principle applies? Developers feel safe admitting mistakes in meetings, and they openly raise concerns. Which principle is being applied? A PM brings end users into requirements sessions from the very first week. Which principle is this? A small startup drops most of the heavy documentation its parent company requires, keeping only what is needed for a two-person project. Which principle is this? The team adds automated tests and code reviews from the first sprint instead of testing at the end. Which principle is this? Before starting, the team lists what could go wrong and prepares a backup supplier. Which principle is this? When a vendor suddenly goes out of business, the team quickly switches to another and keeps going. Which principle is this? The PM helps staff learn the new system and move away from the old process over several months. Which principle is this? A leader adjusts how she treats team members, patient with one who is struggling and direct with another who prefers it. Which principle is this? Nobody can predict how three new technologies and two departments will interact, so the team reviews the situation often and stays alert. Which principle is this? The PMBOK v7 principles are a sequence of steps to be carried out in order. Project Management 12 Principles (PMBOK v7) 1. Stewardship : Act responsibly and ethically. 2. Team: Foster trust, respect, and open communication to empower team members. 3. Stakeholders: involve stakeholders 4. Value: Prioritize outcomes that deliver value 5. Systems Thinking: understand how project elements interact within broader organizational and external contexts. 6. Leadership: Lead with integrity, adaptability, and empathy 7. Tailoring: Adapt methods, tools, and approaches 8. Quality: Ensure quality is embedded from the start 9. Complexity: Embrace uncertainty and complexity 10. Risk: Identify, assess, and respond to risks 11. Adaptability and Resiliency: Be flexible and ready to pivot 12. Change: Support transformation and continuous improvement 21
Project Management

A domain is something you must keep paying attention to. Think of driving: steering, speed and mirrors aren’t steps you do in order, you handle them all at once throughout the journey. Domains work the same way, and they influence each other. That is why “phases”, “steps” and “in order” are wrong answers. Each one asks its own question. Stakeholders : who cares about this? Team : are the people working well? Development approach and life cycle : how will we build it? Planning : what’s the plan? Project work : how’s the day-to-day? Delivery : are we producing what’s needed? Measurement : how are we doing? Uncertainty : what might surprise us? Chapter 1.2 covers each in depth. Sentence for the eight: S ome T eams D on’t P lan P roperly, D elaying M any U pdates (Stakeholders, Team, Development, Planning, Project work, Delivery, Measurement, Uncertainty). Domains = driving : you do them all at once, not in sequence. Which of the following best explains the nature of project performance domains? Which of these is NOT one of the 8 performance domains? A PM tracks progress against targets and reports trends to the sponsor. Which domain is this? Performance domains are carried out one at a time: when the Planning domain ends, the Project Work domain begins. Key Terms and Concepts (section)

Section divider. The next five slides define the terms the exams test most. Similar-sounding pairs like program and portfolio, or project and product, are used on purpose, so learn what separates them. Key Terms and Concepts 23
Key Terms and Concepts

An outcome is the difference something makes, while an output is the thing itself. A hospital’s new appointment app is an output. Fewer missed appointments is the outcome, and that outcome is why anyone paid for the app. If the app ships but missed appointments stay the same, you have an output with no useful outcome. A portfolio is how leadership looks at everything the organization is investing in, grouped by strategy. The items don’t have to relate to each other, like a new R&D program, a marketing campaign and a data center upgrade. It is also the only grouping here that includes ongoing operations . The question it answers: “Is this the right mix of work for our strategy?” A product is something real you can count. “Quantifiable” means you can point at it and measure it: one mobile app, 500 units. “End item or component” means a login module counts as a product just like the whole app does. Output = the thing. Outcome = the difference it makes. Portfolio = your investment portfolio : stocks, bonds and property that have nothing to do with each other, chosen together for one goal. “Projects, programs, subsidiary portfolios, and operations managed as a group to achieve strategic objectives” defines a: A team ships a new online ordering system, and average customer wait time falls by 30%. Which is the outcome? A company groups an R&D program, a marketing campaign and an infrastructure upgrade together for strategic oversight, though they are unrelated. What is this? Which of these fits the definition of a product? Outcomes can include outputs and artifacts, but they focus more broadly on the benefits and value the project was undertaken to deliver. Key Terms and Concepts • Outcome • An end result or consequence of a process or project. • Outcomes can include outputs and artifacts, but have a broader intent by focusing on the benefits and value that the project was undertaken to deliver. • Portfolio • Projects, programs, subsidiary portfolios, and operations managed as a group to achieve strategic objectives (Examples: A company’s R&D programs, marketing campaigns, or infrastructure upgrades) • Product • An artifact that is produced, is quantifiable, and can be either an end item in itself or a component item. 24
Key Terms and Concepts

A program exists because the pieces are worth more together. A bank might run mobile, branch and call-center upgrades as separate projects, but coordinated together, customers get one consistent experience, which none of the projects could achieve alone. That extra is “benefits not available from managing them individually”. No extra benefit means there’s no reason for a program. A project has two defining features. Temporary means it has a start and an end, not that it is short: a five-year metro construction is still temporary. Unique means the result has not been produced in exactly this way before. Monthly payroll is neither, so it is an operation. “Or a phase of the project work” means phases have their own beginning and end too. A project doesn’t have to belong to anything. A small company might run one website redesign without any program or portfolio around it. An exam option saying projects “must” be part of a program is false. A team spends $50,000 protecting against a risk that could cost at most $2,000. Which response test does this fail? A risk response is agreed, but nobody is named to carry it out. Which test does this fail? A team’s plan to “hire ten experts next week” for a small project with no budget fails which test? A team has a response plan that the client strongly objects to. Which test does this fail? Hiring a full security team to guard against a minor typo in a help page fails which test? A hospital accepts far less risk than a startup does. What explains this, according to the card? When are risks addressed, according to the card? Optimize Risk Responses 68
Embrace Adaptability and Resiliency

The card says to build these in, so it’s something you prepare ahead of time, not something you hope for. Keeping backups, cross-training staff and working in small increments all make a project able to handle shocks. Adaptability works before and during a change: it’s adjusting to new conditions. A new law requires different data storage, so you change the design. Note the card’s last point: focusing on outcomes rather than outputs helps, since if you care about the goal more than the original feature list, you can change your route to it. Resiliency works after a hit: it’s absorbing the blow and getting back up. A server fails, and the team restores from backup and resumes the same day. Exams test the difference between them: changed conditions call for adapting, and setbacks call for recovering. Adaptability = bend. Resiliency = bounce back. A tree bends in wind (adapts) and regrows after a storm (recovers). A critical server failure takes the test environment down, and the team restores it from backups and resumes work within a day. Which quality does this show? A new regulation means the team must change its data-storage design midway through. It redesigns and continues. Which quality does this show? Which helps a project adapt, according to the card? Resiliency is the ability to absorb impacts and to recover quickly from a setback or failure. Embrace Adaptability and Resiliency 69
Enable Change to Achieve the Envisioned

A system can be delivered perfectly and still fail if nobody uses it. So this principle is about the people affected, not the technology: getting them ready, helping them adopt the new behaviors, and keeping them from sliding back. “Sustainment” is the often-forgotten part: people must stay with the change after the excitement has faded. A structured approach means planning the transition rather than just announcing it: explain why, train people, support them through the switch, and collect feedback. Change comes from inside (a new CEO) or outside (a new law). Either way, not everyone will welcome it, because people often lose familiarity or status in the process. Change fatigue is what happens when people get too much change too quickly. They start ignoring announcements and resisting even useful changes, since they’re worn out rather than because the change is bad. The fix is pacing and motivation: spacing out changes, engaging stakeholders, and showing them why it’s worthwhile. Deliverable ≠ adoption. Ask: “Are people actually working the new way?” Too much change, too quickly → fatigue . Treat it by slowing down and engaging people, not by pushing harder. A ministry rolls out a new ERP, a new HR system and a new workflow in the same month. Staff start ignoring announcements and avoiding the new tools. What is happening? What should the PM do in that situation, according to the card? All stakeholders will embrace a change if it benefits the organization. Change can originate from: What does a structured approach to change help with? Months after go-live, staff are slowly going back to the old spreadsheets. Which word on the card addresses this? Enable Change to Achieve the Envisioned Future State 70

n: Slide 1

Chapter 1 listed the 8 domain names; this deck opens each one in turn. The number badge (1–8) on each domain’s title slide keeps the order: stakeholders, team, development approach and life cycle, planning, project work, delivery, measurement, uncertainty. For each domain learn its purpose, its key terms (many are examined as definitions), and one or two practices you could describe in a scenario answer. Project Performance Domains SE423: Software Project Management 1 d
Project Performance Domains

Think of a domain as one area a PM must keep an eye on, such as “are the stakeholders on board?”. It is a group of related activities rather than a single task, and it is critical because neglecting it damages the outcome, whatever else goes well. Interdependent means a problem in one area spreads. If nobody engages stakeholders, requirements come in wrong, so planning is built on bad information and delivery gets rejected. That’s why the domains are interactive, interrelated and interdependent rather than separate checklists. You never “finish” a domain and move on. On the last day of a project you are still managing stakeholders, measuring and handling uncertainty. So they run concurrently whether you ship weekly or once at the end. They are not phases done in order, which is exactly the trap in the real MCQ. Which of the following best explains the nature of project performance domains? 5111 all The we coverdcostus principles Project Performance Domains The GuidedBehaviors whichare ProjectPerformancdeomain The • A project performance domain is a group of related activities that are critical for the effective delivery of project outcomes. • Project performance domains are interactive, interrelated, and interdependent areas of focus that work in unison to achieve desired God project outcomes. go 095 • Performance domains run concurrently throughout the project, regardless of how value is delivered (frequently, periodically, or at the end of the project). 2
Slide 3

The definition is deliberately broad. A neighbor annoyed by construction noise is a stakeholder, even with no role in the project. So is someone who only believes the project will take their job: perceive itself to be affected counts, because their reaction can still affect you. You can’t give everyone equal attention, so stakeholder analysis works out who matters and how. Numbers such as budget influence, plus judgment such as attitude toward the project, tell you whose interests to take into account first. Teams tend to list only friendly people inside the company. Include people internal and external , and especially those who oppose the project: a regulator or an unhappy department can block you late, when change is most expensive. Edugate scheduling system: identify three main stakeholder groups for this project, describe their roles, and explain how their input will shape the system. 1 Stakeholder Performance Domain https://vt.tiktok.com/ZSHsX4HEr/ • Stakeholder • An individual, group, or organization that may affect, be affected by, or perceive itself to be affected by a decision, activity, or outcome of a project, program, or portfolio. • Stakeholder Analysis told • A method of systematically gathering and analyzing quantitative and qualitative information to determine whose interests should be taken into account throughout the project. • includes stakeholders who are internal and external to the organization, those who are supportive of the project, and those who may not be supportive or are neutral. 3
Stakeholder Performance Domain

Technical PM skills matter, but interpersonal and leadership skills for working with stakeholders may matter more. Most stakeholder problems (resistance, conflicting expectations) are solved by listening, negotiating and building trust, not by a better Gantt chart. The circles diagram groups stakeholders from the core team outward to customers, end users and regulators. A PM has a flawless schedule, but a key department keeps blocking the project. What does the slide suggest is most needed? Stakeholder Performance Domain • Technical project management skills are important, but having the interpersonal and leadership skills to work effectively with stakeholders is maybe more important. 4
Checking Outcomes: Stakeholder Performance Domain

The “checking outcomes” table: the left column is what success looks like for the domain, the right column is the evidence that it happened. You won’t be asked to reproduce it, but it is a good structure for a written answer about the domain. Here: a productive working relationship with stakeholders throughout, checked by observing it and by how stakeholders move along the engagement continuum (unaware → resistant → neutral → supportive → leading). Many scope changes keep arriving from stakeholders. According to the checking-outcomes table, what might this indicate? Checking Outcomes of Stakeholder Performance Domain 5
Team Performance Domain
Which is a desired outcome of the Team performance domain? 2 Team Performance Domain StakeholdersTeams 6
Project Team Management and Leadership

One person often does both jobs in the same meeting. Fixing the agenda and the timeline is management , while getting a discouraged tester back on board is leadership . A project needs both kinds of effort, so neither one replaces the other. Management is about the machinery: are the plan, the tracking and the process working? A team can be happy and still miss the deadline if nobody manages the means . Leadership is about whether people want to and can do the work. A perfect plan fails if the team doesn’t trust it. A quick way to remember it: manage things, lead people. Influencing, motivating and listening to the team are examples of which kind of activity? Project Team Management and Leadership • Project management entails applying knowledge, skills, tools, and techniques for management activities as well as leadership activities. • Management activities focus on the means of meeting project objectives, such as having effective processes, planning, coordinating, measuring, and monitoring work, among others. • Leadership activities focus on people. • Leadership includes influencing, motivating, listening, enabling, and other activities having to do with the project team. • Both are important in delivering the intended outcomes. 7
Project Team Management and Leadership

Anyone can show leadership, for example by helping a stuck teammate or raising a concern, without any title. Management is different, because someone has to be assigned tasks like budgets and reporting, and an organization can give them to one person or share them out. Accountability means that when something goes wrong, there is a known person who has to answer for it. Centralizing it makes things clear: everyone knows who decides and who to escalate to. Being named PM isn’t enough, since you need the right to spend money and pull people from other departments. The project charter is the document that formally gives that right, so nobody can later ask who authorized it. On a project with centralized management, who usually carries accountability? What gives a PM approval to form the team and use resources? Project Team Management and Leadership • Centralized Management and Leadership • While leadership activities should be practiced by all project team members, management activities may be centralized or distributed. • In an environment where management activities are centralized, accountability (being answerable for an outcome), is usually assigned to one individual, such as the project manager or similar role. • In these situations, a project charter (see example in notes below) or other authorizing document can provide approval for the project manager to form a project team to achieve the project outcomes. 8
Project Team Management and Leadership

Here the PM’s tasks are split up, such as one person tracking budget and another handling risks, while the rest of the team builds. It suits teams that are experienced enough not to need one central decision-maker. To self-organize means nobody assigns the work: the team decides among themselves who does what and how. It depends on a mature team, because it collapses if nobody takes responsibility. A facilitator doesn’t give orders. They run the conversation and remove obstacles, as a Scrum master does. The role can shift because it isn’t a rank, so whoever suits the current stage can take it on. A team has no designated PM. One member runs discussions this month, and another may next month. What is this person? In distributed management, leadership is limited to the person who is the facilitator. Project Team Management and Leadership • Distributed Management and Leadership • Sometimes project management activities are shared among a project management team, and project team members are responsible for completing the work. • There are also situations where a project team may self-organize to complete a project. • Rather than having a designated project manager, someone within the project team may serve as facilitator to enable communication, collaboration, and engagement. • This role may shift among project team members. 9
Centralized vs. Decentralized

Decentralized : middle and lower-level managers have decision power, and authority goes to those closer to the stakeholders ; units are self-sufficient. Decentralized gives faster decisions and more creativity but is more expensive (duplicated resources and skills in each unit). Centralized gives more standardization and control and is less expensive , with limited creativity. Learn it as three opposite pairs: speed vs. control, more vs. less expensive, creativity vs. standardization. In decentralized project management, decision-making authority is primarily: Which is a characteristic of decentralized management, according to the table? Project Team Management and Leadership AW 10
Project Team Management and Leadership

These come first because missing them causes problems no process can fix. If people disagree on the goal or on who owns what, you get duplicate work and gaps. Agreeing on team operations (how meetings, decisions and communication work) avoids daily friction. Guidance isn’t only top-down. The PM keeps the whole team heading the same way, while the most experienced person on a task may guide others on it, such as the database expert advising on queries. Growth needs honesty in both directions. Naming what works keeps it going, and naming what doesn’t gives the team something specific to improve. That’s what a retrospective does. Sentence, in slide order: V ery R ich P eople G et G old. Vision and objectives, Roles and responsibilities, Project team operations, Guidance, Growth. During a retrospective, the team notes what went well and sets goals to improve. Which aspect of team development is this? Which is NOT one of the common aspects of team development? Project Team Management and Leadership • Common Aspects of Team Development • Regardless of how the management activities are structured, there are common aspects of project team development that are relevant for most project teams. • These include: • Vision and objectives. • Roles and responsibilities. • Project team operations. • Guidance. • Guidance can be directed to the overall project team to keep everyone headed in the right direction. • Individual project team members may also provide guidance on a particular task or deliverable. • Growth. • Identifying areas where the project team is performing well and pointing out areas where the project team can improve helps the project team to grow. • Working collaboratively, the project team can identify goals for its improvement and take steps to meet those goals. 11
Project Team Culture

Put two teams in one company and they can still feel completely different, in how they argue, how fast they reply and whether they admit mistakes. A team’s own culture always forms, so the only question is whether anyone shapes it. A culture built deliberately starts with agreed rules: “we review every pull request within a day.” If nobody agrees anything, culture forms informally from behavior, for example if the PM ignores late work, the team learns lateness is fine. A team can’t ignore its company’s rules, so a bank’s project team still follows the bank’s compliance culture. Inside those limits, it can still set its own habits. Think of a family living under a country’s laws. A team agrees that every pull request gets reviewed within a day. How has this part of its culture been established? A project team’s culture operates independently of the organization’s culture. Project Team Culture • Each project team develops its own team culture. • The project team’s culture may be established deliberately by developing project team norms, or informally through the behaviors and actions of its project team members. • The project team culture operates within the organization’s culture but reflects the project team’s individual ways of working and interacting. 12
Project Team Culture

People hide bad news if speaking up gets them punished, and hidden problems are the expensive ones. A safe, respectful, nonjudgmental environment makes it normal to say “I’m stuck” early, and the PM is the one who sets that tone. Teams copy what you do, not what you say. A PM who admits a mistake in a meeting teaches more than any poster about honesty. Courage matters most here, since it’s what gets problems raised before they grow. Recognition tells people that their effort was noticed, which is a big part of why they keep giving it. Celebrating success can be small, like thanking someone in a review, and works best when it’s specific. CRyPTICS : Courage, Respect, Positive discourse, Transparency, Integrity, Celebrating success, Support. Your team has just completed a major milestone in the project development process. How would you celebrate this achievement collaboratively with your team members? How would you recognize individual contributions to the team’s success? What actions would you take to ensure that team morale remains high as you move forward in the project? Project Team Culture • The project manager is key in establishing and maintaining a safe, respectful, nonjudgmental environment that allows the project team to communicate openly. • One way to accomplish this is by modeling desired behaviors, such as: • Transparency • Integrity • Respect • Positive discourse • Support • Courage • Celebrating success 13
High-Performing Project Teams

A team can’t work together toward something it pictures differently. Open communication surfaces problems, shared understanding means everyone pictures the same goal, and shared ownership means nobody says “that’s not my part” when something breaks. Trust lets people ask for help without fear, and collaboration is what trust makes possible. Without them, people protect their own piece of the work and the pieces don’t fit together. Projects never go as planned. Adaptability is changing course when a requirement changes, and resilience is recovering after a real setback, such as a failed release. Empowerment means people can decide without waiting for approval, which speeds everything up. Recognition makes them want to keep doing it. Empowerment without recognition burns people out. R oller COASTERS : Recognition, then Collaboration, Open communication, Adaptability, Shared understanding, Trust, Empowerment, Resilience, Shared ownership. What are key characteristics of a good team? High-Performing Project Teams • The list below identifies some of the factors associated with high- performing project teams. • Open communication • Shared understanding • Shared ownership • Trust • Collaboration • Adaptability • Resilience • Empowerment • Recognition 14
Leadership Skills

Vision : establish and maintain a shared picture of what the project is for, so decisions point the same way. Critical thinking : weigh evidence, question assumptions and make sound judgments. Motivation : understand what drives each person (intrinsic or extrinsic) and use it. Interpersonal skills : emotional intelligence, decision-making and conflict resolution (next slide). MICE : Motivation, Interpersonal skills, Critical thinking, Establishing and maintaining vision. A PM weighs the evidence and questions assumptions before a decision. Which leadership skill is this? Leadership Skills Establishing and Maintaining Vision Critical Thinking Motivation Interpersonal Skills 15
Components of Emotional Intelligence

Emotional intelligence (EI) has four components: two about yourself, two about others. Self-awareness : how do you affect the team, and how does the team affect you? “Be empathetic” and “employ active listening” belong to which component of emotional intelligence? Components of Emotional Intelligence 16
Tailoring Leadership Styles

No style is always right, so the PM picks one that suits the situation. Autocratic can work in a crisis when a fast decision is needed, while servant leadership suits a skilled team that only needs obstacles removed. Using one fixed style is the mistake. Each variable changes how much direction people need. A team new to this type of project needs more guidance. A mature team would resent it. Strict governance limits what you can leave to the team, and a distributed team needs more deliberate communication because nobody overhears anything. DEMO : Distributed teams, Experience with the project type, Maturity of team members, Organizational governance. How can a project manager balance technical leadership with adaptive leadership in a software team? Tailoring Leadership Styles • leadership styles (ex: autocratic, democratic, laisser-faire, transactional, servant, etc.) are tailored to meet the needs of the project, the environment, and the stakeholders. • Some of the variables that influence tailoring of leadership styles include: • Experience with the type of project • Maturity of the project team members • Organizational governance structures • Distributed project teams 17
Checking Outcomes: Team Performance Domain

The “checking outcomes” table: the left column is what success looks like for the domain, the right column is the evidence that it happened. You won’t be asked to reproduce it, but it is a good structure for a written answer about the domain. Team: shared ownership (members are engaged and take initiative), a high-performing team (trust, collaboration, adapting to change) and leadership shown by all (evidenced by members’ interpersonal skills and initiative). Which evidence best shows “shared ownership” on a team? Checking Outcomes—Team Performance Domain 18
Development Approach and Life Cycle Performance Domain

This domain answers three questions: how do we build it ( development approach ), how often do we deliver ( cadence ), and what stages do we go through ( life-cycle phases )? The answers have to fit together. The approach has to match what you’re building: you can’t construct a bridge in two-week releases. The phases then need to fit the rhythm you promised, so that value reaches people when expected. That’s what consistent with the deliverables means. Which three things does this domain cover? 3 Development Approach and Life Cycle Performance Domain 19
Development Approach and Life Cycle

The test is in two words: unique (specific to this work) and verifiable (someone can check it exists and is correct). “A signed test report” is a deliverable. “Better teamwork” isn’t, since you can’t verify it. This is the “how do we build it?” choice. Predictive plans everything first, while adaptive learns as it goes. Iterative and incremental are ways of working within those. Chapter 4 compares them in detail. Cadence is a rhythm, like a heartbeat. When everyone knows a demo happens every second Thursday, they plan around it without needing extra coordination. A phase is a chunk of work that ends with something to show, such as “design” ending in approved designs. The life cycle is all the phases in order, so a phase is a chapter and the life cycle is the book. In project management, what is the primary purpose of establishing a project cadence? Development Approach and Life Cycle Performance Domain • The following definitions are relevant to the Development Approach and Life Cycle Performance Domain: • Deliverable • Any unique and verifiable product, result, or capability to perform a service that is required to be produced to complete a process, phase, or project. • Development Approach. • A method used to create and evolve the product, service, or result during the project life cycle, such as a predictive, iterative, incremental, adaptive, or hybrid method. • Cadence. • A rhythm of activities conducted throughout the project. • Project Phase. • A collection of logically related project activities that culminates in the completion of one or more deliverables. • Project Life Cycle. • The series of phases that a project passes through from its start to its completion. 20
Development, Cadence, and Life Cycle

Everything flows from what you’re making. Software can be released in pieces, but half a bridge is useless. So the type of deliverable limits your options before anyone chooses a method. Once the method is chosen, it affects how often you can ship. A physical product may ship once, while a website can ship weekly. Promises to the customer about cadence have to respect that. This is the last link in the chain: deliverable → approach and cadence → life cycle . If you plan monthly releases, your phases have to repeat monthly. A single long “build” phase wouldn’t fit. “When and how often does the customer receive something?” is all this means. Don’t confuse it with cadence in general, which covers any rhythm of activity, such as weekly meetings. Delivery cadence is specifically about deliveries . Pick by what the customer needs. A single delivery fits a one-off building, multiple fit a system handed over in stages, and periodic fit something like monthly payroll updates. Earlier deliveries mean earlier value and earlier feedback. What decides how a project’s deliverable can be developed? A payroll system ships an update on the first of every month. Which delivery is this? Development, Cadence, and Life Cycle • The type of project deliverable(s) determines how it can be developed. • The type of deliverable(s) and the development approach influence the number and cadence for project deliveries. • The deliverable approach and the desired delivery cadence determine the project life cycle and its phases. • Delivery cadence refers to the timing and frequency of project deliverables. • Projects can have a single delivery, multiple deliveries, or periodic deliveries. 21
Delivery Cadence

Think of apps that update without you noticing. Continuous delivery is only realistic for digital products, because you can’t ship a physical product’s improvements daily. Why small batches? A small change is easy to test and easy to undo if it breaks something. Automation makes the frequent releasing cheap, because no person has to repeat the build and test steps each time. A project mindset asks “did we finish?”, while a product mindset asks “is it still delivering value?”. With continuous delivery, the team can react to what the market wants this month, not what was planned last year. You’ll see this practice again under DevOps in Chapter 4, where development and operations work as one team. #noprojects is the extreme view that you fund ongoing products rather than one-off projects. A team ships small feature increments to customers immediately, using automation. What is this? Continuous delivery is mainly an option for digital products. Delivery Cadence • For digital products, another delivery option is called continuous delivery. • Continuous delivery is the practice of delivering feature increments immediately to customers, often through the use of small batches of work and automation technology. • From the product management perspective, the emphasis is on delivering benefits and value throughout the product life cycle. • This allows the team to respond to market trends and stay focused on value delivery. • This practice is included in several approaches such as DevOps, #noprojects and Continuous Digital, for example. 22
Development Approaches

It’s the answer to “what way of working will we use to produce this?”. It isn’t the tools or the team. Waterfall and agile are examples of a development approach . If an exam or company uses an unfamiliar name, look at how the work is done, not the label. One industry’s “stage-gate” may be another’s “waterfall”. Different industries use different terms, but the idea is the same. The three common ones are predictive, hybrid and adaptive , a spectrum rather than three boxes: the further toward adaptive, the more iterative and incremental the work. HeAP : Hybrid, Adaptive, Predictive. Which statement about development approaches is correct? Development Approaches • A development approach is the means used to create and evolve the product, service, or result during the project life cycle. • There are different development approaches, and different industries may use different terms to refer to development approaches. • Three commonly used approaches are • predictive, • hybrid, and • adaptive. 23
Development Approaches

Predictive bets that you can know what’s needed before you start, such as a building with approved blueprints. It works when requirements won’t move much. It’s also called waterfall because each stage flows into the next. The second reason is about stakes, not certainty. When a mistake is very costly, like a hospital information system, you want formal checks before spending the next large sum. Heavy reviews would slow a small app down, but here they’re protection. Knowing these early is what makes predictive possible, because you can commit to a price and date up front. If they keep changing, those commitments keep breaking, and that’s the sign you chose the wrong approach. It tries to remove uncertainty before building starts, so most planning happens up front . The cost is that late changes are expensive, as you’d be undoing finished work. A government payroll system must implement fixed legal rules that will not change during the project. Which development approach fits, and why? Development Approaches • Predictive approach • A predictive approach is useful when the project and product requirements can be defined, collected, and analyzed at the start of the project. (Waterfall approach) • May also be used when there is a significant investment involved and a high level of risk that may require frequent reviews, change control mechanisms, and replanning between development phases. • The scope, schedule, cost, resource needs, and risks can be well defined in the early phases of the project life cycle, and they are relatively stable. • This development approach allows the project team to reduce the level of uncertainty early in the project and do much of the planning upfront. 24
Development Approaches

Hybrid is about mixing, not compromising. You use the predictive way where things are stable and the adaptive way where they aren’t, in the same project. It’s useful when you’re sure about some parts and not others. A payment system’s rules may be fixed by law, while its user interface needs trying out with real users. Using one approach for both would be wrong for one of them. Pieces that can be built separately can be run differently. Modularized means the parts connect but don’t depend on each other’s way of working, like a fixed back-end integration planned predictively with a user-facing app built in sprints. Edugate scheduling system: given the evolving requirements (student usability, advisor requests, IT integration rules), which development approach (Agile, Waterfall, or Hybrid) would you recommend, and why would it be the best fit for this project? Development Approaches • Hybrid approach • A hybrid development approach is a combination of adaptive and predictive approaches. • This means that some elements from a predictive approach are used and some from an adaptive approach are used. • This development approach is useful when there is uncertainty or risk around the requirements. • Hybrid is also useful when deliverables can be modularized, or when there are deliverables that can be developed by different project teams. 25
Iterative vs. Incremental

Iterative (top row): try different ideas to clarify scope, approach and requirements, refining the same thing after each round of feedback (sketch → mock-up → prototype → app). The customer needs a way to capture ideas that might change. Incremental (bottom row): progressively add new features and functions, each a working piece (foundation → frame → walls → finished house), with feedback after each increment. Adaptive approaches use both. Iterative refines; incremental adds. Adding one new working feature to the product in each cycle is best described as: Development Approaches • Hybrid approach 26
Development Approaches

Adaptive assumes that you can’t know everything up front, so it doesn’t pretend to. It suits new products, where users themselves don’t yet know what they want until they try something. Not knowing the details doesn’t mean having no direction. The clear vision is the fixed point, like “students can register online in under a minute”. The features that achieve it can change as you learn from user feedback. Adaptive work repeats ( iterative ) and grows ( incremental ). The further toward the adaptive end, the shorter each cycle gets, since shorter cycles mean faster correction when you’re wrong. In which type of project would an iterative development approach be most beneficial? Development Approaches • Adaptive approach • Adaptive approaches are useful when requirements are subject to a high level of uncertainty and volatility and are likely to change throughout the project. • A clear vision is established at the start of the project, and the initial known requirements are refined, detailed, changed, or replaced in accordance with user feedback, the environment, or unexpected events. • Adaptive approaches use iterative and incremental approaches. However, on the far side of the adaptive methods, the iterations tend to get shorter and the product is more likely to evolve based on stakeholder feedback. 27
Development Approaches

A framework is a set of steps, while agility is an attitude of responding to change. A team can follow every Scrum ritual and still not be agile. The 1–2 week iterations ending in a demo force real progress to be shown often. People commit more to plans they helped make, and they know the real effort better than anyone else. That’s why the team plans each iteration in agile, rather than receiving a plan from above. Because the backlog is prioritized , the most valuable work comes first and whatever doesn’t fit is the least important. If time runs out, you lose the least. The team sets the amount it takes on, which makes its promise realistic. Who determines the scope for an agile iteration? Agility is simply another name for the Scrum framework. Development Approaches • Adaptive approach • While agility is a wide mindset that is broader than a development framework, agile approaches can be considered adaptive. Some agile approaches entail iterations that are 1 to 2 weeks in duration with a demonstration of the accomplishments at the end of each iteration. • The project team is very engaged with the planning for each iteration. • The project team will determine the scope they can achieve based on a prioritized backlog, estimate the work involved, and work collaboratively throughout the iteration to develop the scope. 28
Considerations for Selecting Approaches

The common thread is how much you can know in advance and how cheaply you can change. New ideas, unclear requirements and easy changes all favor learning as you go, like a mobile app. Rule of thumb: high innovation , uncertain requirements , unstable scope , easy change and frequent delivery options push toward adaptive. Strict safety requirements and regulations push toward predictive (they need documented, controlled phases). Sentence, in slide order: D on’t R ush S cope: E very D elivery R isks S afety R ules. Degree of innovation, Requirements certainty, Scope stability, Ease of change, Delivery options, Risk, Safety requirements, Regulations. A medical device must meet strict safety regulations and its requirements are stable. Which way do these product variables push the development approach? Considerations for Selecting Approaches • There are many variables associated with the nature of the product or service that influence the development approach. • Degree of innovation • Requirements certainty • Scope stability • Ease of change • Delivery options • Risk • Safety requirements • Regulations 29
Considerations for Selecting Approaches

The product isn’t the only factor. Even for the same product, the approach can change depending on who’s involved, how soon something is needed and how the money arrives. These are the three project variables to name: stakeholders, schedule constraints and funding availability . Adaptive only works if someone is available to answer questions and give feedback every week. A busy customer who only wants to see the final result is a warning sign. A product owner fills this role by deciding what comes next. Imagine needing to show something at a trade fair in six weeks while the full product takes a year. Delivering something usable early only works when the work is split into cycles, which a single big delivery can’t give you. If next quarter’s money isn’t certain, a big plan risks being stopped halfway, with nothing usable. Working in cycles means there’s always something finished, so you lose less if funding stops… …and there’s a further benefit: an MVP is the smallest version worth releasing. Releasing it tests the idea cheaply, and if the market responds well, that success can help secure more funding. SaFeS : Stakeholders, Funding availability, Schedule constraints. An adaptive project has a busy client who won’t attend reviews. What concern does the slide raise? Funding for next year is uncertain. Which approach does the slide favor, and why? If you know what you need, you can break it down from the top. The WBS is like an outline: a building becomes floors, floors become rooms, rooms become tasks. Instead of scheduling every task for a year, you plan in layers: rough for later, detailed for soon. A timebox flips the usual approach. Normally scope is fixed and time slips. Here time is fixed and scope flexes, so whatever’s finished at the end is delivered. A sprint is the common example. A budget isn’t an arbitrary figure handed down. It starts from what the work is estimated to cost, and it has to be agreed on, because those people will be held to it. Aggregate just means adding up. Every project has things that can go wrong and cost money. A budget with no contingency reserve assumes nothing will, which isn’t realistic, and the first surprise puts you over budget. The SOW matters most: if it’s vague, you get arguments about what was promised. What does a statement of work (SOW) describe? Who develops the RFP and other bid documents? Working with Procurement • Organizations usually have rigorous policies and procedures associated with procurements. The policies identify who has authority to enter into a contract, the limits of authority, and the processes and procedures that should be followed. • Prior to conducting a procurement, the project manager and technically qualified project team members work with contracting professionals to develop the request for proposals (RFP), statement of work (SOW), terms and conditions, and other necessary documents to go out to bid. 62
The Bid Process

Sellers need a fair chance and buyers need comparable offers. So there’s a fixed order: publish what you want, answer questions equally, then choose. Skipping steps invites disputes about the bid process . Use an RFI when you don’t yet know what’s possible. You’re researching rather than buying, so it commits you to nothing. RFP (request for proposal): “how would you build it?”, used once the type of solution is chosen, to invite vendors to propose and bid. RFQ (request for quote): “what’s your price?”, used for a known, specified item (500 laptops with exact specs). A company needs 500 laptops with exact specifications and asks several vendors for their best price and delivery time. Which bid document does it issue? The Bid Process • The bid process includes developing and publicizing bid documents, bidder conferences, and selecting a bidder. • Bid documents can include: • Request for information (Example: A company wants to build a new software platform but isn’t sure what technologies or vendors are out there. They issue an RFI to learn about different capabilities and approaches.) • Request for proposal (Example: After reviewing RFIs, the company decides on a specific type of software and issues an RFP to invite vendors to bid on building it.) • Request for quote (Example: A company needs 500 laptops with specific specs. They issue an RFQ to multiple vendors asking for their best price and delivery timeline.) 63
Learning Through the Project

Learning through the project is knowledge management : capturing and sharing what the team learns so it isn’t lost when people leave. It covers both explicit knowledge (documents, lessons-learned registers) and tacit knowledge (shared through mentoring, pairing, communities of practice). The diagram shows explicit knowledge flowing through information management and tacit knowledge through people. A senior developer’s instinct for which module will break is shared through pairing. What kind of knowledge is this? Learning Through the Project • Knowledge Management • Explicit and Tacit Knowledge 64

You won’t be asked to reproduce it, but it is a good structure for a written answer about the domain. Project work: efficient performance (status reports show the work on track), appropriate processes, good communication, efficient physical resources and procurement, and improved capability through learning.
