Delivery Performance Domain
Which is a desired outcome of the Delivery domain? 6 Delivery Performance Domain 66
Delivery Performance Domain

“Done” means different things to different people. A developer may mean “it runs on my machine”, while a customer means “I can use it”. The definition of done removes the argument by listing what has to be true. Quality is measured against what was required, not how impressive something is. A simple tool that does exactly what was asked is high quality, while a beautiful one that misses a requirement isn’t. Cost of quality (COQ) : all costs over the product’s life from prevention (training, standards), appraisal (testing, inspection) and failure (rework, warranty, lost customers). Chapter 7 develops it. Which three kinds of cost make up the cost of quality? Delivery Performance Domain • The following definitions are relevant to the Delivery Performance Domain: • Definition of Done (DoD) • A checklist of all the criteria required to be met so that a deliverable can be considered ready for customer use. • Quality • The degree to which a set of inherent characteristics fulfills requirements. • Cost of Quality (COQ) • All costs incurred over the life of the product by investment in preventing nonconformance to requirements, appraisal (ˢ̎ɓ ̎ɓ ̷̏) of the product or service for conformance to requirements, ɒ ɒ and failure to meet requirements. 67
Delivery of Value

If you ship in pieces, users benefit from the first piece right away, and it can start earning or saving money. With a single delivery at the end, the value only begins once the project is over . The project team may have disbanded long ago while the product is still earning. So you can’t judge a project’s value on its closing day, and benefits may be measured for years after the project ends . A business case answers “why is this worth doing?”, and it’s what you check later to see whether the value arrived. An adaptive project may use a lighter version, because the details are expected to change. Why can a project with frequent releases deliver value during the project? Business value can continue to be captured long after the project has ended. Delivery of Value h • Projects that use a development approach that supports releasing deliverables throughout the project life cycle can start delivering value to the business, customer, or other stakeholders during the project. • Business value often continues to be captured long after the initial project has ended. • A business case document often provides the business justification and a projection of anticipated business value from a project. • The format of this business case varies based on the development approach and life cycle selected. 68
Quality

Delivering every requested feature can still fail. A system with all its functions but which crashes under load isn’t a success, so more than scope has to be considered. Scope is the list of things the customer gets. Ticking every item off the list tells you nothing about how well each one works. Quality says how well : the performance levels that must be met (response time, reliability, accuracy). A quality requirement only helps if the team can see it, so it needs writing down somewhere they use. Putting “loads in under 2 seconds” in the definition of done means it’s checked each time. A website has every feature requested but takes a minute to load. What’s missing? Where might quality requirements be recorded? Quality • Delivery is more than just scope and requirements. • Scope and requirements focus on what needs to be delivered. • Quality focuses on the performance levels that are required to be met. • Quality requirements may be reflected in the completion criteria, definition of done, statement of work, or requirements documentation. 69
Quality

Quality work is often paid for before your project starts. Standards and quality procedures already exist, which means the sponsoring organization absorbs much of this cost. Company-wide rules, such as “all code needs review”, express its quality policy . Your project inherits them, and you normally can’t opt out. Your project benefits from training and audits without paying for them directly. That’s why the true cost of quality may be hidden from the project’s budget. Perfect quality would cost a fortune and take forever, while no quality causes failure. The right level is where further spending is no longer worth it, which is why projects balance quality against cost. A bug found in review costs little, while one found by customers can cost far more. The cost of quality idea is that money spent on prevention usually saves more than it costs. Who usually bears much of the cost of training and process audits? What is the idea behind the cost of quality? Quality • Much of the costs associated with quality are born by the sponsoring organization and are reflected in policies, procedures, and work processes. • For example, organizational policies that govern how work is performed and procedures that prescribe work processes are often part of the organization’s quality policy. • The cost of overhead, training, and process audit are born by the organization, though they are employed by the project. • Inherent in projects is balancing the quality needs of the processes and products with the costs associated with meeting those needs. • The cost of quality methodology is used to find the appropriate balance for investing in quality prevention and appraisal to avoid defect or product failures. 70
Suboptimal Outcomes

Doing everything right doesn’t guarantee success, because projects create something new. So suboptimal outcomes aren’t proof of bad management, and the question is whether you limited the damage. Here failure is expected and paid for, since the organization knows it’s buying a chance of a breakthrough. A drug company accepts many failures to find one medicine, so a fully experimental project needs judging differently. A project can be delivered perfectly and still be too late. If a competitor launched first, the market opportunity may be gone. This is one more reason why speed of delivery has value. You can reduce the chance and the cost of failure, but not remove them. Good project management spots trouble early and limits the damage, which is why exam answers saying it “eliminates” failure are wrong. A company tests many compounds and most fail before one succeeds. How does the slide describe this? Good project management can eliminate all negative outcomes. Suboptimal Outcomes • All projects attempt to deliver outcomes, though some may fail to do so or may produce suboptimal outcomes. • The potential for suboptimal outcomes exists in every project. • In the case of a fully experimental project, the organization is attempting to achieve a breakthrough, such as the creation of a completely new technology, for example. • This requires deliberate investment in an uncertain outcome. • Companies that produce new medicines or compounds may experience several failures before finding a successful formula. • Some projects may fail to deliver outcomes because the market opportunity has passed or competitors were first to market with their offering. • Effective project management can minimize negative outcomes, but such possibilities are part of the uncertainty of attempting to produce a unique deliverable. 71
Checking Outcomes: Delivery

The “checking outcomes” table: the left column is what success looks like for the domain, the right column is the evidence that it happened. You won’t be asked to reproduce it, but it is a good structure for a written answer about the domain. Measurement Performance Domain
Which is a desired outcome of the Measurement domain? 7 Measurement Performance Domain 73
Measurement Performance Domain

“Progress is good” isn’t a metric . It becomes one when you state what you’re measuring and how: “percent of planned work finished”. That lets two people get the same answer. You can’t say you’re behind without something to compare with. The baseline is the agreed plan, and it’s approved so that it can’t quietly be changed to make results look better. A dashboard gives a quick view. Rather than reading a long report, someone can see in a glance what’s off track and then ask about it. The approved version of a measure that actual results are compared against is called a: Measurement Performance Domain • The following definitions are relevant to the Measurement Performance Domain: • Metric • A description of a project or product attribute and how to measure it (ex: work progress %). • Baseline • The approved version of a measure used as a basis for comparison to actual results (cost of a project, duration). • Dashboard • A set of charts and graphs showing progress or performance against important measures of the project. 74
Measurement Performance Domain

Measuring tells you whether reality matches the plan while there’s still time to act. You can’t correct a budget overrun that you only find out about at the end. Numbers keep things honest. Accountability is easier to show with a record of what was promised and delivered, and stakeholders get facts rather than reassurance. A project can be on time and still heading for no benefit. Data also makes hard discussions easier: “we’ll miss this date, so which feature do we drop?” is better than opinions, and it helps focus conversations . It’s far better to learn that a deliverable will fail before handing it over. Testing against customer acceptance criteria along the way avoids a nasty surprise at sign-off. Which is a reason given for using measures? Measurement Performance Domain • Measures are used for multiple reasons, including: • Evaluating performance compared to plan; • Tracking the utilization of resources, work completed, budget expended, etc.; • Demonstrating accountability; • Providing information to stakeholders; • Assessing whether project deliverables are on track to deliver planned benefits; • Focusing conversations about trade-offs, threats, opportunities, and options; and • Ensuring the project deliverables will meet customer acceptance criteria. 75
Measurement Performance Domain

A report nobody acts on is wasted work. The value comes when someone asks “this number looks bad, so what do we do?”. If no decision comes out of it, the measure isn’t helping. Those conversations also expose bad measures. If people keep ignoring a number, it may be the wrong thing to track. So talking about data helps you measure the right things . Slow decline is the hard kind to notice, since each week looks only slightly worse. Tracking over time reveals the trend, so you can act before performance deteriorates badly. Where does the slide say the value of measurement lies? Measurement Performance Domain • The value of measurements is not in the collection and dissemination of the data, but rather in the conversations about how to use the data to take appropriate action. • It helps to ensure the right things are measured and reported to stakeholders. • Effective measures allow for tracking, evaluating, and reporting information that can communicate project status, help improve project performance, and reduce the likelihood of performance deterioration. 76
Establishing Effective Measures

A KPI is one of the few measures that really shows whether things are going well. Leading indicators are the valuable kind because they warn you early, like dark clouds before rain, while you can still act. Why do these predict trouble? Lots of scope change requests suggest that requirements weren’t understood, so delays are likely to follow. An overloaded team will soon start missing dates, which is why team workload is worth watching now. Lagging indicators report what already happened, like a final exam grade. They’re accurate and easy to measure, but it’s too late to change that result. You can only learn from them. Cost variance can only be calculated after the money is spent, and satisfaction only after people use the product. So you need both: leading to steer and lagging to confirm. Leading looks ahead; lagging looks back. Which of these is a leading indicator? Establishing Effective Measures • Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) • Leading indicators (proactive metrics) • predict changes or trends in the project • Ex: • Rate of scope change requests (frequent changes may hint at poor planning) • Team workload balance (overloaded teams may lead to burnout or missed deadlines) • Lagging indicators (reactive or Backward-looking) • measure project deliverables or events • They provide information after the fact • Ex: • Cost variance (budget overrun or underrun) • Number of deliverables completed • Customer satisfaction scores 77
Establishing Effective Measures

Measurement isn’t free, since every hour spent collecting data is an hour not spent building. So ask of each measure “what would we do differently if this changed?”, and if nothing, drop it. Effective metrics are SMART : Specific, Meaningful , Achievable, Relevant, Timely. Note that in this slide the M is “meaningful”, not the usual “measurable”: a classic trap. On this slide, what does the M in SMART stand for? Why should teams only measure what is relevant? Establishing Effective Measures • Effective Metrics • Measuring takes time and effort, which could otherwise be spent on other productive work; therefore, project teams should only measure what is relevant and should ensure that the metrics are useful. • Characteristics of effective metrics (or SMART criteria) include: • Specific • Meaningful • Achievable • Relevant • Timely 78
What to Measure

There’s no universal set. A safety-critical system tracks defects closely, while a marketing campaign watches customer response. So start from what success means for this project and environment . The categories ask different questions: is it good ( deliverable ), is it flowing ( delivery ), are we on plan ( baseline ), are we using things well ( resources ), is it worth it ( business value ), are people happy ( stakeholders ), where will we end up ( forecasts )? Slides 80–81 give examples of each. Which is NOT one of the common categories of metrics? What to Measure • What is measured, the parameters, and the measurement method depend on the project objectives, the intended outcomes, and the environment in which the project takes place. • Common categories of metrics include: • Deliverable metrics, • Delivery, • Baseline performance, • Resources, • Business value, • Stakeholders, and • Forecasts. 79
What to Measure

These judge the thing being built. A high count of defects warns of trouble even when the schedule looks fine, and technical performance checks things like speed against the target. Delivery : work in progress, lead time (from identifying the need to delivering the result: the customer’s whole wait), cycle time (from starting the work to finishing it), process efficiency. These compare reality to the approved plan. Schedule variance is the gap: a negative number means you’re behind, which tells you how far you’ve drifted and that you may need to act. Lead time measures: Schedule variance belongs to which category? What to Measure • Deliverable metrics • Information on errors or defects, Measures of performance, Technical performance measures • Delivery • Work in progress, Lead time (total elapsed time between the identification of a need and the delivery of the result), Cycle time, Process efficiency • Baseline performance • Start and finish dates, Effort and duration, Schedule variance 80
What to Measure

Comparing plan and actual reveals problems early. Using far more of a resource than planned hints that the estimate was wrong, and that the cost will overrun too. These ask “is this worth the money?” in different ways. ROI compares gain to cost, while NPV also accounts for money later being worth less than money today. They’re what a sponsor cares about. Unhappy people are an early warning sign. NPS asks how likely customers are to recommend you, while morale and turnover show the team’s health. Losing people is expensive and a sign something’s wrong. Forecasts : estimate to complete (ETC: what is left), estimate at completion (EAC : the expected total), variance at completion (VAC = budget − EAC). Net Promoter Score belongs to which category? EAC is the: What to Measure • Resources • Planned resource utilization compared to actual resource utilization, Planned resource cost compared to actual resource cost • Business value • Cost-benefit ratio, Return on investment (ROI), Net present value (NPV) • Stakeholders • Net Promoter Score (NPS), Mood chart, Morale, Turnover • Forecasts • Estimate to complete (ETC), Estimate at completion (EAC), Variance at completion (VAC) 81
Stakeholder and Team Health Dashboard

An example dashboard for the stakeholder and team metrics of slide 81. Each row has a current value, a trend arrow, a target and a red/amber/green status. Stakeholder engagement : 82% active participation, rising, green. NPS +45 against a target of >30 (green). Mood chart and morale (7.2/10 vs. >8) are amber. Presenting Information

Dashboards : summary displays of the key measures, usually electronic (slide 84). Information radiators : large, visible displays placed where everyone sees them without asking (slide 85). Visual controls : task boards, burn charts and other charts that show the flow of work (slide 86). DIV , like the HTML tag: Dashboards, Information radiators, Visual controls. A big burndown chart hangs where everyone on the team can see it. What is this? Presenting Information • Dashboards • Information Radiators • Visual Controls 83

Information Radiators

(Also called a “big visible chart”.) How can a burn chart help a project manager track progress and identify if the team is ahead or behind schedule? Presenting Information • Information Radiators 85

Uncertainty Performance Domain

Outcomes: awareness of the environment (technical, social, political, market, economic), proactive exploration of and response to uncertainty, awareness of how variables depend on each other, anticipating threats and opportunities, delivery with little impact from surprises, and opportunities realized. Which is an outcome of the Uncertainty domain? 8 Uncertainty Performance Domain 88
Uncertainty Performance Domain

Uncertainty is the umbrella term, meaning you simply don’t know something, like whether a new technology will work. The other terms on this slide are different kinds of not knowing. The key feature of ambiguity is unclarity rather than lack of data. Several answers seem possible and you can’t tell which is right, like not knowing which of multiple options fixes a bug. Many parts affecting one another make results hard to predict. Complexity isn’t the same as being difficult: a hard math problem can be solved, while a system of people and interacting parts can surprise you. Think of how volatility works in a market: a steel price jumping 30% in a month. You may understand it well, and it can still change without warning. A risk is specific: “the vendor may deliver late”. It may happen or not. Exam trap: the definition includes positive effects, so a risk isn’t always bad. CRAVe : Complexity, Risk, Ambiguity, Volatility. “The possibility for rapid and unpredictable change” defines: Uncertainty Performance Domain • The following definitions are relevant to the Uncertainty Performance Domain: • Uncertainty • A lack of understanding and awareness of issues, events, paths to follow, or solutions to pursue. • Ambiguity • A state of being unclear, having difficulty in identifying the cause of events, or having multiple options from which to choose. • Complexity • A characteristic of a program or project or its environment that is difficult to manage due to human behavior, system behavior, and ambiguity. • Volatility • The possibility for rapid and unpredictable change. • Risk • An uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive or negative effect on one or more project objectives. 89
Uncertainty Performance Domain

This slide steps back. Whenever you can’t say for sure what will happen or what’s true, that’s uncertainty , and the next three terms describe why. Compare them by what’s unknown. Risk : a specific future event may happen. Ambiguity : you aren’t sure what the current situation means. Complexity : too many interacting parts to predict. Each one needs a different response, which is the reason to separate them. “We can’t tell what this requirement really means right now.” Which nuance of uncertainty is this closest to? Uncertainty Performance Domain • Uncertainty in the broadest sense is a state of not knowing or unpredictability. • There are many nuances to uncertainty, such as: • Risk associated with not knowing future events, • Ambiguity associated with not being aware of current or future conditions, and • Complexity associated with dynamic systems having unpredictable outcomes. 90
Uncertainty Performance Domain

Many surprises come from outside the project. You can’t respond to what you never looked at, so scanning the larger environment comes before responding. Use it as a checklist when asked where uncertainty comes from. Economic : costs change. Technical : new technology may not work. Legal : the rules may change. Each is something the team doesn’t control but must plan for. Political influences, inside or outside the organization. (A PESTLE-style checklist.) PLATE SPinning : Political, Legal, Ambiguity, Technical, Economic, Social and market, Physical. A new law may change what the product must do. Which aspect of the environment is this? Uncertainty Performance Domain • Successfully navigating uncertainty begins with understanding the larger environment within which the project is operating. • Aspects of the environment that contribute to project uncertainty include, but are not limited to: • Economic factors such as volatility in prices, availability of resources, ability to borrow funds, and inflation/deflation; • Technical considerations such as new or emerging technology, complexity associated with systems, and interfaces; • Legal or legislative constraints or requirements; • Physical environment as it pertains to safety, weather, and working conditions; • Ambiguity associated with current or future conditions; • Social and market influences shaped by opinion and media; and, • Political influences, either external or internal to the organization. 91
Ambiguity

Two people can read the same sentence differently and both feel sure. Conceptual ambiguity is fixed by defining terms: agree on what “done” or “on track” means before relying on the word. The slide’s schedule sentence shows how easily it happens. Here the words are clear, but you can’t tell which path will turn out best. With situational ambiguity , the way forward is trying options on a small scale or making them comparable, rather than arguing. Team members argue in a status meeting because they mean different things by “done”. Which kind of uncertainty is this? Ambiguity • There are two categories of ambiguity: • Conceptual ambiguity • The lack of effective understanding—occurs when people use similar terms or arguments in different ways. • For example, the statement, “The schedule was reported on track last week,” is not clear. • It isn’t clear whether the schedule was on track last week or whether it was reported on last week. • Situational ambiguity • Surfaces when more than one outcome is possible. • Having multiple options to solve a problem is a form of situational ambiguity. 92
Complexity

This isn’t about the amount of work. A huge but predictable job can be merely large. Complexity comes from people and systems reacting in ways you can’t fully foresee. Interconnected is the key word: change one thing and others respond, and those responses cause more change. Think of a new policy that makes one department’s work easier and creates a backlog in another. What makes something complex, according to the slide? Complexity • Complexity is a characteristic of a program, project, or its environment, which is difficult to manage due to human behavior, system behavior, or ambiguity. • Complexity exists when there are many interconnected influences that behave and interact in diverse ways. 93
Complexity

The whole can behave differently from its parts. Each person can act sensibly and still produce a traffic jam. That’s what unintended outcomes means, and it’s why testing parts alone doesn’t guarantee the whole works. This changes how you should act. Since you can’t predict results, a detailed long-term plan offers false confidence. Instead, try small steps, watch what happens and adjust. Each family tackles it from another angle: systems-based changes the system itself, reframing changes how you look at it, and process-based changes how you work. Next three slides. What is the effect of complexity on prediction? Complexity • In complex environments, it is not uncommon to see an aggregation of individual elements leading to unforeseen or unintended outcomes. • The effect of complexity is that there is no way of making accurate predictions about the likelihood of any potential outcome or even of knowing what outcomes might emerge. • There are numerous ways to work with complexity; some of them are systems-based, some entail reframing, and others are based on process. 94
Systems-Based Complexity

If everything is connected, every change affects everything. Decoupling cuts those links so you can work on one piece safely. Software modules with clear interfaces are the familiar example, as you can change one without breaking the rest. When you can’t test the real thing, learn from something similar. A simulation doesn’t have to use the same industry: an airport can learn from shopping malls how customers spend, at low cost and before anything’s built. A team designing a new airport’s retail area studies shopping malls to predict consumer buying habits. Which complexity technique is this? Systems-Based Complexity • Examples of working with complexity that is systems based include: • Decoupling • Disconnecting parts of the system to both simplify the system and reduce the number of connected variables. • Determining how a piece of a system works on its own reduces the overall size of the problem. • Simulation • There may be similar though unrelated scenarios that can be used to simulate components of a system. • A project to build a new airport that includes an area with shopping and restaurants can learn about consumer buying habits by seeking out analogous information on shopping malls and entertainment establishments. 95
Reframing Complexity

One person only sees part of a complex system. Diversity brings in other views to uncover what you’d miss. Starting broad and narrowing later keeps you from settling too soon on the first idea. Delphi-like processes then narrow things down. Relying only on past data misses what’s coming, and relying only on forecasts ignores what really happened. Balance uses both, and the slide’s other point is like a hedge: elements that counteract each other limit the total damage. A team brainstorms many views of a system, then uses a Delphi-like process to narrow them. What is this? Reframing Complexity • Examples of working with complexity that entail reframing are: • Diversity • Complex systems require viewing the system from diverse perspectives. • This can include brainstorming with the project team to open up divergent ways of seeing the system. • It can also include Delphi-like processes to move from divergent to convergent thinking. • Balance • Balancing the type of data used rather than only using forecasting data or data that report on the past or lagging indicators provides a broader perspective. • This can include using elements whose variations are likely to counteract each other's potential negative effects. 96
Process-Based Complexity

If you can’t predict the result, make small changes and watch. Iterating turns a big unknown into many small experiments, and each one tells you what to try next. Assumptions are where complex projects go wrong. Asking stakeholders regularly replaces guesses with facts. Engaging them also means they’re less likely to be surprised, or to resist the final result. Fail safe : for critical elements, build in redundancy or graceful degradation so a component failure doesn’t take the whole system down (a backup server). lIFE : Iterate, Fail safe, Engage. Adding a backup server so a critical system keeps working in reduced form if its main server fails is which complexity technique? Process-Based Complexity • Examples of working with complexity that is process based include: • Iterate • Build iteratively or incrementally. • Add features one at a time. After each iteration, identify what worked, what did not work, customer reaction, and what the project team learned. • Engage • Build in opportunities to get stakeholder engagement. • This reduces the number of assumptions and builds learning and engagement into the process. • Fail safe • For elements of a system that are critical, build in redundancy or elements that can provide a graceful degradation of functionality in the event of a critical component failure. 97
Volatility

Compare it with ambiguity. Volatility isn’t about being unclear: you may understand a market well, and prices can still jump next week. It often comes from fluctuations in available skills or materials (a key specialist leaves; chip prices spike). Sudden shortages and price jumps show up directly as more money or more waiting. So cost and schedule are where you plan protection, which is what the next slide covers. A key specialist unexpectedly leaves, and chip prices jump. What is the project experiencing? What does volatility usually affect? Volatility • Volatility exists in an environment that is subject to rapid and unpredictable change. • Volatility can occur when there are ongoing fluctuations in available skill sets or materials. • Volatility usually impacts cost and schedule. 98
Volatility

You can’t stop the changes, so prepare for them with two tools: have other options ready and keep something in reserve. That’s why alternatives analysis and reserves go together. If your one specialist leaves, what then? Alternatives analysis answers before it happens: train someone else, reorder the work, or outsource . Having options means a shock doesn’t stop you. Prices may rise no matter what you do, so a cost reserve absorbs the jump without needing a new approval. Without it, every price change would become a crisis. Prices rise and the budget runs short. Which response fits? Which is an example of alternatives analysis? Volatility • Alternatives analysis and use of cost or schedule reserve address volatility. • Alternatives analysis • Finding and evaluating alternatives, such as looking at different ways to meet an objective, such as using a different mix of skills, resequencing work, or outsourcing work • Reserve • Cost reserve can be used to cover budget overruns due to price volatility. 99
Risk

Uncertainty is the broad state of not knowing. A risk is one specific thing you can name, assess and plan a response to, and that’s why it’s manageable. Two parts make up the definition: it might not happen (uncertain), and if it does, an objective is affected. If it has already happened, it’s no longer a risk but an issue. Remember the effect can be positive . Separate words help because you act in opposite ways: you try to stop threats from happening and try to make opportunities happen. Exam questions often turn on that difference. Having never done this exact thing before means you can’t know everything in advance. So “no risks” in a plan means that nobody looked, and every project has them because each is unique . A vendor might deliver late. It hasn’t happened yet. What is this? All projects have risks. Risk • Risks are an aspect of uncertainty. • A risk is an uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive or negative effect on one or more project objectives. • Negative risks are called threats, and positive risks are called opportunities. • All projects have risks since they are unique undertakings with varying degrees of uncertainty. 100
Risk

Separate risks can each look fine while the project as a whole is shaky. Overall project risk looks at the total picture, and a very complex, unclear, fast-changing project is risky even if no single item stands out. Same toolkit, larger scale. Rather than buying insurance for a single event, you might split a whole project into phases, or partner with another firm to share the project as a whole ’s exposure. If overall risk is too high, the organization may cancel the project: a legitimate outcome, not a failure of risk management. Overall project risk is often a function of: If overall risk is too high, what may the organization do? Risk • Overall risk is often a function of complexity, ambiguity, and volatility. Responses to overall project risk are the same as for individual threats and opportunities, though responses are applied to the overall project rather than to a specific event. • If the overall risk on the project is too high, the organization may choose to cancel the project. 101
Risk (Threat)

A threat is still only a possibility. That’s why you have choices about it, including accepting it or preventing it, which you wouldn’t have once it has happened. Avoid : eliminate the threat or protect the project from it (change the plan, drop the risky feature). Escalate : the threat is outside the PM’s authority or scope, so pass it to the right level (program, portfolio, sponsor). Transfer : shift ownership and impact to a third party (insurance, a fixed-price contract). Mitigate : reduce the probability or impact (extra testing, a prototype). Accept : acknowledge it without action, perhaps with a contingency reserve. Threats, the A TEAM : Accept, Transfer, Escalate, Avoid, Mitigate. Buying insurance against a data-centre fire is which threat response strategy? Risk (Threat) • A threat is an event or condition that, if it occurs, has a negative impact on one or more objectives. • Five alternative strategies may be considered for dealing with threats, as follows: • Avoid • Escalate • Transfer • Mitigate • Accept 102
Risk Reduction over Time

The table scores five risks each month (impact × probability = severity), and the threat profile chart stacks their severities over time. The total (dashed line) falls from about 26 in January to about 11 in April. Some risks disappear as they are dealt with ( permits obtained drops to 0 once permits are secured; “site not ready in time” too), while “pump capacity” stays. A falling profile is the evidence that risk responses are working. What does a falling threat profile suggest? Risk Reduction over Time 103
Risk (Opportunities)

Same event logic as a threat, but here you want it to happen. Since an opportunity can be missed, ignoring one has a cost too, so it deserves as much attention as a threat. Finishing early sounds like simple luck, but a PM should plan for it. Under a time-and-materials contract, you pay for hours worked, so an early finish saves money directly, which can be reused elsewhere. Exploit : act to make sure the opportunity happens (raise its probability to 100%). Share : give part of the ownership to a third party better able to capture the benefit (a partnership). The difference from exploit is the guarantee. Enhance improves the odds or the size, such as adding staff to raise the chance of finishing early, without promising it. Escalate and accept apply to opportunities too. Opportunities, in slide order: E ach E xtra S hare E arns A gain. Exploit, Escalate, Share, Enhance, Accept. A team identifies a chance to finish early and takes action to ensure that the opportunity occurs. Which strategy is this? A firm partners with another company so that both can capture a positive risk neither could capture alone. Which opportunity strategy is this? Risk (Opportunities) • An opportunity is an event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive impact on one or more project objectives. • An example of an opportunity could be a time and materials-based subcontractor who finishes work early, resulting in lower costs and schedule savings. • Five alternative strategies may be considered for dealing with opportunities, as follows: • Exploit • Escalate • Share • Enhance • Accept 104
Risk (Management and Contingency

Reserves are a planned cushion, not padding. Being explicit means people can see what’s there for risk and track how it’s used, instead of hiding extra days in every task. You’ve named the risk and estimated the possible hit, so this is planned money. Since it’s tied to identified risks, it’s normally part of the cost baseline and the PM can use it. Nobody can name these events yet, so you can’t assign the money to specific risks. Management reserve stays outside the baseline, and using it takes approval (see slide 47). True or false: contingency reserve is set aside for unknown, unplanned events. Risk (Management and Contingency Reserve) • Reserve is an amount of time or budget set aside to account for handling risks. • Contingency reserve is set aside to address identified risks should they occur. • Management reserve is a budget category used for unknown events such as unplanned, in-scope work. 105
Risk (Risk Review)

Risks change as a project moves, so a list written once goes stale. A regular cadence catches new ones, and more varied people mean more chance someone spots what others can’t see. Nobody has to run a separate risk meeting for this. Daily stand-ups already ask what’s blocking people, which is where threats first appear, while they’re still small. A small delay today can become a missed milestone if it continues. A blocker is a threat in its early form, so treat a repeat report as a warning, not just an update. Good news deserves a follow-up too. If a team finds a faster method, could another team use it? A breakthrough is an opportunity only if someone notices and acts on it. People react differently to something real than to a description. Showing a working piece early with a demonstration makes misunderstandings visible while they’re still cheap to fix. A blocker keeps being reported at daily stand-up. What might it become? A team finds a much faster testing method. What should it consider? Risk (Risk Review) • Establishing a frequent rhythm or cadence of review and feedback sessions from a broad selection of stakeholders is helpful for navigating project risk and being proactive with risk responses. • Daily standup meetings can be used in any project and are a source for identifying potential threats and opportunities. • Reports of blockers or impediments could become threats if they continue to delay progress. • Likewise, reports of progress and breakthroughs might point toward opportunities to be further leveraged and shared. • Frequent demonstrations of increments of the product or service, interim designs, or proof of concepts can surface threats and opportunities. 106
Checking Outcomes: Uncertainty

The “checking outcomes” table: the left column is what success looks like for the domain, the right column is the evidence that it happened. You won’t be asked to reproduce it, but it is a good structure for a written answer about the domain. Uncertainty: awareness of the environment (environmental factors considered in estimates and plans), proactive responses (risk register and responses kept current), awareness of interdependencies, anticipation of threats and opportunities, little impact from surprises, realized opportunities, and effective use of reserves. Which evidence supports “proactive responses” in the Uncertainty domain? 107

decks.c: SE423 · Chapter 1.3: Tailoring, Models, Methods, and Artifacts
n: Slide 1

Tailoring means fitting the project-management approach to the project. Models, methods and artifacts are the toolbox it picks from. This finishes Chapter 1: principles (how to behave) and performance domains (what to manage) are applied through a tailored selection of tools. Tailoring, Models, Methods, and Artifacts SE423: Software Project Management 1
Outline

The first half answers “how do we adjust our way of working to fit this project?”. The second half is the toolbox you choose from once you’ve decided what fits. Outline • Tailoring • Models, Methods, and Artifacts 2
Tailoring (section)
Section divider: tailoring. Tailoring 3
Tailoring

Tailoring is a decision made for a reason. Skipping steps because you’re in a hurry isn’t tailoring , while dropping a step because you can show this project doesn’t need it is. Deliberate is what separates the two. Nearly everything about how a project runs can be adjusted. So when a question asks whether something can be tailored, the answer is usually yes, including the development approach and even who gets involved. The higher the cost of a mistake, the more control you need. And with more people involved, there’s more to coordinate. So criticality and the number of stakeholders push you toward more formality. If a reactor fails, people can die, so every step is checked and recorded. An office building still needs care but not that level of rigor. Exam trap: more critical means more process, never less . Which statement best defines tailoring? Tailoring • Tailoring is the deliberate adaptation of the project management approach, governance, and processes to make them more suitable for the given environment and the work at hand. • In a project environment, tailoring considers the development approach, processes, project life cycle, deliverables, and choice of people with whom to engage. • Many variables factor into the tailoring process, including the criticality of the project and the number of stakeholders involved. • Using these variables as an example, it is evident that the rigor, checks and balances, and reporting required for a critical project (e.g., building a nuclear reactor) are much greater than those for building a new office building. 4
Tailoring

You can’t fit an approach to a project you don’t understand. A student app and a banking system need different things, and only their context and goals reveal what. Projects must balance competing demands : speed, low cost, value, quality, regulatory compliance, diverse stakeholder expectations, and adapting to change. No project can maximize all seven at once (the fastest delivery is rarely the cheapest or the most thoroughly checked), which is why the approach has to be tailored to what matters most here. COMPADreS : Creating high-quality deliverables, Optimizing value, Minimizing costs, Providing compliance, Adapting to change, Delivering quickly, Satisfying stakeholders. Why must an approach be tailored rather than simply maximizing speed, cost, quality and everything else? Tailoring • Tailoring involves understanding the project context, goals, and operating environment. • Projects operate in complex environments that need to balance potentially competing demands that include, but are not limited to: • Delivering as quickly as possible, • Minimizing project costs, • Optimizing the value delivered, • Creating high-quality deliverables and outcomes, • Providing compliance with regulatory standards, • Satisfying diverse stakeholder expectations, and • Adapting to change. 5
Why Tailor?

Direct benefits show up on this project, while indirect ones build up over time, such as a team that gets better at choosing how to work. The next three items say what they are. People follow rules they helped write more willingly than rules handed to them. So letting the team shape the approach is a way of earning commitment , not just a courtesy. A standard process is built around the process. Tailoring asks “what does this customer need from us?”, which keeps a customer-oriented focus on things they actually value. More efficient use of resources : effort goes where the project needs it, not into unneeded process. Which is a stated benefit of tailoring? Why Tailor? • Tailoring produces direct and indirect benefits to organizations. • These include, but are not limited to: • More commitment from project team members who helped to tailor the approach, • Customer-oriented focus, as the needs of the customer are an important influencing factor in its development, and • More efficient use of project resources. 6
What to Tailor?

This is the biggest decision, the overall way the work is organized. Slide 8 explains the life cycle and development approach . Slide 9 covers processes : the specific steps inside the approach, and which to keep. Slide 10 covers engagement : who’s involved and how much they can decide. Slide 11 covers tools : what software or equipment the team uses. Slide 12 covers methods and artifacts : techniques and documents, scaled to fit. Remember all five with TEMPLe . TEMPLe : Tools, Engagement, Methods and artifacts, Processes, Life cycle and development approach. Which is NOT one of the project aspects that can be tailored? What to Tailor? • Project aspects that can be tailored include: • Life cycle and development approach selection, • Processes, • Engagement, • Tools, and • Methods and artifacts. 7
What to Tailor?

You aren’t stuck with a standard set of phases. A research-heavy project might add a feasibility phase, for example, so picking the phases is itself tailoring. The life cycle is the shape of the project, while the delivery approach is how the results reach people. Each is a separate choice you can adjust. Why two approaches in one building? The walls can be fully specified up front, but the computing needs are still being discovered. Each part gets the approach that suits what’s known about it. Whether something is hybrid depends on where you’re standing. No single team feels hybrid, since each follows its own approach, but the project as a whole mixes them. A new data center is built in fixed construction phases, while its computing capabilities are worked out in iterations. What is the overall approach? What to Tailor? • Project aspects that can be tailored include: • Life cycle and development approach selection, • Deciding on a life cycle and the phases of the life cycle is an example of tailoring. • Additional tailoring can be done when selecting the development and delivery approach for the project. • For instance, building a new data center could involve • (a) the use of predictive approaches for the physical building construction and finishing and • (b) an iterative approach for understanding and establishing the computing capabilities required. • Viewed from a project level, this combination of approaches represents a hybrid approach, but the construction team and the computing team may only experience a predictive or iterative development approach. 8
What to Tailor?

Choosing an approach doesn’t mean accepting all of its steps. Process tailoring goes through them and asks about each one, using the five verbs below. Added (extra rigor, e.g. a security review), modified (changed to fit, e.g. a lighter weekly report), removed (dropped as unnecessary), blended (elements from different methods combined into one, e.g. Scrum ceremonies with a predictive budget process) or aligned (harmonized so definitions and terms are consistent across teams). A RuMBA : Aligned, Removed, Modified, Blended, Added. Combining elements of two different methods into one process is which process-tailoring action? What to Tailor? • Project aspects that can be tailored include: • Processes, • Process tailoring for the selected life cycle and development approach includes determining which portions or elements should be: • Added • Modified • Removed • Blended • Aligned 9
What to Tailor?

A process only works if the right people are involved at the right level. Engagement tailoring settles that, and the next note gives the three things to decide. People : who is on the team and with which skills and capabilities. Empowerment : how much responsibility and local decision-making the team gets (a mature team gets more). Integration : how contractors, partners and other organizations are brought into the team. PIE : People, Integration, Empowerment. A mature team is given more decision-making power. Which part of engagement tailoring is this? Contractors from a partner company are brought into the team’s way of working. Which is this? What to Tailor? • Project aspects that can be tailored include: • Engagement, • Tailoring engagement for the people involved in the project includes: • People • Empowerment • Integration 10
What to Tailor?

Tools shape how people work, so the choice matters. A distributed team may need a shared board where a small co-located one needs only a whiteboard, which is why picking tools counts as tailoring. The people using a tool every day know what actually helps, so ask them. But the “best” tool may cost too much, so someone has to weigh the benefit against the cost . A company may require one tool for security or licensing reasons, even if the team prefers another. Tailoring happens within such constraints , so the team works around them instead of ignoring them. Leadership requires a specific corporate tool that the team dislikes. What does the slide say about this? The project team usually has the best insight into which tools suit the work. What to Tailor? • Project aspects that can be tailored include: • Tools • Selecting the tools (e.g., software or equipment) the project team will use for the project is a form of tailoring. • Often, the project team has the best insight into the most suitable tools for the situation, but those choices might need tempering based on the associated costs. • Additionally, organizational leaders can impose constraints that the project team cannot change. 11
What to Tailor?

A method that works in one place can fail in another. Open retrospectives suit a culture where people speak freely, but may need adjusting where criticizing others is uncomfortable. Hence fitting to environment and culture . Artifacts (documents, templates) are tailored so they are appropriate for the project and organization: a two-page charter for a small internal project, a full one for a regulated contract. A small internal project uses a two-page charter, while a regulated contract uses a full one. What is this? What to Tailor? • Project aspects that can be tailored include: • Methods and artifacts • Tailoring the means that will be used to achieve the project outcomes is performed so that the methods are suited for the environment and the culture. • Tailoring the documents, templates, and other artifacts that will be used on the project helps to make sure the artifacts are appropriate for the project and the organization. 12
The Tailoring Process

The tailoring process, step 1 : select the initial development approach : choose the approach best suited to the endeavor (the ticked set of gears). Step 2 : tailor for the organization : modify it to fit organizational requirements and constraints. Step 4 : implement ongoing improvement : inspect and adapt; the loop arrow shows it never ends. Put the four steps of the tailoring process in order. The Tailoring Process 13
Selecting the Initial Development

Step 1 in pictures: choose the base approach, e.g. agile or waterfall (the handwritten note). Step 2: one set of gears becomes the organization’s adapted version. Step 3: elements are removed (the crossed boxes) and adjusted for this project. Step 4: the remaining process keeps being refined. What is the first step in the tailoring process? Selecting the Initial Development Approach Selecting the Initial Development Approach Tailoring the Approach for the Organization waterfall exagile Tailoring the Approach for the Project Implement Ongoing Improvement 14
Assessing the Organizational and Project

Tailoring happens at two levels . At the organizational level, a general PM methodology and development approach are adapted into the organization’s own methodologies, e.g. one for small projects and one for large or sensitive projects. Both levels are guided by environmental factors , general guides, and the available models, methods and artifacts. A company creates one methodology for small projects and another for large, sensitive ones. At what level is this tailoring? Tailoring can happen at both the organizational level and the project level. Assessing the Organizational and Project Factors When Tailoring 15
Tailoring for the Project

Knowing the project’s features tells you how far to adjust. Rather than a long list, the slide groups them into three questions: what are we making, who’s making it, and in what kind of workplace? Each one has its own slide next. Remember them as what ( product/deliverable ), who ( project team ) and where ( culture ). CoPPer : Culture, Project team, Product or deliverable. Which three groups of attributes influence tailoring for the project? Tailoring for the Project • Many attributes influence tailoring for the project. • These include, but are not limited to: • Product/deliverable, • Project team, and • Culture. 16
Tailoring for the Project

The thing you’re producing limits your choices. A heart monitor and a game can’t follow the same process, even with the same team, which is why product/deliverable comes first. Compliance and criticality decide how much proof and checking you need. A medical product needs a paper trail, so a short time frame or new technology can’t remove that need; it only makes planning harder. Stability of requirements (stable favours predictive, volatile favours adaptive) and security needs. Sentence, in slide order: C ats T ake I n T oo T iny S nacks, S adly. Compliance, Type of product, Industry market, Technology, Time frame, Stability of requirements, Security. A heart monitor needs strong evidence of safety. Which attribute drives this? Very unstable requirements usually favor which kind of approach? Tailoring for the Project • Product/Deliverable • Attributes associated with the product or deliverable include, but are not limited to: • Compliance/criticality • Type of product/deliverable • Industry market • Technology • Time frame • Stability of requirements • Security. 17
Tailoring for the Project

The same process can work for one team and fail for another. So look at who’s doing the work before deciding how much structure they need. These are the project team factors. Five people in a room can just talk. Fifty people across time zones need written decisions and scheduled meetings, so size and geography raise the amount of formal communication needed. Team experience (an experienced team needs less prescribed process) and access to the customer (adaptive approaches need frequent customer input). SAGE O wl: Size of the team, Access to customer, Geography, Experience, Organizational distribution. An adaptive approach needs frequent input, but the customer is hard to reach. Which consideration does this raise? Why might an experienced team need less prescribed process? Tailoring for the Project • Project Team • Project team considerations include: • Project team size • Project team geography • Organizational distribution • Project team experience • Access to customer 18
Tailoring for the Project

Culture is how things really get done, which may differ from official policy. If everyone knows that bad news gets punished, that’s culture, even if no document says so. A process only works if the workplace accepts it. Daily self-organizing meetings can fall flat where people wait for orders, so check the fit first: is it formal and hierarchical , or agile and collaborative ? An agile process forced onto a strictly hierarchical culture struggles. These tell you how much change people will accept. Without buy-in , people quietly ignore the new way of working. Without trust and empowerment , they won’t make decisions on their own. TO BE : Trust, Organizational culture, Buy-in, Empowerment. An agile process is forced onto a strictly hierarchical company and struggles. What was not considered? Which is a culture consideration? Tailoring for the Project • Culture (refers to the shared norms, beliefs, and practices within a company.) • When tailoring a project, you assess how the project management approach fits with this culture—whether it's formal and hierarchical, agile and collaborative, risk-averse, or innovation-driven. • Evaluating the culture includes considerations regarding: • Buy-in (gaining support and commitment from key stakeholders, especially those who influence or are affected by the project) • Trust • Empowerment • Organizational culture 19
Implement Ongoing Improvement

The first version is a best guess about what will work, and you’ll know more later. So treat tailoring as not a one-time exercise , or you’ll keep following a process that stopped fitting. Progressive elaboration means details get clearer as you go. As they do, so do the problems: if reviews keep catching the same errors, you’ve found where the process needs adjusting. You don’t need extra meetings to improve. Retrospectives and phase gates are already scheduled pauses, so use them to ask “is the way we work still right?”. True or false: tailoring is done once, when the project is initiated. Implement Ongoing Improvement • The process of tailoring is not a single, one-time exercise. • During progressive elaboration, issues with how the project team is working, how the product or deliverable is evolving, and other learnings will indicate where further tailoring could bring improvements. • Review points, phase gates, and retrospectives all provide opportunities to inspect and adapt the process, development approach, and delivery frequency as necessary. 20
Situations and Tailoring Suggestions

The pattern in this table: name the problem, then tailor in the missing control. Poor quality deliverables → add feedback, verification loops and quality-assurance steps. Members unsure how to proceed → add guidance, training and verification. Too much work in progress or scrap → value-stream mapping and kanban boards to visualize the work and find the problems. Disengaged stakeholders → check information sharing and feedback loops; deeper engagement may work better than simply communicating. Lack of visibility of progress → make sure the right measures are collected, analysed and discussed, and validated with the team and stakeholders. Recurring surprises → root-cause analysis of gaps in the process. A team keeps waiting several days for approvals before it can proceed. What tailoring change does the table suggest? 21
Summary

Considered is the same point as “deliberate” on slide 4: you adapt for a reason you can state. That’s the idea to carry into a written answer. This tells you what can be changed, so a good answer names all three: people, processes and tools . Changing only the paperwork isn’t enough if the team and tools stay wrong. The order runs from general to specific and then keeps going. Remember “ Smart Teams Tailor Iteratively ”: select a base, fit it to the organization , fit it to the project , then keep improving . The order matters here: S mart T eams T ailor I teratively. Select the initial approach, Tailor for the organization, Tailor for the project, Implement ongoing improvement. What is the correct order of the tailoring process? Summary • Tailoring involves the considered adaptation of approach, governance, and processes to make them more suitable for the given environment and the project at hand. • It involves the analysis, design, and deliberate modification of the people elements, the processes employed, and the tools used. • The tailoring process involves four steps: • Select initial approach • Tailor for the organization • Tailor for the project • Implement ongoing improvement 22
Models, Methods, and Artifacts (section)
Models, Methods, and Artifacts 23
Models, Methods, and Artifacts

You only need to know what each one is for, not how to run each in detail. A high-level view helps you recognize which tool fits a situation. It is not exhaustive or prescriptive : a menu of options to tailor from, not a checklist to use every time. Teams must use every model, method and artifact in this section. Models, Methods, and Artifacts • This section provides a high-level description of some commonly used models, methods, and artifacts that are useful in managing projects. • The items listed in this section are not intended to be exhaustive or prescriptive, but rather to help project teams think about the options available to them. 24
Models, Methods, and Artifacts

A model helps you make sense of what you see. It doesn’t tell you what to do step by step: Tuckman explains why a new team is arguing, so thinking is its job. A method is something you carry out, like running a retrospective. If you could schedule it and do it, it’s a means for achieving something. An artifact is something you can hold or file, like a risk register. Model = think, method = do, artifact = thing answers most “which one is this?” questions. MaMA : Model, Method, Artifact. A risk register is best classified as a: Give an example of a project management tool or technique that you might use to manage a complex software development project, and explain how it could help you ensure project success. Models, Methods, and Artifacts • Model • A model is a thinking strategy to explain a process, framework, or phenomenon. • Method • A method is the means for achieving an outcome, output, result, or project deliverable. • Artifact • An artifact can be a template, document, output, or project deliverable. detitarable is a Goodexamk project 25
Principles, domains and the toolbox together

The whole PMBOK 7 picture in one diagram. At the top, the 12 principles … …the 8 performance domains (the circle), which are carried out with models, methods and artifacts (left and right) to produce deliverables. Everything sits inside the system for value delivery and the internal and external environments, and is tailored to fit the project context (bottom). According to the diagram, what do the 12 principles do? 26
Models, Methods, and Artifacts

No tool is free. Even a simple template takes time to fill in and learn. So “this tool is useful” isn’t enough: the benefit has to beat its costs . Teams should weigh these before adopting one. Avoid anything that duplicates work or adds unnecessary effort, isn’t useful to the team and stakeholders, produces incorrect or misleading information, or serves one individual’s needs rather than the team’s (a report one manager likes but nobody reads). A manager wants a weekly report that nobody else reads. What should the team do, according to the slide? Why do models, methods and artifacts need weighing before use? Models, Methods, and Artifacts • As with any process, the use of models, methods, and artifacts has associated costs related to time, level of expertise/proficiency in use, impact on productivity, etc. • Project teams should consider these implications when deciding which elements to use. • As much as possible, project teams should avoid using anything that: • Duplicates or adds unnecessary effort, • Is not useful to the project team and its stakeholders, • Produces incorrect or misleading information, or • Caters to individual needs versus those of the project team. 27
Commonly Used Models

Situational Leadership II : the PM adapts style to each member’s development level (competence and commitment): directing a beginner, coaching, supporting, then delegating to an expert. The instructor’s note: understand these models, don’t memorize them. Coaching works by asking, not telling. OSCAR walks through the goal, where things stand now, what the options are, what to do next, and how it went, so the person solves their own problem. Not every message suits every channel. A sensitive problem needs a conversation, while a date change suits an email you can refer back to. Channels differ in clarity, speed and recordability, so pick the one the message needs. Execution asks “how do I do what I want here?” and evaluation asks “did it work?”. When users can’t answer them, you have a gulf . It’s from UX, but it fits any process people find confusing. Which model helps a project manager adapt leadership style to each team member’s development level? •a Commonly Used Models understand don't memorize • Situational leadership models • Situational Leadership® II (helps project managers adapt their leadership style based on the development level of their team members) • OSCAR Model (useful in project management for guiding conversations, solving problems, and supporting team development) • Communication models • Cross-Cultural Communication (set of principles that help people from different cultural backgrounds communicate effectively) • Effectiveness of Communication Channels (Clarity, Speed, Richness, Recordability, Accessibility, Suitability) • Gulf of Execution and Evaluation (a concept from UX that focuses on the gap between a user's goal and the system’s ability to help them achieve it and the gap between the system’s response and the user’s ability to interpret it) 28
Commonly Used Models

Good pay stops people being unhappy but doesn’t make them excited. That’s the key insight: fixing hygiene only gets you to neutral, while motivators like recognition produce real effort. A pay rise is hygiene, not a motivator. Intrinsic motivation comes from the work itself (it excites you); extrinsic from outside rewards (pay, grades). People can’t care about growth while worried about their job or safety. So if a teammate is struggling with a basic need, inspiring talk won’t help until that’s dealt with. That’s Maslow’s order: lower needs first. Theory X : people dislike work and must be controlled. Theory Y : people want to work and should be empowered. Theory Z : long-term employment, loyalty and involvement. In Herzberg’s model, which of these is a motivator rather than a hygiene factor? A manager assumes employees dislike work and must be closely supervised. Which theory does this reflect? Commonly Used Models • Motivational models • Hygiene and Motivational Factors (Hygene: salary, benefits, working conditions, company policies, job security, etc. Motivational: Achievement, recognition, advancement, responsibility, the work itself, personal growth) • Intrinsic (to the work itself) versus Extrinsic Motivation ex thet.amexcitesYou • Theory of the hierarchy of Needs (physiological->safety->love/belonging- >esteem->self-actualization) • Theory X, Theory Y, and Theory Z (These psychology of management styles models describe different assumptions about employee motivation and behavior) 29
Commonly Used Models

ADKAR explains why one person isn’t changing, by finding the step they’re stuck on. Someone who knows how but doesn’t want to needs Desire, not more training. People resist unless they feel a reason to change, so urgency comes first. Kotter is about moving a whole organization, and the order matters: visible short-term wins come before making the change permanent. Performance usually gets worse before it gets better. If you know that’s normal under the Satir model, you won’t panic and abandon a change during the dip. Bridges points out that people must let go of the old way before accepting the new one. Announcing a change isn’t the same as people having moved through the transition . Which change model focuses on the individual, through awareness, desire, knowledge, ability and reinforcement? Commonly Used Models h • Change models • ADKAR® Model (focuses on individual transformation) • The 8-Step Process for Leading Change (Create a Sense of Urgency -> Build a Guiding Coalition -> Form a Strategic Vision and Initiatives -> Enlist a Volunteer Army -> Enable Action by Removing Barriers -> Generate Short-Term Wins -> Sustain Acceleration -> Institute Change) • Virginia Satir Change Model (is a psychologically grounded framework that explains how individuals and organizations emotionally respond to change. ) • Transition Model (a powerful framework for understanding the emotional and psychological journey people go through during change) 30
Commonly Used Models

Cynefin sorts situations into obvious (apply best practice), complicated (analyse with experts), complex (probe and experiment) and chaotic (act first). It stops teams applying rigid processes to unpredictable projects. Ask two questions: how sure are we about what’s needed, and about how to build it? Sure about both suggests waterfall, and unsure about both suggests agile. That’s all the Stacey matrix is doing. Which model helps decide between waterfall, agile and hybrid approaches based on how uncertain the requirements and technology are? Commonly Used Models • Complexity models • Cynefin Framework (help PMOs and project leads avoid applying rigid processes to unpredictable projects) • Stacey Matrix (Helps determine whether to use Waterfall, Agile, or hybrid approaches.) 31
Commonly Used Models

This chapter (from Pinto’s Project Management ) looks at the three organizational features that shape how projects are run: strategy (why projects exist), structure (who reports to whom and how resources are shared) and culture (the unwritten rules people follow). Projects and Organizational Strategy

It’s just the organization deciding where it wants to go and getting there. Cross-functional matters, because a goal like “enter a new market” needs sales, engineering and finance to act together, and so do the projects that carry it out. You can’t choose a path without a destination, so vision and mission come first. After that comes a loop, because evaluating results may send you back to change the strategy. This is the test for any strategy: did we reach our objectives ? A beautifully written plan with no results has failed. What is the main purpose of strategic management? Projects and Organizational Strategy Strategic management: the science of formulating, implementing, and evaluating cross-functional decisions that enable an organization to achieve its objectives. Consists of: • Developing vision and mission statements • Formulating, implementing, and evaluating • Making cross-functional decisions • Achieving objectives Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. The table’s point: projects are how strategy gets implemented . Each strategic intention on the left becomes a type of project on the right. See the pattern: a business goal becomes concrete work. “Sell to more customers” stays vague until someone runs a new product development project. “Be more efficient” becomes reengineering , which redesigns how the work is done. If a project can’t be linked to a row like this, ask why it’s being funded. For example, reverse engineering studies a competitor’s product to match it. Pick one or two rows as examples when explaining how PM supports strategy. How does project management contribute to organizations in achieving their strategic objectives? Please elaborate. Strategy example: the Airbus A380

The A380 was an engineering achievement, and the planes flew. It still failed commercially, so the lesson is about strategy : delivering the wrong thing well doesn’t help. Same data, opposite conclusions. That’s the point: facts don’t choose a strategy, and people’s interpretation does. Airbus bet on giant planes flying between hub airports. Boeing concluded that medium-sized wide-body jets flying directly between more cities fitted the future better, and the market followed Boeing. Lesson: a project can be well run and still fail if the strategy behind it is wrong. What is the main lesson of the Airbus A380 case? What did Airbus conclude from the growth in air traffic? What went wrong for the A380? Much of the blame rests on the strategic decisions taken by Airbus and its view of the future of global aviation. At the beginning of the millennium, Airbus and Boeing looked where their business was heading and saw similar facts: air traffic doubling every 15 years, including estimates that the number of travelers would hit four billion by 2020—and came to radically different conclusions for the future. For Airbus there was need for much bigger planes for sustainable growth at congested airports. For Boeing, medium-sized wide-body jets best matched future globalization pressures and anticipated higher frequency of travel among major and multiple growing cities. Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Projects and Organizational Strategy

A vision is where we want to be, while a mission is what we do and for whom. Without them, nobody can judge whether a proposed project fits, so every department pulls its own way. Projects are how a strategy actually happens: a plan to enter a market means nothing until a project builds the product. That’s why they’re called the key ingredients in strategy implementation . Strategy fails if each department decides alone. Cross-functional decisions weigh the whole organization, and achieving objectives is the measure of whether it all worked. The TOWS matrix turns SWOT into strategies: SO (use strengths to seize opportunities), ST (use strengths against threats), WO (overcome weaknesses using opportunities), WT (minimize weaknesses and avoid threats). The order matters here: D on’t F orget M y A im. Developing vision and mission, Formulating strategy, Making cross-functional decisions, Achieving objectives. In a TOWS matrix, a strategy that uses internal strengths to take advantage of external opportunities is called: Projects and Organizational Strategy Strategic management consists of the following elements 1. Developing vision statements and mission statements. Vision and mission statements establish a sense of what the organization hopes to accomplish or what top managers hope it will become at some point in the future. 2. Formulating, implementing, and evaluating. Projects, as the key ingredients in strategy implementation, play a crucial role in the basic process model of strategic management. A firm devotes significant time and resources to evaluating its business opportunities through developing a corporate vision or mission, assessing internal strengths and weaknesses as well as external opportunities and threats, establishing long-range objectives, and generating and selecting among various strategic alternatives 3. Making cross-functional decisions. 4. Achieving objectives. TOWS Matrix Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Stakeholder Management

A project can pollute a river or upset a community and still be on budget, but those people can stop you. So you can’t just focus inward: external effects come back to the project. Mapping who wants what shows where the PM stands and whose support is needed. That’s the purpose of stakeholder analysis : seeing the politics clearly enough to plan for them… …and it shows that some conflicts have no clean answer. When groups want opposite things, you can’t please everyone, so the PM manages the trade-off. That’s why they’re called irresolvable conflicts (a new system that helps sales may burden operations). The test is whether they have an interest and can affect the outcome. Note the wording, positively or negatively : a supplier can speed you up, and a protest group can hold you back. What makes someone a project stakeholder, according to the slide? Stakeholder analysis can reveal conflicts that seem impossible to fully resolve. Stakeholder Management Organizations and project teams cannot operate in ways that ignore the external effects of their decisions. One way to understand the relationship of project managers and their projects to the rest of the organization is through employing stakeholder analysis. Stakeholder analysis is a useful tool for demonstrating some of the seemingly irresolvable conflicts that occur through the planned creation and introduction of new projects. Project stakeholders are defined as all individuals or groups who have an active stake in the project and can potentially impact, either positively or negatively, its development. Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Identifying Project Stakeholders

These people work inside your organization, and you can usually reach them through its hierarchy. Each has different concerns: the accountant cares about spending, while top management cares about strategy. You have less control over these, so you must persuade or plan around them. Competitors count even though they aren’t involved, because their moves can make your project pointless. They aren’t customers or partners, but they can still stop you. Intervenor groups are easy to overlook, which is exactly why the slide’s pipeline case hurt: the project was held up for years by lawsuits and lobbying. Edugate scheduling system: identify three main stakeholder groups for this project, describe their roles, and explain how their input will shape the system. Identifying Project Stakeholders Internal Stakeholders External Stakeholders • Top management • Clients • Accountant • Competitors • Other functional managers • Suppliers • Project team members • Environmental, political, consumer, and other intervenor groups • Hydraulic fracturing technology has been widely embraced in USA which led to going from being a net importer of natural gas in 2012 to a net exporter in 2016. Environmental groups, however, continue to oppose these steps, using litigation and political lobbying to resist the development of these energy sources. They were initially successful in halting completion of the Dakota Access Pipeline project and have delayed for years the development of the 1,700-mile-long Keystone XL oil pipeline from Canada’s oil sands region to refineries in Texas. These types of external stakeholders are called intervenor groups (possessing the power to effectively intervene and disrupt the project). Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. A functional manager lends you a good engineer and loses them for months, so don’t be surprised at some resistance. Their goal, keeping their own department running, conflicts with yours even though nobody’s wrong. The client has paid and wants the benefit, so speed is their priority. That can conflict with quality, or with the time your team needs: their view of as quickly as possible isn’t the same as yours. Top management supports you, but also needs to keep an eye on you, as it’s their money and risk. So expect both help and limits. That’s why control sits next to support in this diagram. Accountants : support and actively monitor project budgets . The PM sits in the middle, balancing all of them. Why might a functional manager resist your project?
