Organizational Structure

Everyone should know who decides what. A small span of control means close supervision but many layers, while a wide one means more freedom and fewer layers, and more layers slow every decision. Why group at all? Putting similar people together builds expertise, but it also creates the walls between departments that projects have to cross. Grouping creates walls, and these systems are the doors. Without them, departments don’t share information. Projects cut across departments, so this third element is where they succeed or struggle. A manager has 25 people reporting directly to them. What term describes this number? Which element of structure is where projects most often struggle? g11 Organizational Structure Consists of three key elements: 1. Designates formal reporting relationships, Who reports to whom? – number of levels in the hierarchy – span of control 2. Identifies groupings of – individuals into departments – departments into the total organization 3. Design of systems to ensure – effective communication – coordination – integration of effort across departments Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Forms of Organization Structure

Think of a school arranged by subject: all math teachers together. Functional organizations are great for building expertise, but nobody owns work that spans several departments. Here the project is the main unit, and people belong to it until it’s over. A project organization suits firms that earn their money from projects, like construction companies. A matrix tries to get both benefits at once. It keeps expert departments and still has strong projects, at the cost that a person may have two bosses : a functional manager and a project manager. PerFuMe : Project, Functional, Matrix. How are employees grouped in a functional organization? Which statement best describes a project organization? Forms of Organization Structure • Functional organizations—group people performing similar activities into departments • Project organizations—group people into project teams on temporary assignments • Matrix organizations—create a dual hierarchy in which functions and projects have equal prominence Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved

A functional structure: departments (engineering, manufacturing, marketing, finance, accounting) under the president, each with its own sub-units. The vertical arrows show communication channels running up and down inside each function , not across. Coordinating a cross-functional project means going up one chain and down another, which is slow: the root of the silo weakness on the next slide. In a functional structure, how does communication mainly flow? Why is cross-functional work slow in this structure? Table 2.2 Strengths and Weaknesses of

There’s nothing to reorganize, so you can start right away. For a small project staying within one department, this is the simplest option, since you just assign it within the existing structure . Specialists sit together and learn from each other. That builds deep knowledge in one field, which is very valuable for technically hard work. A person’s next role is clear, like junior to senior engineer. That’s reassuring to staff, unlike project-based work where the next assignment is uncertain, so career paths are a real strength. People protect their own department’s view. Each one may do its piece well, but no one takes care of how pieces fit together. So siloing is the weakness to name first. People are rewarded by their department, so that’s who they work to please. Nobody owns the customer’s whole experience, which is what lack of customer focus means. Longer project times (slower communication through the hierarchy) and varying interest or commitment, since the project is nobody’s main job. Project Organizational Structure

Think of each project as a small company. A dedicated team works only on it, so nobody’s attention is split with other work. People join for the time they’re needed and then leave. This keeps costs down compared to holding someone for a whole project, but it also means they move on once their part is done. Their income comes from delivering projects, so it makes sense to organize around them. A hospital is mostly routine operations, while a construction company is mostly projects. Which kind of company most naturally uses a project organization? In a project organization, resources are assigned for as long as the project needs them. Project Organizational Structure Within the project organization, each project is a self- contained business unit with a dedicated project team. The firm assigns resources from functional pools directly to the project for the time period they are needed. Project organizations are those that are set up with their exclusive focus aimed at running projects. Construction companies, large manufacturers such as Boeing or Airbus, pharmaceutical firms, and many software consulting and research and development organizations are organized as pure project organizations. Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Table 2.3 Strengths and Weaknesses of

There’s no need to negotiate with other managers for decisions or staff. One person can decide, so problems get fixed fast, and that’s what sole authority gives you. A team working on just one thing talks all the time, with no layers between them. That’s why communication and decision-making improve, and doing projects all day also builds real PM experts. A competitor launches something and you can react right away, because you’re not waiting for several departments to agree. That’s the value of a rapid response . The costs add up: every project needs its own full set of staff and equipment, even if another team has spares. Such duplication is what makes it expensive . People identify with “their” project. They may also make decisions that help it but hurt the company, and specialists who leave take their knowledge with them, so loyalty cuts both ways. What happens to me when this ends? If no job is waiting, good people may start looking elsewhere just when you need them most for the finish. That’s why they worry about their future . Difficult to maintain a pooled supply of intellectual capital (contractors hired 4. Creation of project temporarily for the project then leave management experts the organization) 5. Rapid response to market 4. Team member concern about future opportunities once project ends Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved

Read the chart as a grid. The rows are projects, run by project managers reporting to the VP of projects . It’s the “project” half of the matrix… …but the PMs must work closely with the functional departments (columns) to staff their teams through loans of personnel from each function: the “2 resources”, “1.5 resources” cells show how many people each department lends to each project. In this matrix, how do PMs get their staff? Figure 2.7 Example of a Matrix Organizational Structure The vice president of projects controls the activities of the project managers under his authority. Table 2.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of

When priorities change, people can be moved between projects without reorganizing the company. That’s why it’s suited to dynamic environments , unlike a rigid structure. Neither side automatically wins, so expert departments stay strong while projects also get attention. That’s the intent behind equal emphasis , though keeping the balance takes constant work. Because a person belongs to both a department and a project, information moves between them naturally. So coordination across units improves. If you only have one security expert, a matrix lets three projects share them part time. So it’s a good fit when specialists are in short supply, which maximizes scarce resources . Your project manager wants the task today and your department head wants something else. Whose priority wins? That’s the daily experience of two bosses , and it causes stress for the people in the middle. Nothing is given automatically, so managers must agree on who gets whom, and when. Negotiation takes time and depends on relationships. “Two bosses” is never a strength. What is the main weakness of the matrix structure? Equal emphasis on project 2. Negotiation required in management and functional order to share resources efficiency 3. Promotes coordination across 3. Workers caught between functional units competing project and functional demands 4. Maximizes scarce resources Blank Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Heavyweight Project Organizations

Normal structures are slowed by approvals and competing priorities. For an urgent, high-stakes goal, a company may remove those limits. A heavyweight team is that exception, and it’s costly, so it isn’t for every project. Why would it work? Few people, top talent, no red tape. Skunk Works teams built advanced aircraft fast this way, because they could decide without waiting for anyone outside the team. The PM gets real power, like a senior executive, and doesn’t need to ask for permission. That’s the meaning of PM authority expanded , compared with a PM who has to persuade people… …departments no longer shape the work. The team goes after what the market wants and reports directly to the top, so its news doesn’t get diluted on its way up… …and success gets judged by the external customer , not by how well internal rules were followed. That keeps the team’s attention on what really counts. Which describes a heavyweight project team? Skunk Works is best described as: Heavyweight Project Organizations Organizations can sometimes gain tremendous benefit from creating a fully dedicated project organization. All Rights Reserved

A survey of managers’ perceptions of how effective each structure is for project success, from functional through functional matrix, balanced matrix and project matrix to project team . The trend: the more project-oriented the structure, the more effective managers judge it for projects; for new product development the project matrix and project team score highest. (A survey result to understand, not to memorize.) What does the survey suggest? Project Management Offices

Without a PMO , each PM reinvents their own way of working. A central office brings consistency, so that projects can be compared and lessons shared across them. They act as resource centres for technical details , expertise , a repository (templates, lessons learned, past project data) and a center of excellence for PM practice. A PM buried in schedules and reports has no time to lead people. So moving that work to support staff frees them up, which is why the PMO shifts some of the burden . CRaTE : Center for excellence, Repository, Technical details, Expertise. What is a Project Management Office (PMO) and its role in organizations? Project Management Offices Centralized units that oversee or improve the management of projects Resource centers for: • Technical details • Expertise • Repository • Center for excellence Using a PMO as a resource center shifts some of the burden for PM activities (activity scheduling, resource allocation, monitoring, control processes, etc.) from the project manager to a support staff that is dedicated to providing this assistance Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Alternative Levels of Project Offices

The higher up it sits, the wider its view. A corporate office can compare all projects and advise on which matter most, but it’s further from daily project details. One department’s projects may need specific methods, say for engineering. A business unit office gives that closer support, while staying aware of more than one project. Level 1, project : decentralized to the individual project, giving direct support. The numbering runs upward: Level 1 is the narrowest scope, Level 3 the widest. A PMO that serves the needs within one specific business unit is at which level? Alternative Levels of Project Offices The PMO may be situated at a corporate level (Level 3), where it serves an overall corporate support function. It can be placed at a lower functional level (Level 2), where it serves the needs within a specific business unit. Finally, the PMO can be decentralized down to the actual project level (Level 1), where it offers direct support for each project. Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Forms of P M O s and Control

Think of it as advice you’re free to ignore. A supportive PMO offers templates and training and has little power, so it works where project teams are already capable… Now there are rules to follow, and someone checks. Controlling brings consistency across projects, at the cost of some freedom for each PM. It no longer advises, because it runs the projects itself. Directive gives the most control, and it suits critical work where the company wants central authority. SCoreD , from low control to high: Supportive, Controlling, Directive. A PMO that requires projects to comply with its adopted standards and templates, but does not run the projects itself, is which form? Forms of PMOs and Control Three forms of PMOs, varying with degrees of control and influence include: • Supportive, low control; consultative and provide PM resources and training • Controlling, moderate control; requires compliance to adopted PM standards/processes • Directive, high control; directly manages projects Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Models of P M O s

Think of a weather report: it tells you what’s happening but doesn’t change it. A weather station PMO only reports status, so if management asks “what’s going on?” and nothing more, this is the model. A control tower guides planes without flying them. A control tower PMO is about improving how PM is done, through better methods and helping PMs use them. Need a PM for a new project? Ask the pool. Like staff in a talent agency, the resource pool supplies people, so its value is having skilled professionals available. CRoW : Control tower, Resource pool, Weather station. A consultancy keeps a bench of certified project managers and assigns them to client projects as needed. Which PMO model is this? Models of PMOs In addition to the forms of PMO and varying levels of control, there are three models of PMOs with various purposes for companies: • Weather station—the PMO is typically used only as a monitoring and tracking device (management wants to keep an eye on the status of the projects without directly attempting to influence or control them) • Control tower—project management is a skill to be protected and supported (focus on improving methodology and practices and help PM apply them) • Resource pool—maintain and provide a cadre of skilled project professionals (supplying project managers and other skilled professionals to the company’s projects) Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Organizational Culture

After strategy (why) and structure (who reports to whom), this asks how people really behave. It’s the third contextual variable , and it’s the hardest to see, since nobody hands you a chart of it. What a new employee learns by the second week, without being told: is it OK to disagree with the boss? Do people actually leave at 5? That’s what the definition means by unwritten rules . The four parts: unwritten (rarely written down); rules of behavior (how to react to events); held by a subset (not necessarily company-wide: engineering can have a different culture from sales); taught to new members (newcomers pick it up by watching others). Example: a culture that rewards collaboration between functional groups. HURT : Held by a subset of the organization, Unwritten, Rules of behavior, Taught to new members. Newcomers pick up how to behave by watching others. Which part of the definition of culture is this? Engineering behaves differently from sales in the same company. Which part of the definition explains this? Organizational Culture • The third key contextual variable in how projects are managed effectively is that of organizational culture • Definition of culture: “organization’s culture refers to the unwritten rules of behavior, or norms that are used to shape and guide behavior, that are shared by some subset of organizational members and that are taught to all new members of the company” – Unwritten (are often not written down) – Rules of behavior (guidelines as to how best to react to these events) – Held by some subset of the organization (may or may not be companywide) – Taught to all new members (New members of an organization pick up the behaviors as they observe others engaging in them) • Ex: Company X has a strong supportive culture that emphasizes and rewards positive collaboration between functional groups. Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Key Factors That Affect Culture

Each factor pushes behavior a certain way. Fast-changing technology favors experimenting, while a highly regulated environment favors caution. Geography matters too, since workplace habits differ between countries. … reward systems , rules and procedures, and key organizational members. GE’s jet-engine division and Rolls-Royce make the same product for the same markets, yet GE rewards aggressiveness and high commitment (with high burnout) while Rolls-Royce is paternalistic and rewards loyalty and long tenure, largely because of what each rewards. New people are careful and polite, and they look to the leader for direction. Forming feels calm, but little gets done yet, because people are still working out what’s expected of them. Building Trust

Everything else in the pyramid depends on this. If people don’t feel safe, they hide problems and avoid arguments, so trust comes first as the foundation. Managing Conflict

Think of healthy debate as a fight about ideas where nobody’s attacking the person. It only works if you trust that disagreement won’t be used against you, which is why healthy conflict sits above trust. If everyone is always comfortable, tough topics probably aren’t being raised. So some uncomfortable moments are a good sign, not something to fix. What’s normal in one team feels rude in another. Agreeing the rules up front, such as “challenge the idea, not the person”, stops arguments about how to argue. That’s what conflict norms are for. If nobody challenges a weak design because it would feel awkward, the mistake ships. That’s the cost of avoidance , and groupthink is what it looks like: everyone nods, and nobody really agrees. Why is healthy conflict important in teams? A team values harmony so much that it stops critically evaluating ideas. This is: Managing Conflict • Good (healthy) conflict among team members requires trust, which is all about engaging in unfiltered, passionate debate around issues. • Even among the best teams, conflict will at times be uncomfortable. • Conflict norms will vary in each team, and must be discussed and made clear: oNorms = rules of engagement: These define what’s acceptable in debate—tone, language, timing, emotional expression. • The fear of occasional personal conflict should not deter a team from having regular, productive debate: oAvoidance is costly: Teams that fear conflict often fall into groupthink (psychological phenomenon where a cohesive group prioritizes harmony and consensus over critical thinking and realistic decision-making), suppress dissent (actively prevent or silence disagreement, criticism, or opposition), or make poor decisions. 14
Managing Conflict – How?

This asks “what’s really causing this?” and tackles that. It takes longer, but the problem doesn’t come back, which is why confronting isn’t the same as being aggressive. Compromising : both sides give something up to reach a middle ground. Quick, but nobody gets what they needed. These two feel peaceful, but the cause stays there and tends to return bigger. Withdrawal can buy time when emotions are high. Smoothing can suit minor issues, or when the relationship matters more than the point. Each side’s view contributes something, so you may end up with a better answer than either started with. Collaborating takes time, so save it for decisions that matter. Sometimes there’s no time to discuss, like during an outage. Forcing gets a quick decision, but people who were overruled won’t feel committed, so use it rarely. Define the real/root problem 2. Analyze the problem 3. Identify Solutions 4. Pick a Solution 5. Implement a solution 6. Review the solution, and confirm that it solved the problem 15

Commitment

Ever left a meeting and found that everyone understood something different? Commitment fails that way, so a decision needs to be both understood and accepted. A simple habit fixes most of this: end each discussion by stating what’s been decided and who does what next. Without that clarity , people act on their own assumptions. People can accept a decision they argued against, as long as they feel it was fair and their view was heard. That’s why buy-in comes after debate rather than instead of it. Waiting for everyone to agree can freeze a team. Great teams argue, decide, and then back the decision (“disagree and commit”). A common trap: “commitment requires everyone to agree” is false, because buy-in does not require consensus . CuB : Clarity, Buy-in. Achieving Commitment • Commitment requires clarity & buy-in: • Clarity ensures everyone knows exactly what was decided, why it matters, and what’s expected next. • Buy-in means team members support the decision—even if they didn’t fully agree—because they trust the process and feel heard. • Clarity requires that teams avoid assumptions and ambiguity, and end discussions with a clear understanding about what they’ve decided upon. • Buy-in does not require consensus. Members of great teams learn to disagree with one another and still commit to a decision. 17

A chief-programmer team carries high project risk because the project fails if both the chief and the deputy are unavailable. Problems • This chief programmer approach, in different forms, has undoubtedly been successful • However, it suffers from a number of problems • Talented designers and programmers are hard to find. Without exceptional people in these roles, the approach will fail • Other group members may resent the chief programmer taking the credit for success so may deliberately undermine his/her role. • High project risk as the project will fail if both the chief and deputy programmer are unavailable • Organizational structures and grades may be unable to accommodate this type of group 32
Team Models

Distance from the main organization removes interruptions and rules, and the team feels the result is really theirs. That’s the appeal of skunk works , and the reason for high ownership . If they’re off on their own, nobody can easily tell how it’s going. Fine for exploring a new idea, but a narrow, well-defined job doesn’t need this freedom, and little visibility would just be a risk. Compare the two: skunk works is about freedom to explore, while SWAT is about precise skills for a known goal. They already work well together, so they can be dropped into a problem and start immediately. A team of database experts is brought in to fix Oracle performance problems. This is a: A company sends a few creative developers off-site to explore a new product idea with little reporting. This is a: Team Models • Skunk works Team • Put a bunch of talented, creative developers away from the mother ship • Off-site literally or figuratively • Pro: Creates high ownership & buy-in • Con: Little visibility into team progress • Applicable: exploratory projects needing creativity • Not on well-defined or narrow problem • SWAT Team • Highly skilled team • Skills tightly match goal • Members often work together • Ex: security swat team, Oracle performance team 33
Team Models

In large teams communication paths grow with roughly the square of the team size. The exact formula is n(n − 1) / 2 : 50 people → 1,225 paths (the slide rounds to 1,200); 7 people → 21. With that many paths, informal chat can’t keep everybody informed. A hierarchy reduces the paths, since people talk within small groups and leads talk to each other. Why so small? In a small team, everyone knows what’s going on and feels their work matters, and that’s what builds cohesiveness . The other roles sit around this core so it stays small. Calculate the number of communication channels for a project team of 7 members. Your team grows from 5 to 10 people. By how much do the communication channels increase? Notice that “using available people” is a real limit: you rarely get to choose your ideal team. And motivating comes up here because a plan only happens if people want to do it. Plans and estimates can look purely technical, but “how fast” depends on who’s doing it. The same task can take one developer a day and another a week, so estimating is about people too. Controlling doesn’t mean micromanaging; it means knowing whether the work is on track. Organizing is about who works with whom and how, which shapes how well they do. Motivation

Needs-based means that to motivate someone, you first ask what they’re lacking. The same reward can motivate one person and do nothing for another whose need is different. Think of the groups as moving outward: staying alive, feeling valued, then belonging. A manager has most influence on personal and social needs, since those arise at work. Maslow’s hierarchy : physiological → safety → social → esteem → self-realization (self-actualization). Maslow from the bottom up, where the order matters: P lease S tudents, S tudy E very S ession. Motivating people

A paying job with a safe office usually covers the basics. So a manager can start higher up, which is why physiological and safety needs aren’t the usual focus. Once the basics are covered, what makes people try harder is belonging, feeling respected and growing. These are the needs a manager can really act on, so social, esteem and self-realization matter most. But if a lower need stays unmet for a long time (e.g. job security during layoffs), people shift focus downwards to it until it is satisfied again, and higher motivators stop working. During layoffs, recognition stops motivating someone who fears for their job. Why? Motivating people • People’s Motivations depend on satisfying needs • It can be assumed that physiological and safety needs are satisfied • Social, esteem and self-realization (self-actualization) needs are most significant from a managerial viewpoint • If a lower set of needs is continually unmet for an extended period of time, the individual will temporarily shift focus downwards those needs – dropping down to that level until those lower needs are reasonably satisfied again. 39
Need satisfaction

People work better with colleagues they know. Break rooms and casual chats look like wasted time, but they’re how social needs get met and how information spreads. People want to feel their effort was noticed. A specific “thank you” in front of the team can matter as much as a bonus, so recognition doesn’t have to be expensive. Here people want to grow and be trusted. So training and real responsibility motivate strong staff, while doing the same simple task for years drives them away. Your team has just completed a major milestone in the project development process. How would you celebrate this achievement collaboratively with your team members? How would you recognize individual contributions to the team’s success? What actions would you take to ensure that team morale remains high as you move forward in the project? Sending a developer on a cloud-architecture course mainly satisfies which need? Need satisfaction • Social • Provide communal facilities (shared spaces, break rooms, collaborative zones, etc.) • Allow informal communications (support casual conversations, team chats, non- work-related exchanges such as during lunch, etc.) • Esteem • Recognition of achievements • Appropriate rewards (bonuses, promotions, certificates, symbolic gestures, etc.) • Self-realization • Training – people want to learn more • Responsibility (empower team members to make decisions) 40
Personality types

Maslow suggests everybody wants the same things in the same order, and real people aren’t like that. Two teammates at the same level can want very different things, hence personality type . Task-oriented : the motivation is the work itself (they love solving the problem). The same project might be a means to a promotion or to buying a house. Self-oriented isn’t a criticism, but it tells you these people respond to personal benefit. For them, an isolated task with no contact is demotivating, even if it’s interesting. Interaction-oriented people keep a team talking, and that has real value. SIT : Self-oriented, Interaction-oriented, Task-oriented. A developer works mainly to save for a house. This personality type is: Personality types • The needs hierarchy is almost certainly an over-simplification • Motivation should also take into account different personality types: • Task-oriented • The motivation for doing the work is the work itself • Self-oriented • The work is a means to an end which is the achievement of individual goals – e.g. to get rich, to buy a house, to travel etc. • Interaction-oriented • The principal motivation is the presence and actions of co-workers. • People go to work because they like to go to work 41
Motivation balance

Real people have elements of each class , and the balance changes with personal circumstances (a new baby makes someone more self-oriented for a while). Even someone working mainly for money may stay because they like the team. So building a good group and culture is a motivation tool that doesn’t cost much. A new parent becomes more focused on income for a while. What does this show? Motivation balance • Individual motivations are made up of elements of each class (from previous slide). • Balance can change depending on personal circumstances and external events • However, people are not just motivated by personal factors but also by being part of a group and culture. • People go to work also because they are motivated by the people that they work with 42
Group composition: group working

Real software is too big for one person, however talented. Working out how people fit together is therefore central, because this is a group activity by necessity. Group interaction is a key determinant of performance, so how the group works together matters as much as individual skill. You rarely get to hand-pick a dream team, so plan around who you actually have. That’s why group composition is listed as limited: adapt the work to people’s strengths. Why can’t a manager just choose the ideal group? Group composition: group working • Most software engineering is a group activity • The development schedule for most non-trivial software projects is such that they cannot be completed by one person working alone • Group interaction is a key determinant of group performance • Flexibility in group composition is limited • Managers must do the best they can with available people 43
Time distribution

About 50% of an engineer’s time is spent interacting with other people (meetings, reviews, discussions), so communication skills matter far more than people expect. Don’t plan a person’s time as if they code all day. With only 30% alone, an estimate that assumes eight hours of solo work will be far too optimistic. Group composition

Mixing types is deliberate. People with identical motivations tend to clash or leave gaps, just like a team of only goalkeepers, which is why having the same motivation is a problem. Each extreme has a weakness on its own: nobody coordinates, everybody competes, or nobody finishes. That’s why you look at the mix, not only at individuals: task , self , interaction . Since most engineers enjoy the work itself, you’ll often lack people who keep communication going. So value the interaction-oriented member, even if they write less code. A team where “everyone wants to be the boss” is dominated by which personality type? Group composition • Group composed of members who share the same motivation can be problematic: • Task-oriented – everyone wants to do their own thing • Self-oriented – everyone wants to be the boss • Interaction-oriented – too much chatting, not enough work • An effective group has a balance of all types • Can be difficult to achieve because most engineers are task-oriented 45
Group composition: group leadership

A manager with a title can be ignored in practice if nobody respects them, while a respected senior developer gets followed. So respect is what actually makes a leader. Good engineers aren’t always good at budgets and reports, and vice versa. Splitting the role into technical and administrative leaders lets each person do what they’re good at. Skilled people often know more than their manager about the problem. Letting them contribute to decisions gets better answers and more commitment. That’s why democratic leadership works in software. Support a technical career path so good engineers don’t have to become managers to progress. Why might a group have both a technical and an administrative leader? What does leadership depend on, according to the slide? Group cohesiveness

When people care about the group, they help each other and protect its standards, rather than only their own task. That’s what cohesive means in practice. Standards the group sets for itself get followed, while rules imposed from outside are often dodged. Working closely also means people quickly learn what they don’t know, rather than hiding it, which is how ignorance shrinks. If only one person understands a module, you have a risk. When people learn from each other , the team can cope with someone being away. Egoless programming : members try to improve each other’s programs and don’t treat code as personal property. In a cohesive team, which of the following is an advantage? Developing cohesiveness

You can’t simply order people to bond. A blaming organizational culture works against it, and some personalities need more time, so treat it as something to encourage. A shared name or space sounds trivial, but it gives people something to belong to. Group identity is what turns individuals into “us”. Openness with information is the simplest tool: when everyone knows what is going on, everyone feels part of the group. Which is the simplest way to help everyone feel part of the group? A team picks a name and has its own space. What’s being developed? Group loyalties

A close team defends its members, which helps morale. But loyalty can also stop people from speaking up when the group is wrong. Groupthink : preserving the group regardless of technical or organizational considerations (defending a bad design because the group made it). A team can’t easily see its own blind spots, so bring in someone who isn’t invested. That’s what external involvement does: outsiders can ask the awkward questions. If one developer changes a design and nobody hears about it, others build on something that no longer exists. So status and design decisions must be shared, and sharing them also makes people feel included. Juniors may have the answer but stay quiet. A good PM deliberately asks them first, so the status of a senior person doesn’t shut the discussion down. If everyone is quiet, nothing gets raised, and if everyone is dominant, nobody listens. More people mean many more communication paths, so past a certain size you spend more time coordinating than working. That’s why you break big projects down instead. A developer who doesn’t understand banking can write clean code that does the wrong thing. That’s why application domain knowledge often matters more than knowing a specific language. Technology also changes constantly, so communication and adaptability can outlast any one technical skill. You can’t measure these from a CV, so they’re hard to judge, but a bad fit can harm a whole team. There’s no ideal “programmer personality ”; what matters is whether they fit this team. Culture problems can kill a project just as a technical flaw can, and yet nobody tracks them. Treat team culture as you would technical issues : look for it, discuss it and fix it. A role that seems fine on day one may turn out badly, and people rarely volunteer that they’re unhappy. Keep asking about satisfaction , especially during launch , when a change costs almost nothing. Don’t assume a job title means someone can do the task. A role mismatch shows up late as missed dates, and checking early is much cheaper than finding out after the schedule has slipped. You won’t find team mood in a report. Watch how people talk in meetings. Your behavior sets the tone too, so the cultural climate responds to your own example. When is it easiest to change someone’s role? What can a role mismatch lead to? Project Culture • Monitor team members’ satisfaction with their role. • You will need to monitor team role satisfaction throughout the project. • It is especially important during project launch when roles can be changed easily. • Monitor the engineering task-to-people fit to make sure each person can perform the engineering task. • Role mismatches lead to project problems and schedule slip. • If you don’t review task-to-people fit, you will be unaware of each person’s ability, or lack thereof, to perform tasks. • Monitor the cultural climate of the team as a whole. • Monitor project culture by watching and listening to each team member. • Guide the cultural views of the project by your own example. • You need to be able to monitor the team culture throughout the project in order to build confident people and a confident team. 65
Managing People

A project rarely fails because the technology was impossible. It’s more often poor communication or a team that doesn’t work together, and that’s what sociological means here. Peopleware (DeMarco and Lister) is the recommended optional reading on managing people. Promoted engineers tend to treat people as a puzzle with a correct answer. But people aren’t logical systems, so one person’s idiosyncrasies , like needing quiet, can decide whether they do great work. According to the slide, what are the main problems in our work? Managing People • The main problems of our work are not so much technological as sociological in nature • (optional reading) One of the most enlightened sources for information about managing people is: Peopleware: Productive Projects and Teams, Third Edition, • Most technical managers come from technical backgrounds and manage that way as if they are solving an engineering problem • Most managers do not consider individual idiosyncrasies (personal strange habit), yet these can make or break a project 66
Managing People

Gain visibility without micromanagement : know the status through boards and reviews, not by watching over shoulders. Criticizing someone’s ability makes them defensive, and they stop listening. Discussing the process puts everyone on the same side against the problem, as the slide’s two sentences show. Tricking or pressuring people may work once, but it destroys trust. Coordinate by explaining why, and if someone’s effort is going to the wrong place, redirect it rather than discouraging them altogether. People notice when you’re protecting your position rather than helping. When your attention is on what the project and team need, they respect you without being told to. That’s why you focus on needs . Which statement follows the guideline “review process and products, not people”? Managing People Guidelines for Managing People: • Gain visibility without micromanagement. • Review process and products, not people. • Say: “This testing regime allows too many bugs to slip through to the customer; what can we do to correct this?” • Not: “You all don’t seem to know how to write unit tests properly.” • Coordinate, don’t manipulate. • Use your knowledge, not your position of power. • Channel people, don’t put dams in front of them. • Redirect misplaced energy or effort, don’t cut it off • Focus on project and people needs, not your authority as manager. • This will maintain your leadership role without explicit effort 67
production line efficiency

Factory methods assume that identical work gets repeated. Software is different each time, so applying production-line thinking to it causes the errors listed below. On a line, an error is a defect, while in design it’s often how you learn. Someone staring out a window may be solving your hardest problem, so treating that as goofing off drives out your best thinking. A new person takes months to reach full speed, so people aren’t interchangeable like machine parts. Plans that assume a smooth steady state ignore the expensive start and end of work. Strict rules suit repeated tasks, but software keeps meeting new problems. If trying something new isn’t allowed, you won’t find better ways, so eliminating experimentation is harmful. A manager treats a developer thinking at their desk as “goofing off”. What’s the error? Why is treating workers as interchangeable an error? How NOT to manage ‘thought workers’: production line efficiency • The application of production line efﬁciency principles to thought workers can be a sign of disaster for a project • Common errors include: • Squeeze out error – make the ‘machine’ run as smoothly as possible • Take a hard line about people goofing off on the job (Assuming that any non- visible output equals laziness: creative people need time to reflect) • Treat workers as interchangeable pieces of the machine • Optimize the steady state – don’t worry about start up and shut down • Standardize procedure – run by the book (rigid processes) • Eliminate experimentation (Discouraging trial-and-error or creative risk-taking) • Consider how each of these errors might impact your own work 68
Making People Better

It’s usually the first thing dropped under pressure, unless it’s a stated goal. Treating professional development like any other goal means time and money get set aside for it. You need both. Short-term learning helps this project now, while long-term learning keeps people growing, and it’s a large part of why good staff stay. People work harder at goals they chose. A competency framework just gives them a useful list to pick from, so that “improve” turns into something specific. Most people don’t know where their time really goes, and the results often surprise them. It only helps if it’s safe, so stress that this is for their own awareness , not for monitoring. A team tracks its time in detail for a few weeks. What is the purpose? A short-term development goal focuses on: Making People Better • Make professional development a project goal • Recognize long- and short-term development goals • Short-term goals focus on skills needed for the project • Long-term goals prepare team members for future projects • Let each team member specify personal improvement goals • Starting point: Competency framework goals such as: Technical, leadership, domain, general/personal, communication, and management • For a ﬁxed interval, have team members track their individual time expenditure in detail • This concept goes well beyond the weekly timesheet concept • This is an awareness-building activity, not a monitoring activity • The Personal Software Process (PSP) is a formal application of this idea 69
Making People Better

A weekly timesheet is too rough to teach you anything. Tracking daily gives a developer real evidence, such as how long testing actually takes compared with what they guessed. With your own numbers, your next estimate gets better, and you stop promising what you can’t deliver. That’s how the PSP helps developers make commitments they can meet . What is one thing the PSP shows developers how to do? Leadership

Having a title doesn’t get a group to solve hard problems. Mobilize is the key word: people have to want to take it on, so it’s wrong to equate leadership with authority. If the problem has a known fix, the team just needs someone who knows it. Technical leadership is direct and efficient, and asking “what do you all think?” would just waste time. If nobody knows the answer, a leader giving orders is only guessing. Adaptive leadership helps the group learn its way there, and good questions do more than instructions. When people are exploring, it’s easy to drift. A clarity of purpose gives everyone a reason to keep going without a clear path, and lets the leader pull a discussion back. A novel problem has no known solution. Which leadership is needed? Leadership is mainly a matter of having authority. Leadership • Leadership is the capacity to mobilize a group to solve the most challenging problems (wrong to think that leadership is about authority) • Two types of leadership: • Technical leadership (a.k.a. authority) motivates people when the problem can be solved by known means: the leader directs, instructs and applies best practices. • Adaptive leadership motivates people to solve problems that cannot be solved by known means (needed when the problem is complex or novel) • Requires learning on the part of the leader as well as the group (facilitate learning and research) • Often involves leading with good questions (provoke thinking, guide inquiry) • Requires a deep clarity of purpose (to keep the team anchored toward its goals) : Example: during brainstorming meetings, the leader is the one that needs to stop the conversation from diverging to unimportant arguments, problems and bring the discussion back to the essential questions. 71
Technical vs. adaptive leadership

Ask first: does anyone know how to solve this? The answer decides which approach fits, and using the wrong one either wastes time or gives false confidence. Technical says “here’s what I see for us”, and it works because they know the way. Adaptive doesn’t have that map, so it uses a sense of purpose : why it’s worth working through. Tool for motivation : technical relies on personality : charisma, expertise, confidence, decisiveness. Adaptive relies on progress : learning, iteration and visible movement toward clarity. In short: technical = “follow me, I know”; adaptive = “let’s figure it out together.” How can a project manager balance technical leadership with adaptive leadership in a software team? Technical vs. adaptive leadership Technical leadership Adaptive Leadership Approach Technically-oriented: solves problems Adaptive: approaches problems not solved to problem- by known means by known means solving Vision: personal view of outcome. The Sense of purpose: big-picture view of goals: Motivation leader’s personal vision drives the team The leader anchors the team in shared meaning driver —“Here’s what I see for us.” —“Why does this matter?” Personality: Charisma, technical Tool for Progress: Motivation comes from learning, expertise, confidence, and decisiveness motivation iteration, and visible movement toward clarity. inspire trust and action. 72
Technical vs. adaptive leadership

Neither style is always better, so diagnose first. Fixing a known bug doesn’t need a discussion, and a brand-new product can’t be directed by a checklist. Known means is the deciding question. One project contains both: routine deployment work and a new algorithm nobody’s tried. So a PM has to switch between them, which is why a mix matters. A leader doesn’t need to handle everything personally. Delegation lets the person who knows the answer lead that part, which frees the leader to work on the problems nobody has solved. An adaptive leader should personally solve all known technical problems. Technical vs. adaptive leadership • Need to be aware of which kind of leadership is needed and choose between technical leadership and adaptive leadership for a project based on whether the problem can be solved by known means or not. • Most IT projects have a mix of known and unknown problems. • An adaptive leader can address known problems by delegation–allow one who can lead the team in solving the problem by known means do so when appropriate 73
Working toward consensus

Exam trap: consensus doesn’t require full agreement. People can accept a decision they’d have made differently if they feel they had a fair hearing. That’s why it’s about being heard . On a five-person team, a 3–2 vote leaves two people who may quietly stop trying, and you need all five. That’s why majority rule can do harm, even though it seems fair. Everyone being heard doesn’t mean every argument is good. The leader should strengthen the good points and gently remove the bad ones, because they must curate what the decision rests on. Share an experience from a software project you were involved in where collaboration among team members significantly contributed to its success. Describe the specific strategies or techniques you employed to foster collaboration. Working toward consensus • Consensus simply means ‘general agreement: But in the context of project teams, consensus doesn’t mean everyone agrees—it means everyone feels heard, and the group can move forward with a shared commitment. • If possible, reach consensus on all decisions affecting the team • Simple majority rule can be detrimental on a small team in which everyone’s commitment is essential • To reach that point, leaders must curate the quality of discourse: Valid argument need to be highlighted, invalid arguments need to constructively disqualified to protect decision quality: • Example: In a product design debate, a team member cites user data to support a feature. The leader highlights this as a valuable contribution, reinforcing data-driven thinking. 74
Working toward consensus

Don’t start with solutions: agree on the problem first, and collect options before anybody defends one. The order is what keeps the discussion from turning into a contest. People who were simply overruled will resist later. Spending time to persuade now costs less than dealing with resistance during delivery, which is why the extra time pays off. Beware passive-aggressive agreement : people who say yes but don’t act on it. It is just hidden (subsumed) conflict. The order matters here: P lease S it D own, W e C onfirm. Pose the problem, Solicit input, Discuss pros and cons, Work toward the best options, Confirm the choice. You are leading a cross-functional team tasked with selecting a continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) platform for an upcoming project. The team includes software developers, DevOps engineers, and QA testers, each with distinct expectations regarding automation workflows and pipeline management. Describe your approach to collaboratively choosing the most suitable CI/CD platform. Working toward consensus • Steps to reaching consensus: • Pose the problem to be solved or decision to be made • Solicit input on options for the problem or decision • Discuss and weigh pros and cons of each option • Work toward the options that have the most benefit for the project • When it is clear which option is most suitable, work with its opponents to help them buy in to it–persuade, don’t dictate • Consensus takes more time than mandate, but has huge pay-offs • Beware passive/aggressive agreement–this is simply subsumed conflict 75
Leading People

The same habits that build trust are how you lead day to day. If a question mixes these slides, the answer is the same, as this is a reprise . A nervous leader makes a team nervous. Be confident , without pretending you can do it alone, and you’ll get more from people who feel their talents are being used. A good relationship helps, but a friend may avoid saying hard things. You must sometimes give tough feedback, and that needs boundaries , even with people you like. Why does a PM need to use all the team’s talents? Leading People This is a reprise of our view of establishing a basis of trust • Be confident in yourself and the team • Maintain open communication within the project team– communication barriers create project risks • Be fallible. Take responsibility for making mistakes, correct them, and make it clear how you plan to avoid these mistakes in the future • Lead by example rather than by mandate. Show the team what you expect from yourself and from them • Utilize all the talents of your team. You can’t make the project succeed all by yourself • Complete all your commitments on time. If you cannot do so, give adequate notice and an explanation, not an excuse • Don’t confuse friendship with leadership: Warmth and connection are vital—but leadership requires clarity, boundaries, and accountability 76
Key points

Asking for what people can’t realistically do leads to burnout and resignations. Knowing the human factors tells you what’s reasonable to demand. A good exam summary of slide 53. Domain experience and adaptability often count for more than knowing a specific language. The reason is communication paths: small groups share information easily. Status matters because juniors may stay quiet, even when they’re right. Don’t wait for a culture problem to show up as a missed deadline. If you monitor early, you can act while it’s still cheap to fix. Your environment also affects output every day. Why do managers need to understand human factors? Key points • Managers must have some understanding of human factors to avoid making unrealistic demands on people • Staff selection factors include education, domain experience, adaptability and personality • Software development groups should be small and cohesive • Group communications are affected by status, group size and the group composition and organization • The working environment has a significant effect on productivity • Develop methods to monitor the project culture and technical status early so you can continually monitor these issues as the project progresses. 77

Methodology Concepts

A process is what actually gets done to produce something. Writing and reviewing a requirements document is a process: it’s the real work, not a description of it. A model is a general shape, like a recipe type: “iterative” tells you the idea without saying how your company does it. That’s why it’s called an abstract description . A methodology is the model made specific, with your team’s rules, roles and habits. So Scrum at your company is a methodology, while “iterative” is the model behind it. Waterfall, iterative and spiral are examples of: Methodology Concepts • Process • A collection of work activities, actions and tasks that are performed when some work product is to be created • Process Model or Life Cycle • An abstract description of a software process that presents one view of that process • Waterfall, Iterative, Spiral, Evolutionary, etc. • Process Methodology or Methodology • Instantiations of process models – tend to be prescriptive. • The conventions that a group agrees to – “How we work around here” 5
What a Methodology Addresses?

If a new hire can’t find out how things work, they’re slow for months. A methodology writes down how work is done, so new people ramp up faster, and a replacement can step in. Managers need to know how a project is doing without guessing. Visibility means status is easy to see and accurate, so problems get noticed while they can still be fixed. A new developer learns how the team works from its documented method. What does this help with? What does McConnell mean by visibility? What a Methodology Addresses? • Introducing new people to the process • Substituting people • Delineating responsibilities • Demonstrating visible progress • McConnell’s definition for visibility: “The ease & accuracy with which it is possible to assess the status of a project’s cost, schedule, functionality, or other characteristic.” 6
Evaluating a Methodology

If one person leaves and work stops, the method is failing you. A good one makes roles clear enough that you can substitute someone without losing weeks… …its effect on the sales process (can you show clients a credible way of working?)… Too many rules slow people down and frustrate them, while too few cause chaos. This criterion asks you to judge that balance, or how much freedom people have… If each change means a long approval process, you can’t react when something shifts. How well you respond to change is one of the main differences between methods… Records of who approved what help if a dispute goes to court. A method’s paperwork can be annoying day to day and valuable when it protects the organization. Documented approvals later help a company in a legal dispute. Which criterion is this? Evaluating a Methodology • How rapidly you can substitute or train people. • How great an effect it has on the sales process. • How much freedom (or how constraining) it is to people on the project. • How fast it allows people to respond to changing situations. • How well it “protects” the organization – legally or from other damages. 7

You don’t need to memorize these as one list. The left set is about people: who does the work and what they know. The ten elements are easier to recall in those groups. This set is about the work itself: what order it’s done in, what comes out of it, and what counts as good enough. Slides 10–13 define each. Which is NOT one of the elements of a methodology? Elements of a Methodology • Teams • Process • Roles • Work Products • Skills • Milestones • Techniques • Standards • Activities • Quality 8

Elements of a Methodology

Think of your calendar: reviews and meetings count as activities in the methodology too, since they take real time and need planning. Activities alone don’t tell you the order. Process says what must be finished before something can start, such as code review before merging. A milestone isn’t work that takes time. It’s a moment you pass or don’t. That’s why “60% met” makes no sense: either the design was approved today or it wasn’t. MAP : Milestones, Activities, Process. Milestones mark an instant in time and are either fully met or not met. 10
Elements of a Methodology

Who works with whom affects speed and quality. Putting testers with developers gives different results from keeping them apart, so teams are a real design choice. A role is a job to be done, not a person, and one person may have several. Matching roles to personalities matters because someone who hates conflict may struggle as the negotiator. Giving someone a role they can’t do helps nobody. Listing skills per role tells you who needs training and who to hire. STaR : Skills, Teams, Roles. “How you group people and assign them to roles” defines: Role assignment may need to consider people’s personalities. Elements of a Methodology • Teams • how you group the people and how you assign people to roles. • Roles • the job descriptions of team members: project manager, requirements gatherer, tester, program designer, etc. Roles may need to consider the personalities of the people being assigned to those roles. • Skills • the skills team members should have in order to assume responsibility for their role on the project. 11
Elements of a Methodology

Ask “what does the next person need from me?”. The tester needs test specifications, and that hand-over is a product . If it’s poor, the next person’s work suffers. Two people can make the same product differently. Techniques are how the work is done, like modeling use cases, so a methodology can prescribe skills rather than only results. A technique is the method, and a tool is what helps you apply it. Use case modeling is a technique, while the diagram software is a tool. PuTT : Products, Techniques, Tools. Use cases handed from an analyst to a designer are an example of: Use case modeling is an example of a: Elements of a Methodology • Products • what each person or team hands to another person or team: use cases, class designs, test specifications, framework documentation, interface definitions, etc. • Techniques • the techniques the person uses in their work: requirement session facilitation, Java programming, use case modeling, etc. • Tools • what tools the people use in their jobs, either within a technique or to produce a deliverable according to the standard. 12
Elements of a Methodology

Why have rules on the work product? Everybody can read and combine each other’s work more easily. Notational standards are about how things are written, like which language or diagram style. Leaving some open allows projects to decide for themselves. Quality : which rules, issues or concerns are tracked for each deliverable or activity (e.g. code review required, test coverage). A team requires all code to be in Java. Which type of standard is this? Elements of a Methodology • Standards • what is permitted or not permitted in the work product. There are notational standards (which includes the programming language), management and decision standards, and project conventions. The methodology may leave certain standards open, to be determined on the project. • Quality • what rules, issues or concerns are to be tracked for each deliverable or activity. 13
IT project life cycles

A software project is more than coding: someone also handles contracts, budgets and approvals. So the PLC contains the development work, the SDLC , plus everything around it. The PLC targets project requirements (scope, time, cost, approvals); the SDLC targets product requirements (features, quality). A common trap: don’t swap them. A perfect product can still fail if nobody arranged the budget, and a well-run project can still build broken software. So you need both, because neither is enough alone . The two must line up. A PM who plans a release date without knowing how development works will set dates that can’t be met, which is why integrating them matters. The SDLC is directed toward achieving: IT project life cycles • IT projects have two concurrent life cycles: • Project life cycle (PLC) encompasses all activities of project, including the System/Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) • PLC is directed toward achieving project requirements • SDLC is directed toward achieving product requirements • Both life cycle models are needed to manage an IT project • PLC alone will not adequately address system development concerns • SDLC alone will not adequately address business and product integration concerns • Effective integration of the two life cycle models is essential to improving the likelihood of project success 14

Software Development Process

“We just start coding and fix things” is how many small projects begin. Ad hoc can work for tiny tools, but it falls apart as projects grow, since nothing is defined. These set out in advance what to do and when. Prescriptive doesn’t have to mean waterfall: evolutionary approaches are prescriptive too, and it’s the defined process that matters. Rather than a detailed plan up front, these expect to change course. Adaptive methods like lean and agile treat what you learn as the main input for planning. Code and fix belongs to which family? Plan-driven Methodology

Traditional doesn’t mean bad. Plan-driven comes from fields where you plan carefully because rework is very expensive… …such as building aircraft. It borrows from those fields’ way of thinking, which is why it’s rigorous : define it, measure it and improve it… …and when you’re a big customer, like the US Department of Defense , you want every contractor working the same way, so you can compare and control them… …which is why it values documents . They let different teams, even different companies, hand work to each other, and they leave a record to check. What does plan-driven development value? Plan-driven Methodology • The “traditional” way to develop software • Based on system engineering and quality disciplines (process improvement) • Standards developed from DoD & industry to make process fit a systems approach • Values well defined work products 17
Plan-driven Characteristics

If you run the same process twice, you want similar results. That’s what repeatability is for: being able to predict cost and date, which is exactly what big contracts demand. Writing everything down lets others take over and lets you check against it. An architecture up front avoids expensive redesign, provided requirements don’t change much. Everyone knows exactly what’s expected, which is valuable on very large teams, though it’s heavy for small ones. A process group exists just to keep that machine running. Because you’ve committed early, surprises are costly, so risk gets watched throughout. Verification asks “did we build it right?” and validation asks “did we build the right thing?”. What is the main aim of plan-driven processes? Plan-driven Characteristics • Focus on repeatability and predictability • Defined, standardized, and incrementally improving processes • Thorough documentation • A software system architecture defined up-front • Detailed plans, workflow, roles, responsibilities, and work product descriptions • Process group containing resources for specialists: process monitoring, controlling, and educating • On-going risk management • Focus on verification and validation 18
Sequential (‘waterfall’) methodology

It’s an irony worth remembering: the name most people use comes from a paper that warned against it. Royce is the only historical name you need here. He didn’t think testing only at the end was sensible for big systems. By then, fixing a design flaw is very expensive. So he called the pure version risk-prone . His idea was to go back and improve earlier stages using what you learn. So feedback loops are the part of his paper people forgot. Industry adopted its anti-form , the version without feedback loops. A common trap: “Royce recommended the pure waterfall” is false. Winston Royce’s 1970 paper presented the pure sequential waterfall as an ill-conceived, risk-prone practice. Sequential (‘waterfall’) methodology • The term waterfall was coined by Winston Royce in a 1970 paper titled Managing the Development of Large Software Systems, in the Proceedings of IEEE WESCON • The paper used the sequential waterfall approach as an example of an ill-conceived, risk-prone practice for developing large systems • Royce advocated a series of iterative feedback loops among the development stages, incrementally gaining learning value from working software • Instead of adopting the approach Royce advocated, managers and practitioners adopted its anti-form, without feedback loops 19
Waterfall SDLC

The idea is that you don’t start design until requirements are signed off. Finished deliverables keep control tight, but they also make later changes expensive. Each stage depends on the last: you can’t design what hasn’t been analyzed. Mind the order, and that testing comes near the end: that’s the main weakness. The order matters here: R eal A rchitects D raw, C onstruct, Q uality-check, D eploy. Requirements, Analysis, Design, Construction, Quality assurance, Deployment. What marks the end of each waterfall phase? Which phase comes right after Design in the slide’s waterfall? Waterfall SDLC • Each phase is marked by completion of Deliverables • The primary software project phases: • Requirements • Analysis • Design • Construction • Quality Assurance (aka Testing) • Deployment 20
Waterfall SDLC

Royce’s waterfall: plan → requirements → design → coding → testing, with dashed feedback loops back to the previous step. The note on the left says those loops were in Royce’s paper but have been ignored by managers and practitioners alike. On the right, a more detailed version (concept → requirements → architecture → detailed design → coding → testing → deployment). Either way, testing comes last, which is why problems are found late. What did Royce’s diagram include that people came to ignore? Waterfall SDLC 21
Waterfall system development model

Nothing is combined until late, so the first real proof the parts fit comes at the end. That’s when design flaws appear and are most expensive, hence late design breakage and late risk resolution . Adversarial stakeholder relationships (arguing over signed documents) and a focus on documents and reviews instead of working software. Why does it survive? It’s easy to explain and to contract for, and some projects suit it. Most organizations use a modified version , adding some iteration, rather than the pure form. Why does waterfall suffer from late design breakage? Why might stakeholders become adversarial in waterfall? Waterfall system development model • Highly-sequential process • Failure symptoms: • Protracted integration and late design breakage • Late risk resolution • Requirements-driven functional decomposition • Adversarial stakeholder relationships • Focus on documents and review meetings • Still followed (in name or practice) by many organizations, usually a modified version 22
Waterfall system development model

Every item is a form of “we already know what we’re doing”. If requirements and technology are both familiar, there’s little to discover, so a fixed plan works. If one is missing, sequential gets riskier. When there’s little to learn along the way, planning it all at the start is efficient. Conventional methods are the right call here, so don’t assume agile is always better. FALConS : Familiar technology, Adequate time, Low complexity, Clear requirements, Stable schedule. Given the evolving requirements (student usability, advisor requests, IT integration rules), which development approach (Agile, Waterfall, or Hybrid) would you recommend, and why would it be the best fit for this project? Which project suits a sequential (waterfall) SDLC? Waterfall system development model Sequential: suitable projects and management approaches • A sequential SDLC is suitable for projects with: • Clear, unambiguous, and stable user requirements • Familiar, proven technology • Low complexity • Adequate time • Stable schedule • A project meeting most of these criteria can use conventional project management practices, such a big, up-front planning and conventional risk assessment 23
Evolutionary methodologies

Waterfall needs you to know a lot before starting. Evolutionary approaches accept you don’t, so you begin with what you know and learn the rest by building. It is like a jigsaw puzzle : neither top-down nor bottom-up, but accretionary and convergent (pieces accumulate until the picture emerges). Each benefit comes from working in small pieces. Because you integrate often, you spot problems fast, and early working results, even a “Hello world!”, show the team that things connect. That’s continuous integration in practice. A problem is visible within a day, and teammates can help right away. That’s the value of daily meetings : short feedback, not status reporting to a boss. “Shippable” stops the team from piling up unfinished work to fix later. Each sprint’s increment really is complete, so you always have something you could release. Should a sprint get longer if work isn’t finished? Scrum and sprints • In Scrum, software is developed in sprints, which are fixed- length periods (2 - 4 weeks) in which software features are developed and delivered. • During a sprint, the team has daily meetings (Scrums) to review progress and to update the list of work items that are incomplete. • Sprints should produce a ‘shippable product increment’. This means that the developed software should be complete and ready to deploy. 61

The team pulls the most valuable items it believes it can finish. Because it’s chosen by the team, the sprint plan is more realistic than if someone else had set it. During the sprint the team develops and tests software, with a daily Scrum. A sprint’s result is seen by stakeholders in the review, and what they say feeds the next one. Key Scrum practices

The list changes constantly as you learn. Updating it before each sprint means the team always works on what’s most valuable right now. Fixing the time forces prioritizing: you can’t fit everything, so what’s important has to go first. That’s what makes a timebox powerful. They’re closest to the work, so they often decide best, and people commit to their own decisions. Consensus also spreads knowledge across the team. STeP : Self-organizing teams, Timeboxed sprints, Product backlog. How do self-organizing teams make decisions? Key Scrum practices • Product backlog This is a to-do list of items to be implemented that is reviewed and updated before each sprint. • Timeboxed sprints Fixed-time (2-4 week) periods in which items from the product backlog are implemented, • Self-organizing teams Self-organizing teams make their own decisions and work by discussing issues and making decisions by consensus. 63
Product backlogs

If it’s not on the list, it doesn’t get done. This gives one place to see all remaining work, so the product backlog is what gets prioritized and discussed. A PBI is just the name for a single entry. You’ll see the short form in exam questions, so don’t be thrown by it. It’s not only features! Engineering work needs a place too, or it never gets scheduled. Keeping all varied work on one list forces honest trade-offs. Order matters, since the team always takes from the top. An always prioritized list means whoever is available starts on what’s most valuable next. Where should the next items to implement be in the backlog? A product backlog can include engineering improvements as well as features. Product backlogs • The product backlog is a list of what needs to be done to complete the development of the product. • The items on this list are called product backlog items (PBIs). • The product backlog may include a variety of different items such as product features to be implemented, user requests, essential development activities and desirable engineering improvements. • The product backlog should always be prioritized so that the items that be implemented first are at the top of the list. 64
Examples of Product Backlog Items

Notice the form: who wants it and what they want. A feature is written from the user’s point of view, so everyone can see who’s helped by it. This came directly from what users said they need. A user request may become a feature, but it starts as somebody’s stated need. No user will ever see this, and it’s still needed. Choosing which open-source software to rely on is a development activity that keeps the team able to build. Users won’t notice this directly either, but it protects them or keeps the system healthy. An engineering improvement is easy to neglect if it isn’t on the backlog. “Refactor user interface code to improve performance” is which kind of PBI? Examples of Product Backlog Items (PBIs) 1. As a teacher, I want to be able to configure the group of tools that are available to individual classes. (feature) 2. As a parent, I want to be able to view my children’s work and the assessments made by their teachers. (feature) 3. As a teacher of young children, I want a pictorial interface for children with limited reading ability. (user request) 4. Establish criteria for the assessment of open source software that might be used as a basis for parts of this system. (development activity) 5. Refactor user interface code to improve understandability and performance. (engineering improvement) 6. Implement encryption for all personal user data. (engineering improvement) 65
Product backlog item states

Don’t spend time detailing something that may never happen. At consideration , a line or two is enough, and dropping it costs nothing. Now it’s worth investing some thought, as you’ve decided it matters. Refinement answers the open questions, so that it can be built. The test for this state is whether the team could start tomorrow. If it’s possible to estimate it and nothing is blocking it, the item is ready. CRIb , already in order: Consideration, Refinement, Implementation. An item has a reasonably clear definition, but still needs work to understand it. Which state is it in? Product backlog item states • Ready for consideration These are high-level ideas and feature descriptions that will be considered for inclusion in the product. They are tentative so may radically change or may not be included in the final product. • Ready for refinement The team has agreed that this is an important item that should be implemented as part of the current development. There is a reasonably clear definition of what is required. However, work is needed to understand and refine the item. • Ready for implementation The PBI has enough detail for the team to estimate the effort involved and to implement the item. Dependencies on other items have been identified. 66

DevOps vs. Project Management

Traditional PM assumes a project starts and ends, while DevOps never really stops. That’s the apparent conflict: where’s the finish line, if it seems at odds with project management ? A Gantt chart assumes that you know the tasks and order well in advance. Timelines and milestones suit predictable work, and they’re harder to apply when everything keeps changing. The tools change, while the job remains: know what’s happening and help it go well. So PM can adapt by planning in short cycles. Each sprint’s output becomes the milestone, rather than one distant end date. So PMs plan incremental deliveries , which keeps the benefit of tracking without the fixed end. How can project management adapt to DevOps? DevOps vs. Project Management • Given the fluid nature of DevOps and its continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) process, the methodology may seem at odds with project management strategies that tend to follow timelines with a start and endpoint (waterfall style of PM). • These Project Management approaches (timelines, Gantt charts, milestones, deadlines, etc.) seem more closely aligned with traditional software delivery methods like the waterfall approach. • However, project management styles can adapt to fit the parameters of the DevOps pipeline (flexibility and rapid iteration): breaking work into sprints, focusing on iterative progress, and embracing change. • The key is to shift the focus away from the one final product and instead refactor the timeline to follow the agile approach of incremental deliveries at the end of each sprint. 80
What is DevOps project management?

It’s not choosing one over the other. DevOps project management keeps PM’s planning and tracking, adjusted to fit a continuous way of working. With so many people and tools, someone has to see the whole picture. A coordinator notices when one team’s delay will affect another, and clears the way. A PM who doesn’t understand how code gets built and released can’t spot problems or set sensible expectations. That’s why a deep understanding of development is needed here. What’s a key role for PMs in DevOps project management? What is DevOps project management? • DevOps project management is a union between the two disciplines where project management is tailored to and supports the DevOps model. • In a DevOps project management approach, project managers serve as coordinators between multiple contributors and as trackers of timelines and dependencies (ensure team members collaborate smoothly, removing bottlenecks and resolving conflicts) • However, project managers also need to be closely aligned with the DevOps team and bring a deep understanding of the development process and skills needed to create the end product. • There are several best practices that project managers should follow to achieve this integration with the DevOps pipeline. 81
