Perfect is the enemy of shipped. Immediate value is what to prioritize, since early feedback may change what “perfect” even means. Not a poor product, but the smallest useful one. On the five-point scale, “Likely” means: Quantifying risk probability • For most situations, use of a ﬁve-point Likert scale is appropriate: • Highly unlikely (p < 20%) • Unlikely (20% < p < 40%) • About even (40% < p < 60%) • Likely (60% < p < 80%) • Highly likely (p > 80%) • For less well-deﬁned situations, use a three-point scale: • High (p > 75%) • Moderate (35% < p < 75%) • Low (p < 35%) • Likert Scale: psychometric scale commonly used in surveys and questionnaires to measure people's attitudes, opinions, or perceptions. 44

If you remove the cause, the risk disappears. That’s why avoidance is the strongest response, but it can mean dropping something valuable. It’s cheapest early on, before work depends on that part. With a fixed price, the seller pays for any overrun, so expect them to raise their price to cover that risk. Here you pay whatever the work costs. Under a cost-reimbursable contract, most of the risk stays with: Strategies for negative risks or threats • Contracting • Contracting is a form of risk transfer • The contractor accepts certain aspects of the risk and responsibility for the cost of failure • Types of contracts: • Fixed-price contract: If costs exceed expectations, the contractor absorbs the loss. Contractor increases cost of the contract to compensate for the level of risk they are accepting. • Cost reimbursable contract: The contractor tracks and bills for direct costs and receives compensation for additional costs. Risk Mitigation, Monitoring, and Management

Mitigation tries to stop it, monitoring watches for warning signs, and management is your plan if it happens anyway. Together, RMMM answers before, during and after. MMM , all three start the same: Mitigation, Monitoring, Management. In RMMM, what does Monitoring ask? Strategies for negative risks or threats

You accept that the risk might still happen, but you make it less likely or less painful. Finding a problem through tests now is much cheaper than after release, which is why mitigation pays off. Sometimes a risk can’t reasonably be reduced. Passive acceptance means you’ll deal with it if it comes, while active acceptance sets money or time aside just in case. Running extra performance tests to lower the chance of a slow release is: Active acceptance means setting aside reserves of funds, time or resources. Strategies for negative risks or threats • Mitigation • Risk mitigation attempts to reduce the probability of a risk event and/or its impacts to an acceptable level • Risk mitigation takes the viewpoint that fixing a problem earlier in a project is less costly than fixing it later • Examples: Performing more tests, using simpler processes, perform simulations, choose vendors for reliability over cost • Risk acceptance • The risk is acknowledged, but no action is taken unless the risk occurs • Appropriate when it is not possible or cost-effective to address a speciﬁc risk in any other way • Passive acceptance simply documents that the acceptance strategy has been adopted and leaves the project team to deal with the risks • Active acceptance set aside risk reserves, such as a pool of funds, time, or resources to be used in response to a risk event 69
Strategies for negative risks or threats

Don’t confuse this with mitigation. A contingency plan doesn’t make the event any less likely. It’s just what you’ll do if it happens, which saves panic later. A data center may still fail, but a disaster recovery plan gets you running again. That’s a clear example of planning for after the event. What does a contingency plan do? Strategies for negative risks or threats • Risk contingency plans q • Contingency planning involves planning alternatives to deal with the risks, should they occur • Contingency plans do not seek to reduce the probability or impact of risks, the strategy accepts that the risk may occur and plans ways to respond to the risk • A contingency plan is executed when the risk event occurs • Contingency plans must be in place well before the time the risk may occur • Contingency plans are developed for risks: • With very high impact or: • With response strategies that may themselves be risky (require preparation) • Contingency plans usually entail a signiﬁcant alternative path through part of the project • Example: disaster recovery plan 70
Contingency planning tools

This is the time or money kept back to pay for a problem when it happens. A contingency allowance means you don’t have to find extra resources in a crisis. What if your response doesn’t work? A fallback plan is your Plan B, so it’s kept for serious risks where failure of the first plan would really hurt. What is a fallback plan? Contingency planning tools • Contingency allowances (or reserves): Contingency allowances provide a pool of funds, time, or resources that are held for use in response to an unavoidable risk event • Example: Including contingency time in case of loss of key personnel • Fallback plans: Fallback (or ‘Plan B’) plans are developed for risks with high impact or for risks with strategies that may in themselves be risky • Fallback plans may be used to address secondary risks • Example: Use of a relational database plus object-oriented interface (ORM) in place of pure O-O database. 71
Strategies for positive risks or opportunities

With a threat you hope it won’t happen, and with an opportunity you want it to. Exploitation makes it more certain by acting, while sharing brings in a partner who’s better placed to capture it. Strategies for positive risks or opportunities • Exploitation • Exploitation involves looking for opportunities for positive impacts • Example: Reduce project duration by using more experienced resources on critical tasks • Sharing • Sharing assigns opportunity to a third-party owner who is better able to exploit it • Example: Form a joint venture between a technical software company and marketing and sales firm 72

Residual risk is what’s left, so you decide whether it’s acceptable and keep a reserve to cover it. After hiring an expert consultant as a risk response, the consultant falls ill. This is a: Sidebar: Residual and secondary risks • Secondary risks arise as a result of implementing a risk response, they are the risks inherent in the response • Identify and plan responses for secondary risks using tools such as fallback plans • Example: O-O/RDB expert consultant becomes ill • Residual risks are those that cannot be effectively dealt with within the rest of the risk plan • Example: Some risk may remain. Estimation

Why are software estimates often off by so much? Estimation • Remember, an “exact estimate” is not possible • Estimate how long will it take you to get home from class today • On what basis did you do that? • Experience is useful • Likely as an “average” (based on historical data), probable estimation • For most software projects there is no such ‘average’ Most software estimations are off by 25-100% 5
Estimation: definitions

A target is what someone hopes for, and a commitment is what the team has actually checked it can do. Treating a wish as a promise is how impossible deadlines get born, so learn to say no. More work means more unknowns and more connections between them. So a small estimate may be quite close, while a very large one can be off by half. Uncertainty grows with size. A target date is one the team commits to after building a schedule. Estimation: definitions • Target vs. Committed Dates • Target: Proposed by business or marketing • Do not commit to this too soon! (Learn to say no and how to say it) • Committed: Team agrees to this (based on actual planning) • After you’ve developed a schedule • As project size increases, so does uncertainty: • Small projects (10-99 FPs), variance of 7% from post-requirements estimates • Medium (100-999 FPs), 22% variance • Large (1000-9999 FPs) 38% variance • Very large (> 10K FPs) 51% variance -> push back on target dates, understand that variance is normal 6
Cone of Uncertainty

Early estimates can be 0.25× to 4× the real value; the cone narrows as you learn. Ch 1.2, slide 40 : Estimates change as the project evolves At the feasibility stage, the cone of uncertainty says estimates may range from: Cone of Uncertainty • The upper curve represents the maximum possible overestimation. • The lower curve represents the maximum possible underestimation. • Over time, these curves converge toward 1x, meaning your estimate becomes more accurate and reliable. • Early estimates (e.g., during feasibility or proposal stages) can be wildly inaccurate — anywhere from 0.25x to 4x the actual scope. • As the project moves through requirements gathering, design, and development, uncertainty decreases 7

Estimation Methodologies • Expert Judgment: Relies on the experience and intuition of seasoned professionals. • Top-down: Starts with an overall project estimate, then breaks it down into components. Expert Judgment

Asking someone who’s done it before is fast and cheap. It’s only as good as their experience, though, so a guesstimate from someone whose last similar project was ten years ago may mislead you. What does expert judgment’s accuracy depend on? Expert Judgment • Use somebody who has recent experience on a similar project • You get a “guesstimate” • Accuracy depends on their ‘real’ expertise • Comparable application(s) must be accurately chosen 10
Top-down Estimation

You look at the whole project and judge it from similar size or type. It works early, when you don’t yet have the detail. The weakness is that hidden complexity in individual tasks gets missed, so it’s less accurate . When is top-down estimation especially useful? Top-down Estimation • Based on overall characteristics of project • Some of the others can be “types” of top-down (Analogy, Expert Judgment, and Algorithmic methods) • Advantages • Easy to calculate, quick and strategic • Effective early on (like initial cost estimates) • Disadvantages • Less accurate because may overlook complexity in individual tasks. 11
Bottom-up Estimation

You estimate each small task and add them up, which is why it needs a WBS . Detail improves accuracy, but it takes time, and the detail may not exist yet early on. Top-down = fast but rough (early). Bottom-up = slow but accurate (needs WBS). Which method requires a work breakdown structure and is the most granular? Bottom-up Estimation • Create WBS Work Breakdown Structure, identify individual tasks to be done. • Add from the bottom-up • Advantages • More accurate and granular. • Works well if activities well understood • Disadvantages • Specific activities not always known • More time consuming and depend on detailed information 12
Estimation by Analogy

If last year’s similar project took six months, that’s real evidence, not a guess. The catch is that no two are the same, so you must adjust for the differences. That’s where analogy gets hard. What is the main difficulty of estimating by analogy? Estimation by Analogy • Use past project • Must be sufficiently similar (technology, type, organization) • Find comparable attributes (ex: # of inputs/outputs) • Advantages • Based on actual historical data • Disadvantages • Difficulty ‘matching’ project types • Prior data may have been mis-measured • How to measure differences – no two exactly same 13
Priced to Win

Here the estimate starts from what will win the contract, not from the work. It can win the bid and still lead to overruns or cut corners. So priced to win isn’t really an estimate of effort at all. A vendor underbids to win and plans to raise the cost through change requests. What’s this called? What is the main risk of priced-to-win? Priced to Win 7 estimation outsoursed • The quote may not reflect actual costs or effort required. • Needs information on other estimates (or prices): To price competitively, vendors need access to market intelligence: previous bids, or client budget expectations (competitor pricing is not public). • Purshaser must closely watch trade-offs: Is the low price realistic? Will quality or scope suffer? • Priced to lose? some vendors may intentionally underbid to win the contract, knowing they’ll cut corners, request scope change later, absorb losses for strategic reasons (e.g., market entry) • Strength: Aligns with market expectations. • Risk: May undercut realistic effort, leading to overruns. 14
Algorithmic Measures

These give you a number to feed into a formula. LOC and function points are the two to know, and note the slide’s honest point: most projects don’t use any of these. Which are the most common algorithmic measures? Algorithmic Measures • Lines of Code (LOC) • Function points • Feature points or object points • Other possible • Number of bubbles on a DFD • Number of ERD entities • Number of processes on a structure chart • LOC and function points most common (of the algorithmic approaches) • Majority of projects use none of the above 15
Wideband Delphi

Starting independently stops one loud person from anchoring everybody. Each round shares reasoning without pressure, so hidden factors come out, and the group’s numbers move closer. This is the idea behind Wideband Delphi . It’s useful when you have no past data, since it relies on people’s knowledge. But if everyone shares the same blind spot, they’ll happily agree on the wrong number. Ch 5, slide 22 : Delphi technique for risk identification Wideband Delphi requires historical project data. Wideband Delphi • Group consensus approach • Rand Corp. used original Delphi approach in the 1940’s to estimate future projects • Present experts with a problem and response form: They fill out initial estimates independently. • Conduct group discussion, collect anonymous opinions, then share feedback: This helps surface hidden factors and clarify misunderstandings • Conduct another discussion & iterate until consensus • Advantages • Easy, inexpensive, utilizes expertise of several people • Does not require historical data • Disadvantages • Difficult to repeat • May fail to reach consensus, reach wrong one, or all may have same bias 16
Code-based Estimates

It’s easy to count finished code, but you can’t count code that doesn’t exist yet. And LOC rewards long code: 1,000 lines in one language may be 300 in another, so if people are paid by the line, you’ll get more lines. Why is LOC hard to use for early estimates? Developers are rewarded per line of code. What might happen? Code-based Estimates what • LOC Advantages nomatter Language • Commonly understood metric: intuitive and familiar to most developers and managers • Permits specific comparison • Actuals easily measured: Once code is written, LOC is straightforward to count • LOC Disadvantages • Difficult to estimate early in cycle (Before requirements and design are clear) • Counts vary by language and availability of reusable components and programmer style (avg. programmer productivity: 3,000 LOC/yr) • Many costs not considered (ex: requirements, UI design, etc) • Programmers may be rewarded based on this: If incentives are tied to LOC, developers may write more code than necessary, reducing efficiency and maintainability. • Code generators produce repeated code: Auto-generated code inflates LOC without reflecting actual developer effort, skewing estimates and metrics. 17
Function Points

This measures what the software does for users, rather than how it’s written. So it can be estimated earlier and compared across languages, which is the main advantage of function points over LOC. How do function points measure size? Function Points • Software size measured by number & complexity of functions it performs • More methodical than LOC counts • Four basic steps (next slide) 18
Function Point Process

First you count what the system does, then weight each thing for how hard it is. Then you adjust for the overall situation, such as performance demands. Order matters: count → weight → adjust . How many influence factors adjust the function point count? Function Point Process 1. Count # of business functions per category • Categories: outputs, inputs, db inquiries, files or data structures, and interfaces 2. Establish Complexity Factor for each and apply • Simple, Average, Complex • Set a weighting multiplier for each (0 –>15) • This results in the “unadjusted function-point total” 3. Compute an “influence multiplier” and apply • Based on 14 factors rated from 0 to 5 (such as performance requirements, data communications, transactions rates, reusability, etc) 4. Results in “function point total” • This can be used in comparative estimates 19
Effort Estimation

Size tells you how big it is, and effort tells you how much work that means. A skilled, motivated team needs less effort for the same size, which is why people factors are part of this conversion. Which model estimates effort from past project data? Effort Estimation g2 Man PowerBasically • Now that you know the “size” (function points, LOC, etc.), determine the “effort” needed to build it (in person-months or staff-months) • Various models: • Empirical: Based on historical data and past project performance • Mathematical: Uses formulas and algorithms, example: Effort = a × (Size)^b • Subjective: Relies on expert judgment and team intuition (Wideband Delphi) • Depends on Efficiency/productivity of people • Motivation • Ability of team • Application experience • Range of personnel 20
Duration

Effort is how much work there is, and duration is how long it takes on the calendar. Five people working one day is 5 person-days of effort but only one day of duration . Effort ≠ duration. Adding people can shorten duration but not effort. Five people review a document for 10 hours. Effort and duration are: Duration • What is the duration? The duration of a project is the elapsed time in business working days, not including weekends, holidays, or other nonworking days. • Duration is different from work effort. • Duration = Work Effort ÷ Number of People -> more useful in scheduling • Work Effort = Duration × Number of People -> more useful in cost estimation • Work effort is labor required to complete an activity. • E.g. five people reviewing a document; the duration may be 10 hours but the work effort is 50 staff-hours 21
Duration

Nobody works on a task for all eight hours of a day, with meetings and interruptions. So 40 hours of labor doesn’t mean one week, and treating labor time as clock time makes every schedule too short. A task needs 40 hours of labor, and productivity is about 75%. How long will it take on the clock? Duration • When we talk about estimates and duration, there are two types of time that are not the same: • Labor Time: actual effort required to complete a task (in staff-hours) • Clock time: elapsed calendar time needed to complete the task. • For example, if we estimate that a task would require 40 hours of labor to complete, then in a normal business setting we need at least 50 business hours, Why? • Productivity is usually 50-75% of a business day • a developer might only get 5–6 productive hours per day of 8 office hours (meetings, emails and communication, breaks and fatigue, tasks switching and setup, etc.) 22
Causes of Variation

An estimate assumes an average person on a normal day, and real days aren’t like that. Each cause is a way reality differs from that assumption, so variation is normal, not a failure. The causes, in slide order: V ery U nlucky E stimators M iss. Varying skill levels, Unexpected events, Efficiency of work time, Mistakes and misunderstandings. Which is a cause of variation in duration? Causes of Variation • Since we cannot know what factors will be effective when work is underway on an activity, we cannot know exactly how long it will take. • Causes of Variation in the Actual Activity Duration • Varying skill levels: Our estimate of the activity duration is based on average skilled engineer. We may get a higher or lower skilled engineer assigned to the activity, causing the actual duration to vary from the planned duration. • Unexpected events: Random natural events, vendor delays, power failures, etc. • Efficiency of work time: Every time a worker is interrupted it takes more time to get up to the level of productivity prior to the time of the interruption. These interruptions may have little or substantial impact on the worker's productivity • Mistakes and Misunderstandings: Even in organizations that have a documented process, rework may have its impact on the actual activity duration. 23
Estimation Issues

You need accurate numbers at the start, and you only get them at the end. Recording actual results helps because they make your next estimate better. That’s why past experience is the best basis. Precise estimation data only arrives at the end. Why record it anyway? Estimation Issues • Quality estimations needed early but information is limited • Precise estimation data available at end but not needed anymore • Or is it? What about the next project? • At the end of the project you should have determined just how accurate your original estimate was. • Best estimates are based on past experience • Politics of estimation: • You may anticipate a “cut” by upper management (so you add some contingency duration) • For many software projects there is little or no data for estimation • Technologies change • Historical data unavailable • Wide variance in project experiences/types • Subjective nature of software estimation 24
Over and Under Estimation

Both directions hurt. Too high and it won’t get funded, and any spare time gets filled anyway ( Parkinson’s law ). Too low and people cut corners, usually testing, and morale falls when dates keep slipping. “Work expands to fill the time available” is: Over and Under Estimation • Over estimation issues • The project will not be funded: Conservative estimates guaranteeing 100% success may mean funding probability closer to zero. • Parkinson's Law: Work expands to take the time allowed • Danger of feature and scope creep • Be aware of “double-padding”: project member + business manager • Under estimation issues • Quality issues (shorten key phases like testing) • Inability to meet deadlines • Morale and other team motivation issues 25

Introduction: Activity Duration Estimation

Those closest to the work know how long it really takes, so ask them. As you learn more, estimates improve, which is why they’re progressively elaborated , rather than fixed at the start. Who should provide duration estimates? Introduction: Activity Duration Estimation • Focuses on estimating the number of work periods needed to complete individual schedule activities • Estimates originate from person or groups most familiar with the type of work needed in the activity • Estimate is progressively elaborated: duration estimates are improved as project progresses • Activity duration output • Quantitative activity duration estimates, including range of possible values 30
Controlling factors in duration estimation

More people can lower productivity (Mythical Man-Month, Chapter 6.2). Ch 6.2, slide 56 : Mythical man-month Why might adding people not shorten a task proportionally? A useful rule of thumb

Mixing hours and days causes silly mistakes, like adding 2 days and 3 hours as 5. One unit throughout avoids this, and you convert only for the final presentation. What’s the rule of thumb for time units? A useful rule of thumb • Keep all times in the same units • Don't mix increments • Example: Schedule everything in hours, then convert to days and fractions as a last step • Note: Most PM software tools enforce this rule by using a uniform time unit and increment 32
Estimating tools

A buffer is time you added on purpose because something may go wrong. Slack is spare time that just happens to exist on a task not on the critical path. So one is planned protection, and the other results from the network. One single number hides how uncertain you are. Taking three and averaging builds in that range. This simple version treats all three equally. Ch 6.2, slide 34 : Slack time What’s the difference between buffer time and slack? Estimating tools To improve the accuracy and resilience of project schedules: • Reserve analysis: Contingency or time reserves can be added to schedule to allow for schedule risks (uncertainty) • Contingency reserves may be used or adjusted as more precise project information becomes available • Known as buffer time: Do not confuse with slack time. • Three-point estimation techniques use a mathematical combination of three different estimates: Most likely, Optimistic, and Pessimistic: • Basic: • Estimate = { M + O + P } / 3 : get an average of the three estimations 33

COnstructive COst Model (COCOMO)

It’s a formula built from data on many past projects, and that’s its strength. You give it a size and it gives you effort, so it’s only as reliable as that size estimate . Here’s the catch: you need to know the size early, which is exactly when you know least. So a confident-looking result can rest on a weak guess. The biggest weakness of COCOMO is that it: COnstructive COst Model (COCOMO) • COnstructive COst Model: An algorithmic software cost estimation model • Uses a basic regression formula with parameters that are derived from historical project data and current project characteristics: E = a(KLOC)b • Helps estimate person-months (effort) based on the size of the software: Input – LOC, Output - Person Months • Intermediate COCOMO Adjusts its estimates based on the type of application, size, and “Cost Drivers” • Cost drivers using High/Med/Low levels, include: • Motivation, Ability of team, Application experience, etc. • Biggest weakness? • Requires input of a product size estimate in LOC (needs to be reliable estimate of LOC) 38
Basic COCOMO – More Constants

The exponent b is above 1, which is the important part: doubling the code more than doubles the effort, as bigger projects carry more coordination. Don’t mix these up in an exam: a, b give effort, and c, d give time. Q2.4 · COCOMO organic, 32 KLOC: effort, time, staff Q2.5 · COCOMO organic, 20 KLOC: effort, time, productivity, staff Basic COCOMO – More Constants In COCOMO, projects are categorized to Basic COCOMO: one of three types: • Organic: Small , simple projects with experienced teams and flexible E = a(KLOC)b requirements. • Semi-Detached: Medium complexity, • E is the Effort in staff months mixed experience, some constraints. • a and b are coefficients to be determined • Embedded: Complex, creativity • KLOC is thousands of lines of needed, tightly coupled systems with code • a and b used for (calculate strict requirements (e.g., real-time or Effort from KLOC) safety-critical systems). • c and d used for (calculate Time from Effort) 39
Basic COCOMO – The Modes

Remember size isn’t the only thing that decides. A small project with severe constraints may still be embedded , because it’s the difficulty that drives effort. Note c = 2.5 for all three modes. a goes 2.4 → 3.0 → 3.6 (+0.6 each). d goes 0.38 → 0.35 → 0.32 (−0.03 each). c is always 2.5. hOSE , from small to large: Organic, Semi-detached, Embedded. Which COCOMO mode has a = 3.0 and b = 1.12? In Basic COCOMO, c = 2.5 for all three modes. Basic COCOMO – The Modes • Organic: 2 to 50 KLOC, small, stable, little innovation • Semi-detached: 50 to 300 KLOC, medium-sized, average abilities, medium time constraints • Embedded: > 300 KLOC, large project team, complex, innovative, severe constraints 40
Basic COCOMO – Example

Same amount of code and more than three times the effort. That’s what difficulty does, so picking the right mode matters as much as the size. For the same 200 KLOC, which mode needs the most effort? Time TDEV = c × E^d (months). Uses E, not KLOC. TDEV uses EFFORT (E) as input, not KLOC. What’s the input to the TDEV formula? Basic COCOMO – Development Time TDEV = c(E)d • TDEV is time for development • c and d are constants to be determined • E is the effort 42
Basic COCOMO – Example

Interesting: all three give ~29 months. Harder projects need more PEOPLE, not more time. The three modes all give about 29 months. What does this suggest? Basic COCOMO – Example • Suppose size is 200 KLOC TDEV = c(E)d • Organic • E = 626 staff months • TDEV is time for development • TDEV = 2.5(626)0.38= 29 months • Semi-Detached • E = 1,133 • TDEV = 2.5(1133)0.35= 29 months • Embedded • E = 2077 • TDEV = 2.5(2077)0.32= 29 months 43

Total work divided by time gives how many people you need on average. It’s a check on your plan: if it says 23 people and you have 5, the schedule isn’t realistic. E = 20 staff-months and TDEV = 8 months. How many staff on average? Intermediate COCOMO – Cost Drivers

Basic COCOMO only looks at size, yet a strong team on a familiar platform needs less effort. Cost drivers add these real-world factors, making the estimate more realistic. Why add cost drivers to COCOMO? Intermediate COCOMO – Cost Drivers • The basic COCOMO model assumes that the effort is only a function of the number of lines of code and some constants evaluated according to the different software systems. Each driver is a multiplier: above 1 adds effort, below 1 reduces it. Multiply them together to get C , then scale the basic effort by it. In Intermediate COCOMO the cost-driver multipliers are added together. COCOMO Advantages

Being based on real projects means it isn’t just opinion. Anyone using it with the same inputs gets the same answer, which makes it easy to explain and defend. That’s why repeatable counts for so much. Which is an advantage of COCOMO? COCOMO Advantages • Based on history • Repeatable • Unique adjustment factors • Has different modes • Works well on similar projects • Highly calibrated • Well-documented • Easy to use 50

Each item is something that affects real effort but isn’t in the formula. So treat its result as a starting point. And you must predict size first, which is hard early on. Which is a COCOMO limitation? COCOMO Limitations • Ignores requirements volatility • Ignores documentation • Ignores customer’s “skill” • Oversimplifies security • Ignores software safety • Ignores personnel turnover • Ignores many hardware issues • Personnel experience may be obsolete • Must know the cost drivers • Must be able to predict project size 51

Final Notes 52
Code Reuse and Estimation

Reuse looks free, but someone must still understand, adapt and test that code. Rewriting most of something is often just as hard as new code, which explains the 50% rule. NoRM : New, Reused, Modified. Code is 60% modified. How should it be estimated? About how much effort does reused code take, compared with new? Code Reuse and Estimation • Code reuse does not come for free (understanding the code, adapting, testing, integrating, etc.): consume time and effort. • Code types: New, Modified, Reused • If code is more than 50% modified, it’s “new”: estimated as if totally “new” • Reuse factors have wide range • Reused code takes 30% effort of new • Modified is 60% of new • Integration effort with reused code almost as expensive as with new code 53
Estimation for Agile

Agile doesn’t skip estimating. It estimates smaller things, closer to when they’re built, so each one is easier. Adding up tasks gives a total for the increment that’s easier to trust. How does agile estimation get a total? Estimation for Agile • Agile estimation starts with user stories or scenarios: Each user scenario is considered separately (as a mini-project) • The scenario is decomposed into a set of engineering tasks (UI, backend..) • Each task is estimated separately • May use historical data, empirical model, or experience • Scenario volume can be estimated (LOC, FP, use-case count, etc.) • Total scenario estimate computed • Sum estimates for each task • Translate volume estimate to effort using historical data or COCOMO • The effort estimates for all scenarios in the increment are summed to get an increment estimate 54
Know Your Deadlines

Before fighting for a date, ask why it exists. A legal deadline can’t move, so you’d cut scope, while a date someone just picked may be negotiable. That’s the difference between real and artificial . A contract requires delivery by year-end. What kind of deadline is this? Know Your Deadlines • Are they ‘Real Deadlines’? • Tied to an external event • Have to be met for project to be a success • Ex: end of financial year, contractual deadline, Y2K • Or ‘Artificial Deadlines’? • Set by arbitrary authority • May have some flexibility (if pushed) 55
Estimation Presentation (Communication)

“Six months” sounds like a promise. A range or a confidence level says what you really know, and it leads to better decisions. That’s why how you present it has so much impact. “July 1 with 50% probability” is which presentation technique? Estimation Presentation (Communication) • How you present the estimation can have huge impact • Techniques • Plus-or-minus qualifiers • 6 months +/-1 month -> Communicates a central estimate with a buffer • Ranges • 6-8 months • Risk Quantification • +/- with added information (more info about uncertainty) • Example: +1 month (if new tool not working as expected) • -2 weeks (if hiring new developers happens sooner) • Cases: offer scenario based estimates (if things go well … otherwise ….) • Best / Planned / Current / Worst cases • Coarse Dates : useful when finer estimates are not feasible • Q3 of 2026 • Confidence Factors • April 1 with 10% probability, July 1 with 50% probability, etc. 56
Final Estimates

Known risks get money the PM can use right away, and unforeseen ones need permission. That separation keeps both visible, rather than hiding extra padding in each task. Ch 1.2, slide 47 : Contingency vs. management reserves ARM , already in order: Aggregation, Risk analysis, Management reserves. Who controls contingency reserves in final estimates? How do you access management reserves? Final Estimates • For Time or Cost Estimates: • Aggregation into larger units (Work Packages, Control Accounts, etc.) • Perform Risk Analysis to calculate Contingency Reserves (Controlled by PM) • Add Management Reserves: Set aside to cover unforeseen risks or changes (Total company funds available – requires Change Control activities to access) 57
Estimation Guidelines

Early estimates are rough and later ones are better, so keep updating them. But changing plans too often is chaotic, which is why the slide asks you to balance. Iterative doesn’t mean constant. What does “estimate iteratively” mean? Estimation Guidelines • Estimate iteratively! • Process of gradual refinement • Make your best estimates at each planning stage • Refine estimates and adjust plans iteratively • Plans and decisions can be refined in response • Balance: too many revisions vs. too few 58

Slack Time

Slack is how much a task can slip without moving the end date. It’s worked out by comparing the latest and earliest finish. If there’s no spare time, any delay moves the whole project. So zero slack is how you recognize a critical task. Q4 · network diagram, ES/EF/LS/LF, slack, paths, minimum time Q4 · network diagram and minimum completion time Slack Time • Slack time, also known as float, is the amount of delay expressed in units of time that could be tolerated in the starting time or completion time of an activity without causing a delay in the completion of the project. • Slack time is the difference between the late finish and the early finish (LF-EF). If the result is greater than zero, then the activity has a range of time in which it can start and finish without delaying the project completion date. • If an activity has zero slack, it determines the project completion date. In other words, all the activities on the critical path must be done on their earliest schedule or the project completion date will suffer. • If an activity with total slack greater than zero was delayed beyond its late finish date, it becomes a critical path activity and causes the completion date to be delayed. • The sequence of activities that has zero slack is defined as the critical path • In general, the critical path is the path that has 0 slack. 34
Critical Path Method

A task can’t start until everything before it is done, which is why you take the largest incoming finish time. Going forward tells you the earliest date the project can end. Going back from the end, a task must finish before its earliest successor needs to start, so you take the smallest. This tells you how late each task may be, without delaying the end. Both are spare time, but they differ in who’s affected. Using free float bothers nobody, while using up total float can squeeze later tasks, though the end date holds. Forward = MAX of incoming EFs. Backward = MIN of outgoing LSs. Critical Chain Method

CPM assumes people are always available, which isn’t realistic. CCM asks “is the person actually free?”, so the longest chain may change once you consider resources. CPM ignores resources. CCM includes them. How does the Critical Chain Method improve on CPM? Critical Chain Method • The critical chain method (CCM) is a project management technique that is an improvement of the Critical Path Method as it takes into account the availability of resources. • In software engineering projects, CCM can be used to identify and manage critical tasks, reduce project risk, and improve project delivery time. • CCM focuses on the resources required for project activities, attempting to keep them leveled throughout the project • CCM, assumes that all activities have a statistically-probable range of durations and uses this assumption to create a more ﬂexible and resilient schedule • Resources are assigned to the activities using the most likely durations • The longest sequence of activities in the project is called the critical chain 42
Critical Chain Method

CCM example: mobile app, prototype due in month 4. Which project does the CCM example describe? Critical Chain Method • Suppose a software development team is tasked with developing a new mobile application. • The project timeline is six months, and the team must deliver a functional prototype at the end of the fourth month. • To manage the project using CCM, the following steps could be taken: 1. Identify the critical tasks: The team would begin by identifying the critical tasks that must be completed to deliver the functional prototype on time. These tasks might include developing the user interface, integrating with external APIs, and testing the application. 43
Critical Chain Method

Rather than padding each task, it collects spare time in one buffer at the end. People can’t quietly use it up on each task, so everyone can see how much protection is left. Where does CCM put its project buffer? Critical Chain Method 2. Estimate task duration: Once the critical tasks have been identified, the team would estimate the duration of each task, taking into account any potential delays or obstacles that might arise during the development process. 3. Create a buffer: To account for potential delays and risks, the team would create a buffer at the end of the project timeline. This buffer would be used to ensure that the functional prototype is delivered on time, even if some tasks take longer than expected. 4. Manage the critical chain: Using CCM, the team would manage the critical chain of tasks by focusing on the critical tasks and ensuring that they are completed on time. This might involve reallocating resources, adjusting task priorities, or providing additional support to team members as needed. 5. Monitor progress: Throughout the project, the team would monitor progress and adjust the project plan as needed. This would help to ensure that the project stays on track and that the critical tasks are completed on time. 44
Critical Chain Method

Think of a project buffer as the protection at the end. A delay on the critical chain eats into it, and watching how fast it shrinks tells you how much trouble you’re in. A resource buffer isn’t time but a warning: “your expert is needed in two weeks.” This helps stop a late person from delaying critical work. PReF : Project buffer, Resource buffer, Feeder buffer. A buffer placed where a non-critical chain joins the critical chain is a: Critical Chain Method • Buffer Types: • Project buffer • Contingency time to the whole project inserted at end of the project. Any delay in the Longest Path will consume some or all of the buffer. • Feeder buffers • inserted at the point where non-critical chains feed into the critical chain. This is to ensure that any tasks feeding into the Critical Chain may not delay the Critical Chain. • Resource buffers • Alerts or placeholders to ensure critical resources are ready when needed. 45
Critical Chain Method
How does CCM avoid resource conflicts? Critical Chain Method g Tasks are sequenced to avoid resource conflicts (e.g., no multitasking), ensuring that shared resources aren’t double-booked. 46
What-if analysis

You don’t know what will go wrong, but you can test what happens if it does. What-if shows which delays matter and which don’t, so you know where to prepare. What does what-if analysis test? What-if analysis • It is a scenario-based analysis of schedule to determine effects of various scenarios on different aspects of the project • Example: Delay delivery of a critical component by various amounts to determine effect on schedule; “COTS supplier is unable to provide a critical component at all” • What-if scenario analysis effectively tests the robustness of the project schedule in response to adverse circumstances • Most common technique uses Monte Carlo simulation to generate a population of possible project schedule outcomes • Think of executing the same project 10,000 times with the same resources, different boundary conditions, and no memory between executions • Very useful in preparing contingency and response plans for project risks 47

Measurement and Metrics

Why Measurement and Metrics?

“Good quality” is a matter of opinion until you measure it. Numbers let you compare two methods fairly, and that’s what objective means here. What does measurement allow? Why Measurement and Metrics? • Software measurement is concerned with deriving a quantitative (numeric) value for an attribute of a software product or process (largely qualitative) • This allows for objective comparisons between techniques and processes • Although some companies have introduced measurement programs, the systematic use of measurement is still uncommon • There are few standards in this area 29
Definitions

Think of it as three steps: 10 defects is a measure , counting them is the measurement , and defects per 1,000 lines tells you something useful, which makes it a metric . “The act of obtaining a measure” is: Definitions • Measure • provides a quantitative indication of the size of some product or process attribute • Measurement • the act of obtaining a measure • Metric • a quantitative measure of the degree to which a system, component, or process possesses a given attribute 30
Software Metric

A number on its own means little. The point is what it helps you do: predict or control. So a software metric earns its place by informing decisions. Which is an example of a software metric? Software Metric • Any type of measurement which relates to a software system, process or related documentation • Lines of code in a program, number of person-days required to develop a component • Allow the software and the software process to be quantified • Measures of the software process or product • May be used to predict product attributes or to control the software process 31
Categories

Different questions need different numbers. Product metrics ask “is what we built good?”, while process and project metrics ask “are we working well?”. Which category assesses the design and construction of the software? Categories • Product • Assess the quality of the design and construction of the software product being built. • Process & Project • Quantitative measures that enable software engineers to gain insight into the efficiency of the software process and the projects conducted using the process framework 32
Process Metrics

If people are judged on a number, they’ll improve the number, not necessarily the work. Using metrics to evaluate individuals makes them hide problems and spoils your data. Process metrics should be used to evaluate individual developers’ performance. Process Metrics • Private process metrics (e.g., defect rates by individual or module) are only known to by the individual or team concerned. • Public process metrics enable organizations to make strategic changes to improve the software process. • Metrics should not be used to evaluate the performance of individuals. • Statistical software process improvement helps and organization to discover where they are strong and where they are weak 33
Product Metrics

Dynamic metrics need the program running, like speed. Static ones can look at the code itself, like complexity. So each tells you about different qualities. Cyclomatic complexity measured from source code is a: Product Metrics • A quality metric should be a predictor of product quality • Classes of product metric • Dynamic metrics which are collected by measurements made of a program in execution • Static metrics which are collected by measurements made of the system representations • Dynamic metrics help assess efficiency and reliability; Static metrics help assess complexity, understandability and maintainability 34
Project Metrics

These are for acting during this project, not just reviewing later. Noticing delays or risks early lets the team adjust while there’s still time, which is why inputs, outputs and results are tracked. What should every project measure? Project Metrics • A software team can use software project metrics to adapt project workflow and technical activities • Project metrics are used to avoid development schedule delays, to mitigate potential risks, and to assess product quality on an on-going basis • Every project should measure its inputs (resources), outputs (deliverables), and results (effectiveness of deliverables) 35
Metrics Assumptions

You can easily count lines, but you want to know about maintainability. Metrics only help if what’s countable is genuinely linked to what you care about, and that’s not always so. Which assumption do metrics rely on? Metrics Assumptions • A software property can be measured • The relationship exists between what we can measure and what we want to know • This relationship has been formalized and validated • It may be difficult to relate what can be measured to desirable quality attributes 36
Integrating Metrics with Process

You can’t claim to be improving without a “before” figure. Without a baseline from past work, any change is just opinion, which is why missing old data is such a problem. Why is baseline data needed? Integrating Metrics with Process • Many software developers do not collect measures. • Without measurement it is impossible to determine whether a process is improving or not • Baseline metrics data should be collected from a large, representative sampling of past software projects • Getting this historic project data is very difficult, if the previous developers did not collect data in an on-going manner 37
Software Measurement

Direct measures can simply be counted. Indirect ones, like reliability, have to be inferred from other numbers. That’s why quality attributes are harder to measure. Which is an INDIRECT product measure? Software Measurement • Direct measures of a software engineering process include cost and effort • Direct measures of the product include lines of code (LOC), execution speed, memory size, defects reported over some time period • Indirect product measures examine the quality of the software product itself (e.g., functionality, complexity, efficiency, reliability, maintainability) 38

One project’s data helps a little, but many projects’ data shows real patterns. Keeping it as an organizational resource means the next team doesn’t begin from nothing. Why keep measurement data as an organizational resource? The Measurement Process • A software measurement process may be part of a quality control process • Data collected during this process should be maintained as an organizational resource • Once a measurement database has been established, comparisons across projects become possible 39

Data Collection • A metrics program should be based on a set of product and process data • Data should be collected immediately (not in retrospect) and, if possible, automatically • Three types of automatic data collection • Static product analysis • Dynamic product analysis • Process data collation 41
